Reference Three — marginal note on a Concord relay station maintenance report, ~4,200 BCE, in handwriting that does not match any known Concord administrator:
“Cross-referenced against internal models. Deviation within acceptable range. Monitoring continues.”
(Three documents across sixteen hundred years. The handwriting in the third does not belong to any identified Concord administrator. Someone was reading the Concord’s relay station reports and annotating them for their own records. The annotation is calm. Whatever they found was within acceptable range. The range itself is not defined anywhere in the outer archive.)

V. Administrative Actions
~3,799 BCE — Personnel Transfer Notice, V. Sorath
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, personnel records division. One page. Filed without cover documentation.

NOTICE OF PERSONNEL TRANSFER
Subject: V. Sorath, Administrator, Third Forge District
Issued by: Office of Administrative Oversight
V. Sorath is hereby transferred from his current posting effective the date of this notice.
New posting: [not specified]
Transfer duration: [not specified]
Reason for transfer: administrative reassignment
This transfer is authorized under standard personnel reallocation provisions.
Signed: Overseer-Designate T. Cavren, Office of Administrative Oversight

(V. Sorath wrote On the Certainty of the Mandate approximately eight months before this notice was issued. The treatise was circulated internally. It asked, carefully, a question about why the Witness Body maintains records it does not share. It did not press the question. It explicitly declined to press the question. It was filed without comment.)
(Overseer-Designate T. Cavren does not appear in the outer archive before this document. The title “Overseer-Designate” is not a standard administrative title in the Imperium’s personnel hierarchy. Standard transfer notices are issued by the Office of Personnel Administration. This one was not.)
(V. Sorath does not appear in the outer archive after this document. His new posting is blank. He had served the Third Forge District for nineteen years. He had never been transferred before.)
(The transfer was issued eight months after the treatise. The treatise asked a question. The question was not answered.)

~2,700 BCE — Observatory Maintenance Request, Interior Ranges Station Four
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, infrastructure records division. Filed under routine maintenance, which is the category it was submitted under.

MAINTENANCE REQUEST — INTERIOR RANGES OBSERVATORY STATION FOUR
Submitted by: Station Administrator K. Thren
Request Classification: Routine Infrastructure
Station Four requires the following materials for scheduled maintenance and operational upkeep:
Relay-grade copper sheeting: approximately 1,400 arm-lengths of rolled sheet, 3 finger-widths thick
Arcane resin, grade A: 34 standard casks (each cask sufficient to seal a door frame on all sides, three times over)
Precision lens assemblies: 17 ground-glass units, each the diameter of a spread hand
Structural binding compound: 9 barrels
Arcane-grade binding compound: 21 barrels
Iron framing, load-bearing: enough to frame a building of four large rooms, floor to ceiling
Stellar calibration instruments, Type 3: 6 units
Deep-sky observation apertures: 4 units
Estimated completion of maintenance: 14 months.
Personnel required: 8 specialists, 12 support staff.
Authorization requested from: Office of Infrastructure Administration.

Approved. — Office of Infrastructure Administration. Date of approval: same day as submission.

(Interior Ranges Observatory Station Four has a recorded floor area roughly equivalent to a large house — four rooms, two floors. The materials requested are sufficient to construct a building three to four times that size from the ground up, not to maintain one that already exists.)
(The request was approved the same day it was submitted. The outer archive contains 4,700 infrastructure requests from this period. The median approval time is eleven days. The fastest prior approval was four days.)
(Station Administrator K. Thren does not appear in any other infrastructure request in the outer archive before or after this one. Stellar calibration instruments and deep-sky observation apertures are not maintenance materials. They are construction materials for a new, significantly larger observation platform.)
(The maintenance was completed in fourteen months, per the follow-up filing. The follow-up filing does not describe what was built. It says only: “Maintenance complete. Station Four operational.” The station’s new capacity is not documented.)

~4,100 BCE — Field Personnel Record, Forge District Seven, Cycle 3 Workers
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, personnel records division. One of a very small number of personnel records concerning non-administrative, non-construct workers. The Imperium ran on construct labor. Human workers appear in the record primarily when they filled roles constructs could not — skilled craft, arcane calibration, interpretive judgment. This record covers fourteen of them.

PERSONNEL RECORD — FORGE DISTRICT SEVEN, CYCLE 3
Classification: Non-Construct Labor, Skilled Designation
Filed by: District Labor Coordinator, Office of Personnel Administration
The following individuals are registered as active skilled workers in Forge District Seven for the current cycle. Registration is renewed annually. Workers not renewing registration are considered separated from district service.
Arcane Calibration Specialists (3):
Dorath, M. — 11 years district service. Specialization: relay frequency alignment. Notes: consistently high accuracy. No incidents.
Sorun, T. — 4 years district service. Specialization: construct activation sequencing. Notes: transferred from District Two following restructuring. Performance satisfactory.
Vel, K. — 2 years district service. Specialization: relay frequency alignment. Notes: apprentice designation, under supervision of Dorath, M.
Forge Craft Workers (6):
Arren, P. — 23 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, M-class constructs. Notes: longest-serving non-construct worker in current district roster. Has trained four subsequent workers now in district service.
Bael, S. — 8 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, L-class constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Ceth, R. — 8 years district service. Specialization: lens and optical assembly. Notes: reassigned from observatory support role following Station Three decommissioning.
Forath, N. — 5 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, S-class constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Ilven, M. — 5 years district service. Specialization: structural binding, large-frame constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Thera, J. — 3 years district service. Specialization: lens and optical assembly. Notes: no incidents.
Structural and Physical Labor (5):
Dorn, H. — 16 years district service. Specialization: heavy frame installation. Notes: has requested transfer to District Nine twice. Both requests denied — district retention priority.
Kaen, F. — 9 years district service. Specialization: heavy frame installation. Notes: no incidents.
Orath, L. — 6 years district service. Specialization: material transport, oversized components. Notes: no incidents.
Vorath, S. — 6 years district service. Specialization: material transport, oversized components. Notes: no incidents.
Renvar, C. — 1 year district service. Specialization: general physical labor, unspecified. Notes: new registration this cycle. Origin: transferred from civilian population intake, northern sector.

Filed: Personnel Records, Forge District Seven, Cycle 3. Standard annual renewal.

(Fourteen people. Twenty-three years of service at one end, one year at the other. Arren, P. has been finishing precision components for M-class constructs — the military designation — for twenty-three years. He has trained four of the people who came after him. His name appears in four previous cycle records. The record does not say anything about him beyond his specialization and his years. It does not need to.)
(Dorn, H. has requested transfer twice. Both denied — district retention priority. He has been installing heavy frames for sixteen years. The record notes his transfer requests the way it notes everything else: without comment. He is still there.)
(Ceth, R. was reassigned from observatory support following Station Three’s decommissioning. Station Three does not appear in the outer archive’s infrastructure records as having been decommissioned. It appears in earlier personnel records as active. It does not appear in later ones. Something happened to Station Three. The record of what does not exist in the outer archive.)
(Renvar, C. is listed as transferred from civilian population intake, northern sector. The northern sector in this period was the frontier of the Imperium’s expansion. Civilian population intake is the administrative category for people absorbed into Imperium labor pools from territories brought under control. Renvar, C. has been in the district for one year. The record notes no incidents.)

~3,600 BCE — Operational Closure Notice, Subject: Arven Doth, Trade Liaison
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, administrative correspondence division. Filed under contract termination.

NOTICE OF OPERATIONAL CLOSURE
Subject: Arven Doth, Trade Liaison, Concord Relations Office
Issued by: Office of Administrative Oversight
Classification: Internal
Following review of the subject’s recent correspondence and field activity, the Office of Administrative Oversight has determined that continued operational engagement with the subject is not in the Imperium’s interest.
Effective immediately, all active contracts, correspondence chains, and material arrangements involving the subject are to be closed. Personnel currently in contact with the subject through official channels are to cease contact without explanation and redirect any inquiries to the standard contract termination protocol.
The subject’s access to the Concord relations correspondence archive is revoked.
Our operative at the subject’s current location — the relay waystation at the northern Concord approach road, where the subject is lodged for the second night of his return journey — has been notified and is awaiting confirmation of this notice. The subject’s travel documents and personal correspondence are to be secured before the station resumes morning traffic. The subject will not require them.
This notice constitutes full authorization for all necessary actions to effect closure. No further documentation will be issued.
Signed: Overseer-Designate T. Cavren, Office of Administrative Oversight

(Arven Doth was a trade liaison working across the boundary between the Imperium and the Celestial Concord — one of very few individuals with legitimate reason to move freely between both institutions. The outer archive contains no record of what he found on his last journey, or what he reported, or to whom. The “recent correspondence and field activity” that prompted this notice is not described.)
(The operative at the waystation is not named. The notice was sent ahead of the subject’s arrival — it reached the station before he did. It knew his route. It knew which night he would stop there.)
(Arven Doth does not appear in the outer archive after this notice. His correspondence files were not removed — they were integrated smoothly into the existing record, attributed to a successor, as if he had simply been replaced in the ordinary course of administration. The integration was clean enough that it would only be visible to someone who already knew to look for it.)
(Overseer-Designate T. Cavren signed this notice. The same title appears on V. Sorath’s transfer notice two centuries later. Either it passed to a successor who kept the title, or it did not pass at all.)
(The morning traffic resumed on schedule.)

VI. The Mandate Defended
~3,800 BCE — Theological Treatise, Selected Passage
From On the Certainty of the Mandate:

A reader attentive to the structure of this defense will notice that one category of objection is not represented: those concerning what the mandate is ultimately for. Why unification. Why now, across these specific millennia, with this specific urgency. Why the Witness Body maintains records it does not share.


I do not address these objections because I do not have answers that are mine to give. There are things known at levels of this institution that I am not at.


Whether it is also what the Warden asked is a question I have decided not to ask.

V. Sorath was reassigned from the Third Forge District approximately eight months after this treatise was circulated. His subsequent posting is not recorded.

VII. The Advance
~2,400 BCE — Expansion Directive, Standard Form
From Southern Advance Documents:

Indigenous population assessment: nomadic, mammoth-dependent, estimated three to four thousand individuals across the sector. No fixed settlements. No arcane infrastructure. No construct capability. Classification: pre-integration.


Integration assessment will determine whether the indigenous population requires relocation, absorption, or reclassification. Standard protocols apply.

~2,100 BCE — Field Report, Dissenting
From Southern Advance Documents:

They have a word, in their language, that I am told means approximately the line that follows. They use it for the construct advance. They do not use it as a military term. They use it the way one uses a term for weather.


I am reporting that what the constructs are producing in Zone Nine is the end of a people who have been retreating from us for generations and have nowhere left to retreat to.


I do not know what should be done with this report. I have filed it because not filing it seemed worse.

Filing Code: 7-ASH-NINE-SOUTH. No administrator with that code appears in personnel records before or after this date.
(The third document from this period — the one addressed to someone whose name was removed — is not reproduced here. It will not be reproduced here. This is the only editorial decision in this collection that required more than a moment’s consideration.)

VIII. The Silence
~950 BCE — Resource Reallocation Order 7-PRIME
From Era VI Documents:

Production under this reallocation is classified. Classification level: Internal. Access restricted to personnel holding authorization code 7-PRIME or above. Forge Complex Seventeen is placed under direct administration of the Witness Body for the duration of production.


Completion timeline: not specified. Production targets: not specified in this document.


No further orders regarding this reallocation will be issued through standard channels.

Authorization code 7-PRIME does not appear in the standard personnel records. The constructs produced under this order do not appear in any deployment record. They were built. They went somewhere.

~800 BCE — Notice of Trial Suspension
From Era VI Documents:

The Trial of Succession is suspended, effective immediately, for an indefinite period.


The suspension is authorized under the body’s standing authority over trial administration. No further explanation is required or will be provided.

Four words when it resumed, eleven years later: “Proceedings resume. This date.”
Three members before. Four members after. Total membership unchanged. The arithmetic is precise. The identities are not.

IX. The End of the Record
Pre-Year 0 — Fragment, Deep Vault, Provenance Unestablished
From Era VI Documents:
The text begins mid-sentence. The page before it has not been found.

— and we were not wrong about what is coming. We were wrong about the time.


What we did not account for is that the thing we were watching was also watching. We do not know for how long.


We know that something moved in the southern survey zone that none of our constructs produced.


We may not be the only ones who knew.


The vaults will seal when the network fails. This is designed. Whatever comes after will have to find their own way in, and we have made that —

The sentence does not finish. Whether the document does is not known.

X. After
What follows is not a document. It is an observation.
The Machine Wastes, sixty years after Year 0, contains sections that have not been fully surveyed. The autonomous construct activity in those sections is inconsistent with standard emergency-protocol behavior. Standard emergency protocols do not require coordination. What is observed in those sections requires coordination.
Bogrund knows approximately where the Ashen Seat is buried. He has been deciding what to do about that for three years.
Garvak’s excavation logs contain a section that has been deliberately obscured. The method used is not consistent with weather damage.
CR-9 prevents unauthorized excavation in the Wastes with a consistency that exceeds any documented emergency directive.
These three facts are presented without connection. The reader may connect them or decline to.

One further note, appended separately from the rest of this collection:
The filing code on the dissenting field report — 7-ASH-NINE-SOUTH — shares its prefix with the classification code on the resource reallocation order: 7-PRIME. This may be coincidence. The Imperium used numerical prefixes extensively and inconsistently.
It may not be coincidence. If it is not, it suggests the dissenting administrator had access to — or was assigned to — something classified at the 7-level. Which would mean they were not simply a field administrator who noticed something wrong. It would mean they were someone the body had cleared for internal work, who then filed a report the body could not acknowledge without revealing that they knew who had filed it.
The body filed it anyway. The body did not respond. The body reassigned them to a posting that does not appear in the outer archive.
This note is the last entry in this collection because it is the most uncertain, and uncertainty belongs at the end.

This collection is incomplete. Several documents known to exist have not been included. Several documents that should exist have not been found. The gap between those two categories is not small.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
(I have been assembling this collection for longer than I will say. Some of what is here I found in the outer archive. Some of what is here I found elsewhere. The distinction matters less than what it means that I found it at all.)

lore-and-stories/documents/the-warden-wa.filePath: Lore and Stories/Documents/The Warden Walked Ahead.md
lore-and-stories/documents/the-warden-wa.title: The Warden Walked Ahead
lore-and-stories/documents/the-warden-wa.content:
What follows is a reconstruction of an oral account, committed to writing approximately 4,500 BCE by an unnamed archivist of the early Imperium. The reconstruction is explicitly noted as third-generation — the archivist was working from a written account of a spoken account of a remembered account. The chain of transmission before that point is unknown. The archivist notes, at the end of the document, that two other versions of this account exist and that they differ in ways that cannot be reconciled. Neither of the other versions has been located.

In the beginning there was only the ground, and the ground was hot, and the heat was not suffering but instruction.
They had come from somewhere. Nobody remembered where. The elders said their elders had said their elders had said there was another place before this one, and that the leaving of it was not their choice. A being had come — not a man, not a god, something that moved the way fire moves, with purpose that needed no explanation — and the leaving had happened. Whether he spoke or whether he only walked ahead and expected them to follow was something the elders disagreed about. In some versions he said: this land will be yours and all lands after it, go and make them one. In other versions he said nothing. In the version the archivist prefers, he said only: come, and did not look back.
They followed because something in the way he moved suggested they should.
The new land was volcanic and difficult and theirs. The being of fire did not stay. He pointed — some said east, some said simply there — and then he was gone, and the ground where he had stood was warm for three days after.
The elders called him the Warden. The Warden of what was not specified. Some said of the volcano. Some said of the mandate. Some said of them, specifically, which the archivist finds unlikely but notes without judgment.
They did not look for him after. He had given them the land and the direction and the warmth of three days, and that was what he had come to give. What they did with it was theirs.

Filed under: Oral Histories, Pre-Imperial Period, Provenance Uncertain.
Note, ~4,500 BCE: I have written what I was given. I have not written what I believe. These are not always the same document.

(The gap between the archivist’s note and the document itself is exactly the gap between evidence and conviction that defines this period. Neither can be recovered. Both matter. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/documents/trial-record-.filePath: Lore and Stories/Documents/Trial Record — Contested Succession.md
lore-and-stories/documents/trial-record-.title: Trial Record — Contested Succession
lore-and-stories/documents/trial-record-.content:
One of the earliest surviving trial records. Written in a script that predates the standard Imperial notation by several centuries and required translation before archiving. The translation was performed by an unknown party — the translator’s name does not appear in the record. The original document is held in the outer archive. The translation is what is reproduced here.

RECORD OF CONTESTED SUCCESSION
Third Community, Interior Ranges
Witness Assembly: Eleven representatives, seven communities
The challenge was formally presented on the third day of the dry season. The challenger named himself before the assembly. The incumbent named himself before the assembly. Both were confirmed as eligible by the Witness Body.
First Trial — Endurance of Stone
Both candidates were required to hold position on the heated rock shelf for a period determined by the Witness Body. Duration not recorded. The incumbent withdrew at the point of incapacitation. The challenger remained. The challenger was confirmed as the victor of the First Trial.
Second Trial — Contest of Arms
Standard rules applied. Both candidates provided their own weapons. No substitutions permitted. The contest lasted until one party was unable to continue. The incumbent was unable to continue. The challenger was confirmed as the victor of the Second Trial.
Third Trial — Witness Examination
The challenger was examined by the Witness Body in closed session. Duration not recorded. Questions not recorded. The challenger emerged from examination and was confirmed as suitable to lead.
Outcome
The challenger is recognized as leader of the Third Community by unanimous witness assembly. The succession is binding. Any challenge to this outcome within the standard period requires a new trial before the same Witness Body.
Signed by witness representatives of all seven communities.

Filed: Trial Records, Pre-Imperial Confederation Period.

[In the margin of the original document, in handwriting that does not match the primary text and was not part of the original record, someone has written the following in early Imperial notation — meaning it was added at least two centuries after the document was created:]
The challenger’s name was removed from this record before filing. This was not standard procedure. The removal was authorized by the Witness Body. No reason is given. The challenger led the Third Community for thirty-one years and was not subsequently challenged. His name does not appear in any other document in the outer archive.
[The handwriting of this marginal note does not match any identified historian of the relevant period. It was added by someone who had access to the archive, knew the original record had been altered, and chose to note the alteration without explaining how they knew. No further context is available.]
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/history/the-history-of-.filePath: Lore and Stories/History/The History of the Unnamed World.md
lore-and-stories/history/the-history-of-.title: The History of the Unnamed World
lore-and-stories/history/the-history-of-.content:
Long before the Starfall shattered the world, civilizations rose beneath a sky that was already breaking. Power does not descend from gods in this world — it leaks through fractures in reality itself. Erased constellations. Unstable magic. Cosmic absences that answer when observed too closely. The Starfall marked Year 0 and collapsed empires, rewrote geography, and scattered fragments of impossible power across the land, leaving survivors to rebuild amid monsters, relics, and half-forgotten truths.
What follows is the long account.

Era I — The Age of First Civilizations (~12,000 – 9,000 BCE)
Mortal civilizations emerge independently across multiple continents. Magic exists but is localized, ritualistic, and poorly understood. Early astronomy develops for navigation, agriculture, and religion. Asterion is born human during this era — exceptionally long-lived due to unknown astral magic, and obsessive about the night sky from the beginning. He does not inherit a great world. He helps build the idea of one.
Era II — The Age of Constellations (~9,000 – 6,000 BCE)
Asterion pioneers astral cartography — identifying the stable star-patterns that influence magic, fate, and natural forces, and developing Constellation Lines & Star Points as a discipline for working with them. Nations rise around star-aligned philosophies. Early star-resonant artifacts are created. Asterion’s immortality becomes suspected, then confirmed — not through myth but through his own celestial modeling, which shows him as a fixed point across millennia.
Era III — The Founding of the Celestial Concord (~6,000 – 4,000 BCE)
The Celestial Concord is founded as a transnational scholarly order dedicated to cataloging and safeguarding astral knowledge. Asterion is a founding authority — not its ruler, never its ruler. Massive white-and-gold structures rise: observatories, arcane academies, astral relay towers, all magically linked across continents. Celestial Concord HQ — the Meridian Library — becomes the seat of power. The Great Concord is built as the capital city. The world’s most advanced institution takes shape, and Asterion designs much of its infrastructure while avoiding its throne.
Era IV — The Gilded Age of the Concord (~4,000 – 2,500 BCE)
Concord influence peaks. They act as arbitrators between nations, keepers of magical law, developing star-powered enforcement divisions and institutionalizing astral magic. With that power comes subtle corruption: knowledge hoarding, political manipulation, moral absolutism. The Concord does not become evil — it becomes certain. Certainty is the more dangerous condition.
Era V — The Age of Omens (~2,500 – 800 BCE)
Astral anomalies increase. Some constellations flicker, distort, or vanish entirely. Asterion discovers that erased constellations are leaking back into the world and warns the Concord of a cosmic devourer entity responsible. Concord leadership dismisses his claims. Internal fractures form around the question of what to do about a warning no one wants to hear — fractures that eventually become Lumia’s preservation-focused sect and Serathiel’s judgment-focused sect.
Era VI — The Fracture of the Concord (~800 – 50 BCE)
Asterion is pressured out or leaves voluntarily — even he is uncertain which. The Concord, without its greatest architect and most inconvenient voice, becomes a militarized cabal: dogmatic, politically dominant, developing star-powered weapons and constructs, and treating faith in the Concord as near-religious. Meanwhile, Asterion continues his research in secrecy. The Concord rewrites records. Compresses his legacy. Protects itself from his shadow.
Year 0 — The Starfall
A god-like cosmic entity — possibly The Cosmic Devourer, possibly something else — triggers the Starfall. Massive meteoric impacts devastate the world. The Celestial Concord is obliterated; most of its leadership dies instantly, and its magically linked structures lose their connections forever. The World Scar is born. Technology and knowledge regress by centuries. The Eternis Core falls with the Starfall, embedding deep beneath the volcanic region of Ashenvale Pyrehold. New monsters and altered species emerge from the wreckage.
Asterion survives — not because he planned it, but because he was no longer centralized.
Era VII — The Shattered World (~1 – 10 AD)
The world becomes scattered survivors: villages, nomadic clans, isolated enclaves. Former empires are lost or mythologized. Rhaegor survives within his volcano and protects the surrounding region indirectly — including Cinderhearth, a village near Rhaegor’s Peak, where a girl named Krysta is roughly twelve to fourteen years old. She spends the years immediately after the Starfall defending the village from Starfall-born creatures, earning admiration and resentment in equal measure.
Era VIII — The Age of Shards (~10 – 30 AD)
Starfall Fragments begin surfacing worldwide. Their effects vary wildly: empowerment, corruption, environmental destabilization. New factions and proto-nations arise around them — the seeds of the Fragment Cults that now contest the Starfall Shard Zones. Rhaegor constructs the Trial Chamber Network within his volcano, believing the trials are the key to reaching the Eternis Core. They are not. The Core chooses its own vessel: Krysta, who becomes its chosen bearer after Rhaegor reveals himself to her, roughly ten to fifteen years after the Starfall. She now carries three voices: her own, the Core’s (order, preservation, control), and a third that has been present longer than either of them realized — Varesa’s corruption, which began posing as friendship years earlier. No one knows the full picture: not Rhaegor, not the village, not Krysta herself, initially.
See: The Fractured Heart, The Will of the Survivor, The Whisper in the Ash
Era IX — The Age of Awakenings (~30 – 60 AD)
Champions emerge worldwide. CR-9 reactivates in the Machine Wastes when Velrisa’s unraveling sends shockwaves through the world’s remaining arcane infrastructure. Garvak awakens. Ka’Ruun discovers volatile Starfall power in the High Sky Regions. Asterion resurfaces quietly, tracking constellation echoes that have begun manifesting in the people he encounters — fragments of erased star-patterns that should no longer exist, each one a clue in an unfolding celestial mystery. Rumors of a second Starfall spread.
See: The Dragon’s Temper, Starfire Trajectory, Neutralization Protocol, Siegeborn Awakening
The Current Era — The Unfolding Storm (~60 AD onward)
The world is fractured but awakening. Nations form with conflicting goals: control Starfall power, prevent another cataclysm, exploit what the first one left behind. Asterion hunts The Cosmic Devourer’s traces. The Eternis Core’s will strengthens within Krysta. Serathiel keeps her vigil at the edge of the World Scar, watching for something she cannot name. Lumia wanders the Verdant Rupture, tending to the lost. Thorall and Aaron maintain their alliance across the melting world.
The Starfall is not finished.
See: The Hollow Vigil, The Current That Chose to Move, The Mammoth’s Burden

For all recorded accounts, see The Starfall Anthology.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
This account supersedes the version dated ~45 AD. Differences between editions have not been disclosed.

lore-and-stories/history/the-starfall-an.title: The Starfall Anthology
lore-and-stories/history/the-starfall-an.content:
These accounts have been gathered as received. Not all of what follows was given willingly.

The Overarching Record

The History of the Unnamed World — the long account. BCE through the present era.
When Paths Converge — the epilogue. Every path, one direction.


The Short Accounts
Filed by subject. Descriptions where available.

The Suit With an Attitude — Bogrund & Bonk — A workshop, a restless machine, and a direction neither of them chose.
Embers of Sanity — Velrisa — (no summary provided)
Beneath the Molten Throne — Rhaegor — The mountain speaks first. He answers second.
The Mammoth’s Burden — Thorall — A march toward a breach, and what the ground said before they arrived.
A Light for the Lost — Lumia — A traveler in the Verdant Rupture. Something in the trees that wasn’t an animal.
“The Arrow’s Shadow” — Varesa — (document unavailable)
The Dragon’s Temper — Teostra and Ka’Ruun — A ridge, a shard, and two different ideas about what “it worked” means.
Starfire Trajectory — Ka’Ruun — (see above; filed separately at subject’s insistence)
Siegeborn Awakening — Garvak — A reactivation. Purpose remembered. World above, unwarned.
Neutralization Protocol — CR-9 — A machine scanning the horizon. The horizon does not scan back. Probably.
The Fractured Heart — Krysta, Rhaegor, Varesa — Three forces. One chamber. No resolution yet.
The Current That Chose to Move — Aaron — The Shoals, a departure, and an old alliance recalled.
The First Light — Celestial Concord HQ — Serathiel at the ruins. Varesa in the shadow. An arrow nocked.
Condemned — Serathiel, Garvak — A war-cannon raised. A verdict disagreeing.
Ascension — Serathiel — A siege, a judgment, and the moment dawn became something else.
“The Weight of Seven Stars” — (withdrawn)
[untitled] — Xero & Rita — (not yet received)


The Long Accounts — Asterion
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony, 8,200 BCE — Year 0 — ~30 AD.

The First Anomaly — ~8,200 BCE. A funeral. A shivering star. The first suggestion that someone would need to outlive the sentence.
The City of the Unmoving Reflection — ~4,000 BCE. The Capital at its height. Asterion at the Great Fountain, touching water that had forgotten how to move.
The Edge of the Circle — ~1,500 BCE. The Council Chamber. The last time he addressed them directly.
The Day the Earth Lost its Weight — Year 0. The Meridian Library. Ink rising from a brush.
The Friction of Being — ~28 AD. A nomad camp. A fragment-seeker learning the difference between asking and demanding.
Beneath the Shifting Sky — ~25 AD. A ruined courtyard. An apprentice named Maren. The sea spray hovering in mid-air.
The Whisper in the Ash — ~30 AD. Ashenvale Pyrehold. Krysta training. Something Asterion misread.
The Will of the Survivor — ~30 AD. The Ashenvale slopes. What Varesa said while standing on rocks that appeared to be empty.
The Architecture of Preservation — ~22 AD. The Machine Wastes. Three parties, one site, no agreement.
The Treaty of the Melting World — ~25 AD. The Great Shelf. Thorall and Aaron, a mountain, and a question of whose catastrophe takes priority.
The Hollow Vigil — ~30 AD. The edge of the World Scar. Serathiel standing watch. Asterion sitting down and opening his ledger.


The Molten Vigil — Recovered Records
Filed separately. Provenance mixed — outer archive, indirect recovery, and unnamed sources.

The Molten Vigil — Recovered Transmissions and Records — a collection, not a single account. Begins before the doctrine existed and ends after the Imperium did.
What the Sky Remembers — four voices, one room, the weeks before The Edge of the Circle.
The Variable — Era IV. A logistics administrator. A false panel in a desk drawer.
The Eleven Years — what the eleven-year suspension actually was, as far as it can be reconstructed.


This catalogue supersedes the version dated ~45 AD. Differences between editions have not been disclosed.

lore-and-stories/history/when-paths-conv.title: When Paths Converge
lore-and-stories/history/when-paths-conv.content:
The crater grew brighter.
The tremors grew stronger.
And across the world…
A titan marched.
A machine rolled.
A boy flew.
A dragon snarled.
A sharpshooter nocked ghostly arrows.
A guardian glimmered in the dark.
A mammoth chief prepared his herd.
An enchantress burned.
A lava warden armed himself.
An engineer and his metal child marched to battle.
The Starfall called.
And everything powerful answered.

For the full account, see The History of the Unnamed World.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/contra.title: Contract Row
lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/contra.content:
Told by Sara, the long gun of the Fresh Meat Squad. Some months after Fresh Falls.
Orrin’s tea shop hasn’t sold a cup of tea in years. It sells other things, mostly other people’s problems, and it marks them up.
Contract Row is where the Seam gives up. Chalk boards on every wall, jobs scrawled right out in the open: haul this, burn that, find my dog. The jobs that matter never go on the boards. Those get said in the back of Orrin’s, over a teapot nobody is allowed to touch.
Spank touched it.
“Does this come with a happy ending?”
“It does not,” said Orrin.
“Then what’s it for?”
“Spank,” I said.
“I’m asking questions, Sara. That’s what ears are for.”
“Sit down.”
He didn’t. He drifted around the room picking things up and putting them back wrong while Orrin opened a ledger on the table. Orrin is a round, soft man in a clean shirt who has never thrown a punch and owns a lot of people who have. At the bottom of the page was Deacon’s number. Nineteen thousand four hundred.
“I’d like to make that zero,” Orrin said.
Deacon went the color of old dishwater. “What’s the catch?”
“A truck.”
“Is it a nice truck?” said Spank.
“It’s a Renova truck. My friend would like what’s in it.”
His friend sat in the corner. Tall, gray jacket, a little V stitched on the cuff, the Varkatech mark. She’d bought our eleven shards three weeks back and never given a name, so Spank called her Miss V, and she let him, which I did not like. She watched me the whole time Orrin talked. Not him. Me.
“Foundry Road gate,” she said. “Thursday, dawn. Three trucks, six guards on cycles. The middle truck carries what Renova pulled off the star at Hollowfall.”
“The turned one!” Spank slapped the table. “That’s my star! I called the day, I just got the place wrong. That’s basically a win. Why you’s want it?”
“They’re good shards.”
“Good how?”
“Triple, remember?” She smiled at him, and then at me, and I stopped being comfortable in my chair.
Deacon said yes before she finished. Spank threw both arms up and yelled, “Butter my Biscuit!” in a room that did not contain the Biscuit. A man in the doorway left.
Outside he walked backwards in front of me so he could do the talking to my face. “Debt’s gone, Sara. Free as a bird. A bird in a truck.”
“It’s not gone yet.”
“Glass half full.”
“The glass is on fire.”
“Then it’s half full of fire! Even better!”
I walked around him. He spun and fell into step beside me like a stray, and I let him, because I’m not made of stone, whatever he tells people.

We planned it on the shed floor in Scrapmoor, in chalk. Deacon drew the road. Spank drew the Biscuit, with eyelashes.
“Step one, we hit ‘em,” Spank said. “Step two, we hit ‘em again. Step three, shards.”
“That’s one step,” said Deacon.
“It’s a good step.”
I took the chalk out of his hand and rubbed out the eyelashes.
“Here’s the gate,” I said, and drew it. “Two towers with a wall between them and a rope across the road. Every truck stops at the rope to get checked. That’s when we take it.”
I drew a little box on the road. “Three trucks line up at the rope. Spank waits in the cart line behind them with a tarp over the Biscuit. When they stop, he pulls out and parks across the road behind the last truck. They can’t back out.”
“I like it,” said Spank.
“Deacon hides in the ditch by the road. When I shoot the lock off the middle truck, he runs up and grabs two crates and runs back. Spank, you throw them in the Biscuit and we leave.”
“What do you do?”
“I lie on the roof of a dead hut two hundred yards away with the long gun and shoot anyone who bothers you.”
“Sara,” said Spank, in love, “you’s a genius.”
“It’s a plan. Don’t make it weird.”
Deacon asked how I knew the gate so well. I told him I’d read about it. Which was a lie, and a bad one. I knew the gate captain was a man named Tobin who never woke before six. I knew the rope was the only real lock they had. I knew all this the way I know my own boot size, and I’d drawn it onto the floor like I was still sitting at the desk. There was a screen at that desk, and orders pinned beside it, and a pen I held while a clock ran. I looked at the chalk and waited for it to stop being the desk.
“Where was the Renova skiff?” I asked. “The night your star fell.”
“Over the ridge,” said Spank. “Big gray ugly thing.”
“Then it moved to the crater before you did.”
“Yeah, it was already there when we got in.”
“The star turned. It fell seven miles away. And the skiff was already waiting over the spot.”
Spank worked that out slowly, right there on his face. “That’s a fast skiff.”
“No skiff is that fast.”
“Lucky, then,” said Deacon.
“Renova doesn’t get lucky.”
I left it there. Spank was watching me with his mouth shut, which is a sight. He lasted four seconds.
“Sara.”
“No.”
“I ain’t said nothing!”
“You were about to.”
He clutched his chest. “That hurts, darlin’. Right here.”
“Good.”

He put his fist through the shed wall that night. I didn’t ask why, and I’m still angry at myself about it.
I found him in the Biscuit with his hand hanging out the window like something the cat dragged in. Knuckles open to the bone. I climbed in on the passenger side, which was my side now, and took the tin out of the glove box.
“Give me your hand.”
“I’m fine.”
“Spank.”
He gave it to me. I cleaned it with the flask water and he hissed and made a noise like a wounded pony. “Don’t read into this,” I said. “If it goes bad Deacon makes me drive.”
“Darlin’, I read into everything. I got a library.”
“I know.”
“You’s real gentle, you know that? For a woman who looks like she’s about to kill me.”
“I’m thinking about it.”
He was quiet for a bit. That was the problem with the whole night, the quiet. I wrapped the hand. It was a big, ugly, kind hand, and there was still grease from Gasket’s rag worked into the thumb. He’d never scrubbed it out. I’d never said anything.
“Who’s Tobin?” he said.
“A man.”
“Whose man?”
“Spank.”
“Sara.” Not loud. “Who is he to you?”
“A guy who sleeps in.”
“Stop that.” His hand closed in mine, and he didn’t notice. “That voice. The one that shuts the door. I been talking at you’s for eight months. I know how you take your tea. I know you hate third gear. I know you sleep with that gun like it’s a person. I don’t know where you was born. I don’t know if you got a mama. I buried Gasket in a ditch and I’m sitting here counting who else I don’t know.”
“It’s not your business.”
“Well, it’s gonna be!”
“Why? So you can make it a joke?”
He stopped.
“That’s what you’d do,” I said, and my voice went somewhere I hadn’t sent it. “You’d hear it and make it small. Some pun. And I’d laugh, because you’d be funny, and then it would be a thing that happened to a girl in a story and not a thing I did. I’m not giving you that.”
“I ain’t never laughed at nothing that hurt you’s!”
“You’ve never known what hurts me.”
“That’s what I’m SAYING!” He slammed the other hand on the wheel. The horn went off. We both flinched, and a dog started up somewhere, and he said, much quieter, “I ain’t shouting.”
“You are.”
“I’m worried, Sara.”
I looked out at the shed and the orange smear of cloud over it. There is a way of sitting very still that I learned a long time ago, and I used all of it.
“There was a bell,” I said.
He turned his head.
“I didn’t ring it. People heard too late. That’s what you get.”
“What bell?”
“That’s all of it.”
I thought he’d push. I wanted him to push, which I will not be explaining. He looked at me a long time instead, and I watched him decide, and I watched it cost him.
“Okay,” he said.
No joke. I waited. My hands sat in my lap and nothing came, and I sat in the seat Gasket rode home in and found I was furious about it.
“Don’t look at me like that,” I said. “It’s not like I wanted you to push.”
“Course not.”
“I didn’t.”
“Course not, darlin’.” The ghost of a grin. “I’m still gonna want it, though.”
“I know,” I said, and got out of the truck before my face did anything.

The Foundry Road gate is a stone wall with a tower at each end and a rope across the road. Past it is the Market Belt. This side of it is dirt, and carts, and a lot of people waiting.
At dawn the cart line ran back half a mile. Spank sat in it with the Biscuit under a tarp, looking like a farmer’s wagon, and I’d heard him practicing a farmer’s voice all morning. Deacon lay in the ditch by the road with a rag over his head. I was on the roof of a dead pylon hut, two hundred yards east of the gate, flat on my stomach, with the long gun and a flask of tea from Marit, who keeps the Vigil bunker at Lanternreach.
I could see all of it. The rope. The two towers. Tobin in a chair under the awning, with his hat over his face and his mouth open. He’d put on weight.
“Sara,” said Spank in my ear. Deacon had bought him a little radio and he refused to learn it. “Sara. You hear me?”
“Don’t say my name on the radio.”
“You look like a hawk from down here.”
“I’m on a roof.”
“A pretty hawk.”
“Spank.”
The convoy came over the rise at ten past six. Three gray trucks, six guards on cycles, rolling down the road toward the rope. Everybody in the cart line shuffled aside to let them through. I knew the middle truck by its paint. I’d stood next to trucks like that. I put that away.
They stopped at the rope. A guard hopped off to talk to Tobin. Tobin did not wake up.
“Now,” I said.
Spank threw off the tarp, drove the Biscuit out of the line, and swung it across the road behind the last truck. The brakes screamed. A woman dropped a basket. Spank leaned out the window with a crowbar in his fist and bellowed, loud enough for me to hear without the radio:
“FRESH MEAT SQUAD! HOT DANG!”
He said it like a proposal.
I shot the lock off the middle truck. The door swung out. Deacon came up out of the ditch and ran, and I watched him haul out one crate, then the second, then drag them across the road. Two guards turned on him. I shot the first one in the arm. The second one dropped his rifle and ran, because the first one was screaming.
It was going right. That scared me.
Then I looked at the east tower.
Tobin had pushed back his hat. He was looking up at the top of the tower, where nothing was moving. He looked for exactly as long as it took to decide he didn’t want to know, and put the hat back down.
Something stood up on top of the tower.

I’ll tell you what I saw, in order, because it happened fast.
It was a person-shaped thing in gray armor, with no marks on it. Where a face goes there was a smooth dark plate, so I couldn’t tell if it was a man or a woman or neither. It stood on the edge of the tower for a second. Then it jumped.
It landed in the middle of the guards. It hit the first one with one hand and he went down. It turned and hit the second one. It was fast and simple. It didn’t waste any movement.
Every few steps it stumbled. A little hitch in the left leg, like a stair that wasn’t there. And a sound came with it, a small dry click, like a bad clock.
I knew that hitch.
Renova doesn’t build its soldiers whole. It rents them parts. A better arm, a faster leg, an eye that sees at night. You pay every month, and you stay fast. If you stop paying, the parts start to fail. The soldiers who can’t pay get called lapsed. I’d heard about them. I had never seen one.
I had seen this one. I’d stood across a corridor from her for two years.
The lapsed soldier didn’t even look at the other guards. It walked up to the middle truck, ripped off the back panel with one hand, and took out a crate with a violet stripe down the side. It held it against its chest.
“HEY!” said Spank.
He ran at it with the crowbar. The thing watched him come. When he swung, it caught the crowbar in one hand and bent it in half. Then it grabbed him by the jacket and threw him. He hit the side of the Biscuit hard enough to dent the door, and slid down it, and stayed there.
I stopped being on the roof.
I don’t remember the ladder. I remember dust, and the long gun heavy in my hands, and Deacon shouting. I came around the corner of the hut with the rifle up and fired at the first thing I could hit, which was its knee.
The shot hit. The armor rang. The knee clicked twice, and caught, and the thing turned around and looked straight at me. A hundred yards, and it knew where I’d been the whole time.
“Four Seven,” it said.
The voice was flat and gentle, like someone reading to a child. Nobody had called me that in three years.
“They closed the post,” it said. “Nobody told me.”
Behind it Spank was moving, trying to get an arm under himself. I didn’t look. I kept the barrel on the dark plate. I had a clean shot. I knew if I took it, I’d be shooting myself.
“Don’t follow,” it said.
It climbed the tower with the crate in two jumps. And at the top, with the crate in its arms, the clicking stopped. The hitch was gone. For three steps it moved like someone had oiled every joint at once, smooth and healthy. Then it went over the wall and was gone.

We got the other two crates, because Deacon is brave about money. Spank had a cut over one eye and a rib that didn’t like air, and he sat in the back of the Biscuit and wouldn’t let me look at it.
“Sara,” Deacon said once the gate was a mile behind us. “That thing knew you.”
I opened my mouth.
“Nobody,” said Spank.
“Spank, it said a number.”
“Nobody, Deacon.” He had his eyes on the road and his one good hand on the wheel and his voice wasn’t loud and it wasn’t a joke. “Sit back.”
Deacon sat back. The rest of the mile was long. I looked out the side window. I’m not going to say what I was feeling, because there’s no word for it I’d sign.
Miss V was waiting at the shed. She opened the first crate and the second and looked for the violet stripe, and I watched her find it wasn’t there.
She didn’t swear. She smiled, small and tired.
“They always get that one,” she said.
“Who does?” said Spank.
“Whoever it is.” She counted the money into Deacon’s hands. “Orrin will burn the ledger by morning. You’re clear.” She looked at me one beat longer than she needed to. “I’ll be in touch.”
When she was gone Deacon sat down on an upturned crate and put his face in his hands. Spank went and sat next to him. Neither of them talked. I stood by the door with the long gun, and I found my other hand had grabbed the frame, and the frame was cold.

He drove us back to the road at dusk. I sat in the passenger seat with the tea tin in my lap.
He didn’t talk.
I’d got used to the noise. In eight months he hadn’t gone ten minutes without a sentence, and this silence was the loudest thing I’d ever sat in. I had my answer ready. I’d have said “Don’t,” and he’d have said “I’m just saying,” and we’d have been us again. I held it ready for ten miles.
He ground third gear twice. His hand was soaking through the bandage and he hadn’t noticed.
“Stop the truck,” I said.
“I’m fine.”
“I know you’re fine. Stop the truck.”
He stopped at the next pylon. I took his hand and unwound it and told him he was an idiot and he said he knew. The sun was almost gone. His fingers were shaking under mine.
“I thought it was gonna cut you in half,” he said.
“It threw you into a truck.”
“I seen you’s go at it. Like you’s walking into a fire. You’s never run in your life, Sara. You walk to ever’thing like it’s late for you.” He swallowed. “Then you was running.”
“Don’t make it a thing.”
“It’s a thing!” Quiet again, quick. “It’s a thing.”
I wrapped the knuckles. I wrapped them very well.
“I knew it,” I said. “I know that hitch. That’s all I’ll say about it tonight.”
He didn’t say anything for a while. Then, very softly, in a voice flat as a board and completely wrong, with all the weight on the wrong words:
“Noted.”
It was my voice. It was the worst impression I have ever heard. The dryness was in the wrong place, and he tipped his chin like a man trying to look down his nose and getting a crick.
I laughed. Out loud, once, before I could stop it. He is never going to let me forget it.

Back at Scrapmoor, Deacon went straight to his bunk and was snoring in a minute. I couldn’t sleep. I came out and Spank was sitting on the Biscuit’s bumper in the dark with a blanket over his shoulders, holding his ribs, looking at nothing.
I went inside and came back with two cups. I’d put tea in both. It was from Gasket’s tin.
He looked at the cup and then at me. “That’s Gasket’s.”
“It’s getting old. Somebody should drink it.”
“You’s never opened that.”
“Drink the tea, Spank.”
He drank it. He made a face. “That’s terrible.”
“It’s from a tin that’s been in a glove box for a year.”
“It’s the best tea I ever had.” His voice cracked on it and he looked away fast, and started talking about the stars, because he can’t help himself. I sat down on the bumper beside him. There was room. I left a little bit of room, just so it would look like an accident when my shoulder touched his.
“Sara,” he said after a while. “I’m gonna say something real, and then you’s gonna act like I didn’t.”
“Fine.”
“I’m glad it’s you in that seat.”
“It’s a seat.”
“Course it is.”
“It’s just a seat, Spank.”
“Course, darlin’.”
I didn’t move. It was cold. That’s the only reason.
He leaned his head back against the truck and shut his eyes, and after a minute his breathing went slow. I knew he was pretending. He does it badly. He makes a little whistle in his nose. He wanted me to stay and he’d found the only way he could ask without making a joke of it.
I stayed. I held the tin in my lap.
I’ll tell him the rest. The bell, the desk, the number. Not tonight.

lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/driver.title: Driver Wanted
lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/driver.content:
Told in turns, by Deacon, Spank and Sara. Some weeks after Contract Row.
Deacon
The debt’s been gone six weeks and I still check my pockets for it.
Nobody tells ya what a free man does on a Tuesday. Three years I paid Orrin and never once pictured the mornin’ after. Turns out it’s quiet. I eat breakfast. I count the money. There’s more of it than there’s ever been, and I count it anyway, in case it changes its mind. Sara says I count like a man defusing something. She’s not wrong.
Spank’s driven the Biscuit all six weeks. In that time she’s lost a mirror and most of her third gear, and he’s lost the right to call himself a driver. Sara’s started holdin’ the dashboard with both hands and says it’s for warmth. She’s wearin’ a coat made out of what I think used to be a tent. So I walked down to Contract Row and chalked it myself.
DRIVER WANTED. APPLY AT THE BISCUIT.
Seven came. In order.
Hobb drove in reverse only. Said it was a condition. I asked what condition and he says, “The kind where ya like to see where ya been.” I gave him points for that, and then he backed us through the shed wall. Shed’s fine. Wall’s a door now.
A woman in a shawl whispered to the truck for ten minutes and called it “him.” Spank, who’d been quiet all mornin’, said “Her” in a voice I ain’t heard since the funeral. The woman left. Fast.
Dobbs drove an ice cream wagon for thirty years. The horn plays a tune when he turns the key and he can’t shut it off, and the Biscuit played it for two days after, every time she hit a bump. Nobody had the heart to say which tune. It was cheerful. We all agreed it was the worst thing that ever happened to us.
A soft-spoken fella in a clean apron said he could drive and he could cook. Sara asked what he cooked. “Whatever comes in,” he says, and smiled, and I went back to the Row that night and added a line to the board. It now says NO CANNIBALS under the first one. Somebody underlined it twice. I’d like to meet the person who underlined it once.
A boy of fifteen with a forged licence drove like an angel, then fainted when Sara looked at him. She hadn’t done nothin’. She’d just looked. I’ve been on the receivin’ end. I don’t blame him.
A broad fella named Corvin watched Spank back the Biscuit into a barrel and said he was a mouth with a truck attached. Sara hit him. I don’t think she decided to. She was standin’, and then Corvin was sittin’, holdin’ a tooth. She said “Sorry” and went to wash her hand. Spank asked me who she was apologisin’ to. I said the tooth, probably.
That was six. The seventh never auditioned. She’d watched the whole circus from an upturned crate with a thermos, a woman past sixty with a face like a boot and forearms like fence posts. When the barrel business was done she stood up, took the keys out of Spank’s hand while he was mid-sentence, and drove the Biscuit out of the yard like she’d stolen it.
Gone four hours. I quit countin’ at two and started writin’ a eulogy at three. When she came back the Biscuit was the right way up, which I consider a miracle, with two chickens in the cab and a man’s hat on the dash. She didn’t say where she’d found ‘em. She climbed down and says, “Third’s hard till she’s warm. You shoulder it.”
Spank went white as a plate.
Gasket said that, word for word, a hundred times. Nobody’d told her. Any driver who spends five minutes behind that wheel would say the same. It didn’t help.
“Name’s Rook,” she says. “Ran buses for the Vigil. Evacuation runs. Never lost a kid.” She thought about it. “Lost two buses.”
I hired her on the spot. Nobody else was gonna apply after the tooth, and Spank had stopped talkin’, which scared me worse than the chickens.
Spank
Now I was sulkin’. A little. I had a seat, and it was a good seat, and I’d been in it forty one days. I counted. Don’t tell Sara I counted.
Mornin’ after, Rook’s standin’ at the driver’s door with her thermos. “Move over, boy.”
I didn’t.
“This here’s Gasket’s,” I says.
“Where’s he?”
“Dead.”
“Then it’s mine now.” Flat as a plank. She looked at the wheel, and at my hands on it, and she says, “I never met him. I’ll drive her like he’d want. I’ll cuss at you like he would. That’s all I got.”
Nobody’d said nothin’ nicer to me in six weeks and I wanted to hit her for it.
My hands wouldn’t come off the wheel. They’d learned where to sit. Sara come round to my side of the truck. She didn’t say it soft. She said “Spank,” flat, like always. But she’d walked round the whole truck to say it, and that’s the soft part. I let go.
The Biscuit’s got a bench up front, three across, and a back seat behind it that Deacon claims by lyin’ across it like he paid for it. I never thought about the front bench till then cause I’d had it to my own self and Gasket’s thermos. Rook on the wheel. Sara at the window, where she likes it, which she’ll say she don’t. Me in the middle, with the stick between my knees like a little fella nobody asked for.
Rook shifted. Her hand come down on my knee. “Ma’am.”
“That’s the stick, boy.”
“That’s my knee.”
“It’s both.”
On the other side, Sara’s shoulder was on mine. Had to be. Ain’t no room. “Don’t,” says Sara.
“I ain’t doin’ nothin’!”
“You’re breathin’ on me.”
“I’m alive, Sara! It’s a requirement!”
She smacked the dash. “It’s three across. Don’t make it weird.” And she didn’t move that shoulder, not one inch, the whole way to the Varkatech turn. I checked. Eight miles.
Rook went diggin’ in the glove box for a rag and come out with Gasket’s notebook. Greasy thing, black cover. She opened it on her knee, drivin’ with her elbow, which I did not love. Deacon leaned up between the seats to see.
“‘Property of Gasket,’” she reads. “‘Short for nothing. Do not ask.’”
I laughed so hard I got hiccups, and then I wasn’t laughin’ no more, and Sara put her hand on the back of my neck. Just for a second. Like she was checkin’ a hot pan.
Rook read the rest out loud like a will.
Third is hard until she’s warm. Shoulder it.
Talk to her. She likes it. Do not tell the boy.
The boy cannot be left alone with fuel.
The boy is not to name anything. (Too late. Biscuit. I have given up.)
If you are reading this I am dead or I have lent her to an idiot. Be kind to her either way.
She stopped. Then she turned the page and read the last line, quieter. “‘Those two. Dear God.’”
“Which two?” I says. “Deacon and Sara? Dear God, that’d be somethin’.”
Deacon coughed behind my ear. Sara looked out the window like the window owed her money. Rook shut the book and passed it across me to her. “That’s yours,” she says. Sara put it in her jacket and said nothin’. It’s in there still.
Sara
The place the Seam calls Varkatech is behind a butcher’s, under a hatch that smells like what the butcher doesn’t sell. Below it there’s a cellar the size of a church, lit violet, with racks of arms and legs and eyes in rows like a cold store. Men in aprons were fitting a hand onto a customer who cried politely the whole time. Cheap parts, cheap suits, and weapons with the numbers filed off. Most of it came off a Renova truck. I know what the truck paint looks like.
Miss V was waiting by a table with her sleeves rolled up.
“The violet stripe,” she said. “That’s the fifth in two years. Same thief, same road. It never sells. I’ve checked every broker in the Belt. Somebody is paying for the one crate nobody can buy.”
“So find the crate,” said Deacon.
“Find who it answers to.” She looked at me when she said it. She does that, and she does it a beat longer than she needs to. I’ve decided I’ll ask her why when I know what I’d do with the answer.
“Why’s she always lookin’ at Sara?” Spank asked, which was exactly the kind of thing Spank asks.
“She’s the only one who never asks what’s in the crate,” said Miss V.
Nobody answered that. She gave us a week and fifty in advance.
I’ll say this about Rook. She drives like a woman with an appointment, and the appointment is with whatever’s in front of her. Deacon sat in the back row and gave directions nobody needed. On the front bench, Spank sat in the middle with his knees jammed against the stick, and my shoulder was against his because there was nowhere else for it to go. He kept very still and breathed carefully, like he was holding something that might spill. I should have shifted. It was a long eight miles.
Deacon
Hollowfall first. Rumour was the lapsed one liked high ground.
Hollowfall’s got the most gravity pockets and the fewest folks who mind. A pocket’s where the Starfall left somethin’ undone. Step in and ya weigh nothin’, or double. Everybody in the ward knows where every one is, same way ya know which stair creaks in yer own house. Rook knew too. She drove the Biscuit into one on purpose, and we floated forty feet. Sara’s tea left her cup and hung there. “Better than a funeral bus,” says Rook. Spank cheered. Sara reached out and caught the tea with the cup, which I’d have paid a week’s wages to see her do on purpose. She’ll tell ya it was an accident. She’ll say it with the cup full.
On a plank bridge over a dry ditch, a very small man in a kettle for a helmet wanted a toll. “For the ditch,” he says. “Out of respect.” Spank started a speech. I paid in a button, ‘cause I’m a coward and it was the cheapest thing I had. The man bit it, scowled, and said, “Another one. Had a woman through a few weeks back paid in a button too. Grey coat, bit too big for her. Can’t tell ya what she looked like. Funny, that.” He scratched under the kettle. “Gave her somethin’ off a truck. She never said thank ya.”
I knew the coat. It wasn’t Miss V, who wears a jacket with a V on the cuff and I’d remember. It was the lost woman outside Orrin’s, the day Spank shouted “free as a bird” down the whole street. He’d tipped his hat to her and told her to ride the Ring Line.
“What woman?” says Spank.
“Outside Orrin’s,” says Sara. “You said good morning. She said it was afternoon.”
“I did not.”
“You did.”
I’d been standin’ eight feet away. I remembered a grey coat and an afternoon. I couldn’t have drawn her face for money. Sara had gone very still, and I know better than to ask her anything before lunch.
A bit further on, a man with a cart of glass jars sold Spank a jar of air for two coins. FRESH AIR, said the label in shaky letters. LAST TUESDAY. Spank asked if it was a good Tuesday. The man said it was the best they’d had, and cried a little. I’ve seen better business sense in a ditch. I let it go. A man gets one mistake a week, and Spank spent his on Monday.
Scrapmoor next, for parts. Scrapmoor’s the ward of what other wards threw away, and its mechanics will tell ya anything was built by Varkatech and then sell ya the part. We asked about a grey soldier with bad joints. Three mechanics said Varkatech built it. A fourth said it built itself. A fifth sold us a spanner.
Then Lanternreach, where Marit keeps the bunker. The Vigil digs ‘em, stocks ‘em with bread and bunks, and when a fall comes the children go down first. Bed’s free. Bread costs a little. I’ve never worked out who pays for the rest and I’ve worked out most things. Somebody does.
Spank gave Marit the first page of the notebook. She read it twice. Then she opened her fat book to the gap after the one word, wrote short for nothing in it in ink, and shut it. Spank said thank you in a voice I’d never heard him use. I counted the stew bowls so as to have somethin’ to do with my face.
“Lapsed come through,” Marit told us. “Four this year. One sat in the yard all afternoon and wouldn’t speak. We fed it. It left the cup washed and hung on the wall.” She tapped a nail by the door. The nail was empty. “Never came back for it.”
Spank
By Glasswick we had seven theories and nine different times of day.
Glasswick’s all glass, on account of the fall dust, which melts into windows if ya spit on it right. Houses is glass, walls is glass, the whole ward’s see through, so nobody lies, cause ever’body knows. Folk walk round in dark specs so they don’t have to look at each other’s business. Ask a Glasswick fella if he likes yer truck and he’ll say it’s ugly, ya paid too much, and the paint’s stole. I lasted forty minutes. I wanted to hit a window. Rook said it was the most honest town she ever drove through and she meant it as an insult.
A glass blower told us the grey soldier was Renova’s. “Old soldiers don’t retire,” he says. “They get filed.”
Tickfall’s the one where ever’ clock is wrong on purpose. A fella told me they figure a star cain’t find a place if the place don’t know what time it is. They ain’t never been hit. They ain’t never been on time, neither. Told us it was a quarter to Thursday. It was Monday. They told us the grey one was Varkatech’s, which the Scrapmoor fellas said too, so that’s two votes for Varkatech and a spanner.
Past that there’s a village with no name. Folks call it the Soup, cause the whole place eats from one pot, and I ain’t askin’ what goes in it. The cook says the soldier come through one night, ate a bowl, said “Post’s closed” to the pot, and left. Sara didn’t say nothin’. She went and stood by the truck for a while.
Rook honked at a fallin’ star. A little one, way off east. She honked, and cussed it, and floored it, and the star went out like it was embarrassed. I seen Sara turn her face to the window so nobody’d catch her smilin’. I caught it. I ain’t tellin’ her.
That night at the Soup, with ever’body else eatin’ from the pot, I got the jar out of my coat. I’d had it three days. I’d been tryin’ to think of a way to do it that wasn’t dumb, and I never did.
“Here,” I says.
“What is it?”
“Last Tuesday. The fella said it was the best one they had.” I couldn’t look at her. “I ain’t got much. I thought you could have a good day, for when you ain’t got one.”
She took it. She turned it over twice. “It’s a jar.”
“I know.”
“It’s empty.”
“It ain’t.”
She put it in her jacket and went back to the pot without a word. I thought I’d done it wrong. Then I seen her hand go to that pocket twice before she sat down, just to check it was there.
Sara
The jar was in my jacket. I’d had it two days. I’d taken it out three times to look at it, which is a stupid thing to do with a jar of nothing, and each time I’d put it back before anyone could see. Nobody had given me something because I might like it in a long time. Gasket did, with his tea tin. Now Spank had, and I didn’t have a way to say that, so I kept it where I could feel it.
Cinderside is built on a slag hill that’s still warm, and its bar, the Soft Landing, is dug into the crater of an old fall. You drink in a bowl. The crews come to lie about the week.
“You’re the sky-reader,” said a man named Brask to the whole room. Big, grinning, drink in hand. “The one who got the place wrong. I hear the ward wants to put it on a plaque. Here lies a boy who called it a day early and a mile out.”
Spank gave the laugh he uses when it hurts. “Day was right.”
I put my cup down.
I crossed the bar without a word. Brask was still grinning when I got to him. “Hey, swe-”
My fist went into his mouth before he finished. It landed square and it hurt my knuckles. I hit him again, in the ribs, and when he folded over I got a hand in his collar and drove his face into the table. The table broke. A cup of something bounced off my sleeve. He tried to get up and I put a knee in his stomach and put him back down, and when he reached for a bottle I stepped on the hand until he let it go.
By then there was a sound in the room like a lot of people not breathing.
I stood up. I pulled my sleeve straight. I was out of breath, and my hand was open and shaking, and I could feel Brask’s blood on my knuckles.
“Whoa!” said Spank. He’d come up behind me, eyes huge. “Whoa. Sara.” He took my wrist, turned my hand over and looked at it. “Are you okay? Is it broke?”
“It’s fine.”
“Did you just defend me?”
“No.”
“You put a fella through a table.”
“He was in my way.”
“He was clear across the room.”
“It’s a small room.” It isn’t. It’s a bowl the size of a barn. I picked up my cup anyway and drank, and wouldn’t look at him, because I knew what his face would be doing. I looked, and I was right. He looked like someone had handed him the sky and told him to keep it. I looked away first. I never look away first.
Rook slid a bag of ice across the bar without turning her head. I put it on my hand, and it wasn’t for the hand.
The barman, who had watched all this with enormous patience, said, “East tower. Foundry Road gate. Ask the man who sleeps.”
We drove out there in the dark. Spank sat in the middle the whole way and I let my shoulder stay where it was.
The Foundry Road gate was quiet. The two towers stood black against the sky, the rope across the road was down for the night, and Tobin was asleep in his chair under the awning, same as the day of the heist. I woke him with my boot.
“I don’t know anything,” he said. “That’s how I’m alive.”
“The east tower.”
He sighed. “Has someone on it. Was there before I got the job. I take a bucket of water up on Mondays and leave it on the landing. Bucket’s empty Tuesday. That’s the arrangement.” He looked at the sky. “It said thank you once.”
He showed us a side door and told us not to say he’d shown us.
At the top there was a guard room four paces wide. A cot, made so tight you could have bounced a coin off it. Boots in a line, toes square. A tin cup, washed and upside down on a nail, with a little lantern stamped on its side. On the wall, rows of chalk marks in fives, rubbed out and redrawn so often the wall had gone white in a square. At the bottom, in careful square writing: DAY 1,411. NOTHING TO REPORT.
The crate sat at the head of the cot where a pillow goes. The lid was off. The shards inside lit the little room like a lamp turned low. I held my hand over it. It was warm.
Nobody was in the room. Nobody had to be.
Spank read the wall twice. “Fourteen hundred and eleven,” he said. “That’s near four years.” He swallowed. “I counted forty one.”
I know this room. I slept in forty like it. I told him, “Four Seven was my post.”
He turned.
“At the Bureau. Skywatch. I had a desk with a screen, and the desk was Four Seven. Across the corridor was Four Six.” I looked at the cot. “I never met them. Opposite shifts. A coat on a chair, a mug on the desk, that was all I ever saw of them. It called me Four Seven at the gate, and nobody alive knew my desk but the one across from it.” My voice did something. I waited for it to stop. “It stood its post, and nobody told it the post closed.”
I had never said that much in a row to anyone. “That’s the bell,” I said. “Part of it. I’ll give you the rest when I can.”
He nodded. He didn’t push. He picked up the washed cup, turned it over, and set it back on the nail exactly the way it had been, with the same tilt. He’s careful with other people’s things. He’s never been careful with his own.
We didn’t take the crate. Four Six stands up straight next to it. Take it away and it’s in pieces by Friday, and I’ve seen what pieces look like on someone I shared a corridor with. I took the tea tin out of my jacket, the one from Gasket’s glove box, made a cup, and left it on the crate. I don’t have a reason.
Going down the stairs in the dark, Spank’s hand found mine on the rail. He didn’t say anything. I didn’t pull away. We got to the bottom and neither of us let go until we saw Tobin.
“Find anything?” Tobin asked.
“Nothing to report,” I said.
Spank
We told Miss V it works for nobody.
“That’s not an answer,” she says.
“It’s the truth,” says Sara.
Miss V looked at her a long while. “That’s worse,” she says, and paid us for the week.
Rook drove us home at a speed I ain’t gonna say out loud. Deacon braced both boots on the back of my seat and said a prayer in a language I don’t think exists. I was in the middle, with the stick at my knee, and Sara’s shoulder on mine, and I didn’t say a word the whole road, cause I’m tryin’ to learn.
Somewhere past Tickfall she says, “You talk too much even when you’re quiet.”
“I ain’t said nothin’.”
“I can hear it.”
Then she leaned over and put her head on my shoulder and stayed there. She was comfortable. I could tell, because she didn’t fidget once. I didn’t know what to do with my arms. My heart was goin’ like I’d run the whole way home, and I was scared to breathe wrong and have her move. I didn’t want her to move.
“Don’t get used to it,” she says, eyes shut. “I’m tired.”
“Yes, Sara.”
Rook looked over, saw, and turned her eyes back to the road with a face like she’d seen nothin’ and would swear to it in court.
Before she dropped off she dug the jar out of her jacket, looked at it a long minute, and set it on the dash next to Gasket’s money jar.
Two jars.
“Shade,” she mumbled. “Keeps the sun off the dash.”
“It’s a jar of Tuesday.”
“It’s glass.”
“You could just say you like it.”
She didn’t answer. She was out. I sat there with her breathin’ against my neck, and Deacon snored in the back, and I never moved my arm the rest of the way home.
She never opened the jar. She never would. Rook honked at the sky, and for once I didn’t mind the noise.
Sara
I woke up when the engine stopped.
It was dark, and the Biscuit ticked as it cooled. My face was in Spank’s collar. He smelled like dust and grease and the Soup, and he hadn’t moved. I could tell from how stiff his shoulder was that he hadn’t moved the whole way home, and my stomach did something I don’t have a name for.
“Is she up?” Deacon whispered from the back.
“No,” Spank whispered. “Leave her.”
I kept my eyes shut.
Rook got out, and then Deacon, and the doors closed one at a time, very softly, like people leaving a nursery. Somebody’s boots went off toward the shed. Then it was just the two of us and the engine ticking.
“Sara,” he said, barely a sound. “We’re home.”
I didn’t answer. I wanted to see what he’d do.
He sat there a long while. Then he slid out from under me an inch at a time, holding my head so it wouldn’t knock the window, and got the door open and came round to my side. He picked me up like it was nothing. He’s no giant, but there’s wire in him, and he carried me across the yard as easy as a sack of flour, which I’d never have told him I noticed.
He almost walked into the pump. He said a very small word to it.
My cot was by the shed wall, made, with Gasket’s blanket folded at the foot. He set me down and pulled the blanket up, and then he tugged it straight, and tugged it again, and I could have told him it was fine.
Something clinked. He’d gone back to the truck and come back with the jar. He set it on the crate beside the cot where I’d see it when I woke.
“Night, Sara,” he said.
He stood there. I thought he might say something else, and he did, so low I almost missed it.
“I’m glad you’re here,” he said. “Real glad.”
It wasn’t the voice he uses for the truck or the jokes or the crowd. There was nothing to hide behind in it. I had known him a long time and I had never heard that one, and it went straight through my ribs and sat there. I kept my eyes shut and didn’t move, and the dark came up warm around me, and I started to sink.
I felt his fingers in my hair.
They went slowly, like he was learning the way, and I knew without looking that he was holding his breath. I’d have told anyone that I hate being touched. I opened my eyes.
He was crouched by the cot with the moon on one side of his face. He froze, caught, his hand still tangled in me.
“You’re awake,” he whispered.
“Your hand’s cold.”
“Sorry.” He started to pull away.
“I didn’t say stop.”
He didn’t. We looked at each other for a long time, and neither of us said anything that mattered. The pump dripped across the yard. In the shed Deacon snored, and Rook told her chickens off in her sleep. His fingers moved again, and I closed my eyes.
After a while his hand came down from my hair and rested along my cheek. It stayed there, careful, like he was waiting to be told to go. I turned my face into it a little. I told myself it was to get comfortable.
His thumb moved once across my cheekbone. It was the gentlest thing anyone has ever done to me, and he did it like he’d been practicing for years and never had anywhere to put it.
“Go to bed, Spank,” I said. It came out wrong. It came out like a different thing.
He didn’t answer. His hand didn’t move. I could feel him standing at the edge of something, and I could hear him working out whether to say it, and he waited there for a long time, and so did I.
“Yes, Sara,” he said at last, very quietly.
Then he leaned down and pressed his mouth to my forehead, quick and light, like he’d decided and was scared to be told off for it. I kept my eyes shut. I didn’t breathe. I told myself I hadn’t felt it.
He went away across the yard, and I heard him tell the pump goodnight too.
I lay there in the dark with my cheek still warm and my forehead warmer.
I’d been on watch so long I’d stopped noticing it. Four years of keeping one eye on the door and my hand near the gun, a desk in my head that I never got up from. I’d thought that was just how I was made. I’d looked at Four Six’s cot that night and seen someone I knew, and I’d gone down those stairs holding a hand I hadn’t asked for, and now I was lying under Gasket’s blanket with nothing in the yard to watch, because someone else was out there.
Nobody ever told me the post closed. I’m not sure he’d have known to. But he’d come and stood beside it anyway, and put the jar where I’d find it.
The jar sat on the crate and caught a little of the moon. I picked it up and held it against my chest, and I slept like I hadn’t in four years.

lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/fresh-.title: Fresh Falls
lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/fresh-.content:
Told by Spank, sky-reader and general nuisance to the Fresh Meat Squad.
