You’s writin’ this down? Good. Name’s Spank. Not Spanky. Spank. Grandmaw give me that name on account of the ladle, and I ain’t tellin’ you about the ladle. This here’s the story of the night the star turned.
Rule about falls. Ever’body in the Drift’s got one. Mine is don’t stand under it. Grandmaw’s was don’t stand under it, and never say the sky’s quiet, cause it’s listenin’. I broke the first rule twice and the second one ever’ goddamn day, and I still got all ten fingers. So you’s tell me which one’s the good rule.
I got Grandmaw’s chart. Goat hide, black ink and red, older than dirt. Ever’ star that falls is gonna shiver first, a day or two ahead. Shiver like a wet dog. The chart tells ya which stars to watch and which way they lean, and the lean says where it’s fixin’ to land. Top corner there’s a name wrote down. Asterion.
Grandmaw said he drawed it before there was ever a Meridian. I said ain’t nobody lives that long. She hit me with the ladle. The suits down at the Seam gates say there never was no Asterion, the old families just made him up. The old families say he’s still out yonder somewheres, walkin’ round, drawin’ stuff. I say if he’s alive he kin come git his chart back, cause it’s heavy as a sumbitch.
The Vigil got lookouts on ever’ ward. Sweet folks. They see one comin’ two hours out and ring a bell. Two hours! You’s cain’t git a granny outta bed in two hours. I git a day. That’s why I got a seat in the truck.
The truck was the Biscuit. Six wheels, older than Deacon’s debts. Down the side it said FRESH MEAT SQUAD in red paint, my own handwritin’. Other crews call the new ones fresh meat cause we die first, so I figured if they’s gonna say it I’ll say it bigger. Deacon wanted it painted over. Gasket said it stayed. Gasket said ya cain’t make a thing worse by agreein’ with it.
Deacon ran us. Tall, tired fella who owed a man on Contract Row named Orrin more than the Biscuit was worth, and Orrin added to it ever’ week whether Deacon paid or not. Gasket drove. Old fella with a gray beard and hands black up to the elbow, and he loved that truck more than most men love their wives. Called her sweetheart. Called me worse. She treated him better than most wives treat their men, too, which ain’t hard, I met the wives.
Sara shot. Sara didn’t talk. One word at a time, like it cost her. She was my favorite, and she had the finest ass in the whole goddamn Drift, and I told her so to her face, once. She said “Noted.” That’s one word, and I lived off it for a month.
Night it started we was in a shed in Scrapmoor and I’m up on the Biscuit’s roof with the chart. There ain’t no real dark in the Drift. Just different oranges, cause the Scar light is on the clouds all night. I been watchin’ a star I call the Limper, cause it sits low and crooked. Round midnight it shivered.
I watched it three more times to be sure. Then I kicked the shed door in.
“Up! Fall’s comin’. Before sunup.”
Deacon didn’t move. “How sure?”
“Sure as the ladle.”
“That ain’t a number.”
“It’s a big one.”
Gasket’s voice come up from under the truck. “Where?”
“Hollowfall edge. Burnt flats past the old pylon.”
“How far?”
“Four hours if nobody stops to hit nobody.”
They all looked at me. Rude.
Sara stood up with the long gun. “Sure?”
“Limper’s leanin’ east and it shivered four times. I’m sure.”
She nodded once. That’s how ya know it’s real. Sara don’t move for maybes.
“Sara,” I says, “you gonna say somethin’ else or just stand there lookin’ hot and dangerous?”
“No.”
“I’m takin’ that as a yes.”
We stopped for fuel at Lanternreach. One pump works, and it’s got a nozzle on it so big the Cinder Boys had been sittin’ round admirin’ it half the night. They’d parked across it, lounged on their hoods like it was a porch. The big one slid down and read the side of the truck out loud.
“Fresh meat.”
He started it. I want that wrote down. I hit him with a wrench before he got to the second word. Not hard. He fell down anyway. His buddies come over, Sara put a round in the dirt by their feet, and suddenly ever’body had somewhere else to be. Deacon paid the pump man double for the trouble. Gasket drank tea out of a tin and watched it like a show.
“You could’ve just asked,” says Deacon.
“I did ask. I asked with the wrench.”
Past Lanternreach there’s a Vigil bunker with a green patch on the door. A gray lady with a braid was loadin’ little kids onto a cart. They run a drill ever’ week cause kids forget. Marit, her name. Ever’body knows her.
“No bell tonight,” she says.
“It’ll ring before mornin’. You’s won’t be on the ground.”
She looked at me long. “Yer grandmother said that. Never wrong neither.” Then, “Ground’s hot three hours after. Three, Spank. Not two and a half cause you’s in a hurry.”
“We know.”
“You don’t. It’s always you that don’t.” She shoved a flask at Sara. “Beds here if you’s come back short. We got room.”
I said thanks and meant about half of it.
We got to the ridge at four. Burnt glass all down the flats, flat and shiny like a plate nobody washed. I put my finger on the chart where it was gonna land. Gasket parked the Biscuit nose down so we could go fast. Sara went up on the roof. Deacon got the heat suits out. Two suits, one for him and one for me, cause I’m the only one stupid enough to run into it.
The suit was tight in all the wrong places. Deacon bought it for his own body type and I ain’t got it. Gasket said I looked like a sausage in a sock. Sara checked my straps herself, give ‘em a yank, said “Tight.” I said that’s what she said. She held on to the strap a second longer than she needed to. Maybe I’m lyin’. Maybe I ain’t.
Down the road three sets of headlights stopped. Other crews. Word gets round when somebody calls ‘em early, and I’m a bit famous, which is bad for business. Up over the flats a big grey thing hung a mile high on sacks of sky shard. Renova skiff. Renova don’t ring no bells. Renova just turns up, like a rash.
“Four minutes,” I says.
“You can’t know that,” says Deacon.
“My teeth hurt.”
They do, right before. Never told nobody. Grandmaw’s did too.
Sky opened at five past five. There’s a color it comes in, white and purple at once, and it come down out of the east tearin’ like a bedsheet. The whole ridge lit up. I had the tongs and the crate and I was already countin’ shards in my head.
Sara says, “It turned.”
“What?”
“It turned.”
I looked. She was right. It was comin’ down at my finger and then it bent. Bent like a stick in water. Went off northeast, a long way, and hit the ground seven miles from where I said.
That chart’s never been off more than a stone’s throw. Stars don’t turn.
“GO!” I says.
Gasket was already in the seat. “Hold on to somethin’,” he says, and put the Biscuit off the ridge so hard my crate flipped.
Other crews was runnin’ too. Gasket went straight across the flats, and halfway he took us through the Hollowfall pocket. Gravity’s busted there. Kids learn where it is before they learn their own street. Six seconds the Biscuit was light as a feather and my stomach went out the roof, and Gasket sung. The whole way through. Terrible voice. Hit ever’ note wrong and loved ever’ one.
The skiff beat us. Course it did. A dozen assholes in grey armor, big guns, bigger crates. We come over the rim a minute behind.
The star was in the bottom of a hole. Grey, veined purple, big as a house and cracked all to hell. Ever’ piece of it hummin’. Ya feel it in yer bones. Air tasted like a coin. My teeth was fixin’ to crack.
“Suits,” says Deacon.
We went down. Gasket stayed up on the rim with the engine runnin’, cause Gasket don’t leave the truck. Sara laid on the roof. I went down in the heat and got a shard in ten seconds. Fist-sized and hot, buzzin’ in the tongs like a wasp. Dropped it in the crate. Deacon got two. I got another. Then a dickhead in grey come out of the steam and put a rifle in my face.
I hit him with the shovel.
I enjoyed it. I been waitin’ since Lanternreach. He went down and his gun went off in the air and ever’body in that hole turned round. Then it was on. Two more crews come over the rim. A Renova prick with a net gun got me tangled. Sara shot the net gun. I got untangled. Sara put a round through some fucker’s head about an inch left of my ear and I said thanks and she said “Duck.” Bit late. I’m hittin’ ever’thing grey and yellin’ at Deacon to grab shards and yellin’ at myself to grab shards, and we got six. We got eight. I lost count.
Then a gunner on the skiff line put a burst in the Biscuit.
I seen it. Fifty feet off, crate on my back. The truck jerked. Engine screamed. And she started to roll, slow, then not slow, down the slope with nobody steerin’ right.
I dropped the shovel and ran.
She hit a rock big as a cow and spun once and stopped against the wall with a bang I felt in my feet. I got to the door. Stuck. I pulled it with both hands.
Gasket was still holdin’ the wheel. Like somebody told him not to let go. There was a lot of blood and I ain’t gonna say.
“Spank.” His voice was small. I never heard it small.
“I got ya. I got ya, come on, git out.”
“Nah.” He almost laughed. “Listen. Coupling’s cracked. Hit it left. Left, not right. Ya always go right.”
“Gasket.”
“Don’t let Deacon drive.”
“GASKET!”
He didn’t say nothin’ else. I said his name a few more times. Don’t know how many. Then Sara had me by the back of the suit pullin’ and I kept sayin’ it and she kept pullin’.
After that I don’t remember much. The star cracked again. A big piece split and the whole hole got hotter in a second and ever’body ran. Renova hooked up and went up the lines, cussin’. The other crews took what they had and scattered. Then it was us, three standin’ and one in the driver’s seat, in a hole full of hummin’.
Deacon was cryin’. He didn’t say. He just kept wipin’ his face on the inside of the suit. “We gotta move him.”
“We don’t leave our own on the ground.”
“I know.”
“The Vigil buries ‘em.”
“I know, Spank.”
We carried him round to the passenger side. Took all three of us. Buckled him in cause it was the only way he’d sit. Sara shut his eyes. I stood with my hand on the window till Deacon says we gotta go.
The Biscuit wouldn’t go. Coupling was cracked clean through, like he said. Deacon had Gasket’s little book, greasy, full of pencil drawings of parts. He read it by Sara’s torch and got half of it wrong. Sara held the light, and with her other hand she held on to my sleeve the whole time, and she never said why. They clamped it with a chain. Then it was me.
I ain’t a mechanic. I hit things. That’s my whole skill. But Gasket told me where, and I laid under the truck in the heat and hit the coupling left, left, left, till somethin’ clicked and the Biscuit shuddered like she’d been woke up.
“Did it work?”
“It worked.”
“Gasket’d be unbearable about this.”
“He would.”
Then who drives. Deacon’s a city boy and can’t work the stick. Sara said “No” so quiet I almost missed it. So it was me. The one fucker what’s been told four separate times never to touch the Biscuit. I got in the seat with the blood still on it and put my hands where his hands was.
Worst drivin’ ever. She’s got a hard third, ya gotta shoulder it, and I didn’t know. I ground her on the first rise and the whole truck bucked. Then I did it again.
“I know,” I says to the seat. “I know! She’s got a hard third. Ya told me. Sweetheart, don’t do this to me.”
He didn’t say nothin’. Cause he was dead. I knew he was dead. I kept talkin’ anyway. Told him sorry about the clutch. Told him the other crews was behind us and I’d lose ‘em at the pylon. Talked an hour. Maybe two. Somewhere past the Hollowfall pocket, where the Biscuit goes light and I got no stomach left, I stopped. I’d got to the part where he sings.
It was real quiet after that.
“Spank,” says Deacon.
“I know.”
“He’s been gone two hours.”
“I know.”
“Ya can stop.”
“I’ll stop in a bit.”
We got to the bunker near noon. Marit was at the door like she’d stood there all night. She looked at the Biscuit. She looked at the passenger side.
“Come in,” she says. “There’s room.”
They took him in on a cart. She asked his name and I told her, and she opened a fat book and wrote it down careful. Then she says, “Gasket what?”
I opened my mouth. Nothin’.
I looked at Deacon. He shook his head. Sara shook hers. Nine years he drove us and none of us knew his other name. He was just Gasket. She wrote it like that. One word. Big gap after.
“Fourth from yer end this month,” says Marit. Plain, like a number. “I’ll see he’s put somewhere dry.”
Sara took his boots, hers was burnt through. Deacon took the ammo. That’s how it’s done, nobody argues. I stood in the yard tryin’ to think what I was meant to take. Couldn’t think. Took the rag out his back pocket, the black one he wiped his hands on, and put it in mine.
We sold the shards that night. Deacon put the word out and three buyers come to a loadin’ yard by the Last Pylon Line where the lights go on and off. Eleven shards, grey and purple in the lead crate, still warm.
First was a DeltaPure broker, thin and polite, nice coat. Fair price, said it twice like we’d argue. Second was a prick from Lumen Heights, nicer coat, smilin’ with half his face. His wife’s leg had lapsed, he says, and he don’t wanna wait for no subscription office. Double the broker. I seen his wife once on a poster in the Seam. Good legs, both of ‘em, God rest the lapsed one. I wanted to hit him anyway. I didn’t. I want credit.
Third was a lady in a gray jacket with a little V sewed on the cuff. No name. Tall, sharp, a mouth like she knew somethin’ about ya and wasn’t gonna tell. I wasn’t lookin’. I was lookin’ a little. Sara elbowed me in the ribs so hard I coughed up a noise. I ain’t sayin’ it was jealous. I’m sayin’ it hurt.
The lady looked at the crate then at Deacon. “Triple. All of it. Cash now. No paper.”
“Varkatech,” says Sara. Longest thing she said all night.
“Take it,” says Deacon. He was lookin’ at the floor. Orrin’s due Friday.
Nobody argued. She counted the money out on a crate in neat stacks and I counted it after, cause somebody had to. Gasket’s share went in a jar. Don’t know who for. It’s still on the dash.
She picked up the crate and looked at me. “You’re the one calls ‘em early.”
“That’s me.”
“Did it land where ya said?”
“No.”
She nodded. Little nod. Like she’d been told what she already knew. I opened my mouth to ask how, and she says, “Keep readin’, kid,” and walked off between the trucks with eleven bits of the sky in her arms, and the lights over the yard went off and come back on.
I think about that. I don’t like it.
We drove back to Scrapmoor in the dark. Me drivin’, cause nobody wanted to say I couldn’t. Ground third twice. Seat next to me was empty and I kept talkin’ to it anyway. Told it about the money. Told it Sara said four whole words today, a record. Told it I’d learn the clutch.
Round the old pylon Sara climbed over from the back and sat down in it. She didn’t say nothin’. The seat he rode his last drive in, and she sat in it like it was hers. After a while she put her hand on top of mine on the stick. Third was hard right there. She shouldered it with me, and it went in.
I quit talkin’ to the seat.
When we got in I took the chart out and put it on the hood. Grandmaw’s marks in the corner, little neat ones. Under the old man’s name there’s a gap. I got Gasket’s pencil out of his rag and I wrote one word.
Turned.
Hey, Asterion. If you’s out there drawin’. Yer chart’s been wrong once. I wanna know why.

lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/standi.title: Standing Order
lore-and-stories/stories/meridian/standi.content:
Told in turns, by Deacon, Spank and Sara, with one page from the tower. A few days after Driver Wanted.
Deacon
Miss V took a week to think about “it works for nobody,” and then she sent for us again. We’d all decided she was Varkatech’s somehow, high up or close to it, though she’d never said so and Spank had asked her twice. Same cellar, same violet light, same fella fittin’ the same hand on the same customer, who’d stopped cryin’ and started complainin’ about the thumb.
“Five times,” she said. “That crate’s been stolen five times in two years. Renova keeps a ledger of every theft on its convoys, and the ledger sits in a depot on the east edge of the Seam. I’d like to read it.”
“Read it,” says Spank. “With yer eyes.”
“I’d like it brought to me.”
“Ya mean stolen,” I says.
“I mean brought,” says Miss V, and slid sixty across the table, which in my experience is what folks pay when they mean stolen.

We went to the depot Friday morning.
It’s a long low building of violet glass with a sign over the door: RENOVA RETURNS AND RECLAMATION. WE’LL MAKE IT RIGHT. Under the words there’s a smilin’ hand, and the hand has six fingers. I took it for a printer’s mistake. By the end of the day I’d decided it was policy.
Inside there’s a queue. I’d call it a queue the way ya’d call the Scar a pothole. It went round the walls and out the back and I think into the next ward. A machine gave me a ticket. My ticket said 9114. The board over the windows said NOW SERVING 212. I did the sum, and then I went and sat on a bench with a hundred other people who’d done the same sum.
The fella beside me had a wooden leg with RENTED stamped on the shin. “Crate of lamps,” he says. “Paid in full. Bandit took ‘em on the Foundry Road. Replacement pending.” He patted the bench. “Two years. I’ve been so patient I’ve grown into this.”
A woman across from us had a patch over one eye. “I bought a pair of lenses,” she says. “He took one. Pending.” She leaned over. “It’s a very good lens, I’m told.”
I got to window four after four hours and a very long conversation with a man named Hobb who I swear I know from somewhere. Behind the glass sat a clerk with a tin badge that said HAPPY TO HELP and a smile that looked like it was holdin’ up the rest of him with wire.
“Good afternoon!” he says. “How can Renova make it right?”
“Somebody stole me crate.”
“We’re so sorry. Theft is a normal part of life on the road. Your claim is important to us.”
“Violet stripe. Foundry Road. Thursday dawn.”
The smile didn’t move. His eyes went to the shelf behind him, and came back. “A bandit, sir. Very sad. A replacement is pending.”
“That crate’s been stolen before.”
“It has been stolen on several occasions.”
“Several.”
“Several is the number I’m able to speak to.”
“And the replacement?”
“Pending.”
“Pending what?”
“Pending, sir. It’s a process.” And he stamped my form. He had a rack of stamps by his elbow. I counted. PENDING. PENDING (URGENT). PENDING (RED). And one at the end that said only SORRY, which was the dustiest.
Behind him, on a shelf, sat a book thick as a door with a chain on it. The spine said THEFT AND LOSS. He’d looked at it twice already. A man who’s lyin’ always looks at the thing he’s protectin’.
I thanked him very much. I told him I’d be back. I meant it as a threat and he took it as a promise, and his smile got a little wider, God help him.
Spank
Plan was real good. Deacon would keep the clerk talkin’ at the window. Rook was parked out the back with the engine on and the chickens in the cab. Sara was up on the roof with the long gun, which she said she wasn’t gonna use, but she’d feel better. And me, I was goin’ in by the laundry chute.
Sara found the chute. She says it’s the only door in the place that nobody guards, on account of nobody wants it. I brung the crowbar. It’s still a little folded from where the lapsed fella done it at the Foundry Road gate, but I bent it back most of the way with my knee, and I say it’s got character.
I went in headfirst. That was mistake one.
Halfway down, the chute narrowed and I stopped. I had my arms at my sides and my boots in the sky and a bag of laundry comin’ down behind me that wasn’t gonna stop either. I was in there eleven minutes. A fella come into the laundry room and put a sack on my feet. I said thank you. He said “You’re welcome” and went away. That’s Renova for you. Nobody asks nothin’.
Eventually the laundry won. I come out in a heap of sheets, which was soft, and a smell, which wasn’t.
The back office had one door and it opened right behind the clerk’s chair. I could see the whole shelf. I could see the book and the chain. And I could see the clerk’s back, which was about a yard from my face, wearin’ a clean vest and a cough.
Deacon was at the window and doin’ his best, and I’ll say this for him, he’s a talent. He’d got the clerk on the subject of his poor mother. He’d got his poor mother a bad eye, and then a worse one. He was cryin’. Real tears. Told me after he’d thought about the debt. I hadn’t known he’d missed it.
I got the crowbar into the chain. I pushed. The crowbar slid off and hit the shelf, and the shelf rang like the Soup’s dinner bell.
“MY MOTHER!” Deacon shouted.
The clerk had half turned. Deacon was standin’ on his chair with his arms wide. “She said I’d be a good boy! And look at me!”
The clerk turned back. I’d ducked behind a mop. I put the bar in again, and this time the chain popped, and the book come off the shelf and onto my chest, and it weighed as much as Rook.
I could not lift it. I could drag it. I dragged it across the floor on its back with me on top of it, and the clerk said “Is something falling?” and Deacon said “It’s my grief,” and I got it out into the front room on my elbows.
That was mistake two. The door I’d picked wasn’t the back one. It let me out into the queue.
A hundred people turned and looked at a man crawlin’ out of the wall with a book the size of a door.
Nobody said a word. Then the woman with the patch gave a yell I’ll never forget.
“IT’S THE REPLACEMENT!”
I’d like to say I knew what to do. I got up. I held the book to my chest. And the whole queue rose off its bench like a flock of birds, and the fella with the wooden leg shouted “Is it the lamps?” and I ran.
They followed me. Every one. All hundred, through the front door and into the street, shoutin’ what they’d ordered. Rook saw it all in the mirror and swung the Biscuit round the building like a woman who’d seen worse. I dove into the back, and Sara jumped off the roof onto the hood without hardly touchin’ the ground, and Deacon came out the window of the depot, and I don’t know how.
The Biscuit took off. About twenty folks hung onto the bumper. The fella with the wooden leg kept pace for two miles on his own legs, and I never seen anybody want somethin’ so bad. The last I saw of him, he was wavin’. I waved back. I didn’t know what else to do.
Rook looked at the book, then at me, then at the mirror. “Good book?” she says.
“It’s heavy,” I says.
“They’re all heavy,” she says, and honked.
Sara
We read it in the shed that night with one lamp.
Eleven thefts in two years, all on convoys. All on the Foundry Road. All at dawn, within a day of a Thursday. Every one of them marked bandit, unknown, and every one of them marked replacement pending, in the same blue stamp, and not one of them marked closed.
“Five of ‘em’s the violet stripe,” said Deacon, running a finger down the margin. “Different buyer each time. Every one paid in full up front. Look, here’s the amounts.”
He read them out. Nobody said anything after the third.
“I don’t get it,” said Rook. “Why steal what you already sold?”
“I’ll tell ya,” said Spank. He’d gone red the way he does when he’s sure of something. “Say I sell ya a biscuit.”
“Spank.”
“A real good one. Ya pay me. Then I sneak back round the corner and take the biscuit off ya, and tell ya a bandit done it, and I’m real sorry, and I’ll get ya another one directly. I never do. But I’ve got yer money, and I’ve got the biscuit, and now I sell the same biscuit to the next fella down the road. And he gets robbed too.” He took a breath. “That’s all of it. Nobody ever loses a biscuit. Just the fella who paid.”
“That’s Renova,” said Deacon slowly.
“That’s Renova. And ever’body says it’s bandits. Even them in the queue. There was a hundred folks in that room and I bet not one of ‘em thought Renova done it to me.”
“Because they’d have to be fools to rob themselves,” I said.
“Or clever,” said Rook.
I turned another page. Down the corner of each one ran a column of tiny boxes, and the last was marked SUPERVISOR’S INITIALS. Nobody had ever initialled it.
I knew that box. I’d looked at it every day for three years. The Bureau used the same forms, the same stamp in the corner, the same margin for notes nobody wrote. I’d sat at a desk with that box in front of me and thought it was a government.
The depot ran on Skywatch paper. It had been the same office the whole time, writing both.
I didn’t say so. Spank looked at me over the lamp. He didn’t ask, and I was grateful, and angry that I was.
“Who’s the bandit?” said Deacon.
“One bandit,” I said. “Same road. Same crate. She never fights the guards, she just walks up and takes it.” I closed the book. “You don’t hire a bandit like that. You issue one.”
Nobody said what we all knew. Rook put a chicken in my lap, which is how she says a thing is bad.

We carried it down to the cellar the next morning, because it was too heavy to carry anywhere else. Miss V read it standing up. She turned each page fast, then slower, then stopped at the fifth violet stripe and set her hand flat across it, like she was holding it down.
“Eleven,” she said.
“Eleven,” said Deacon. “Every one of them pending.”
She didn’t answer. She stood very still, and I watched her face do something between relief and being sick. It wasn’t what I’d expected from someone who’d asked for a crate. Somebody wanted this book a great deal more than they wanted what was in the crate.
“Thank you,” she said. It was the first time. She paid double and didn’t count it, and Deacon, who counts everything, didn’t either, which is how I knew the room had changed.
She took the book through the door behind the racks and shut it.
“Don’t go back to that depot,” she said through the wood.
Four Six
Some days later, in the east tower.
The post is quiet. That’s good. Quiet means nothing to report.
I write it on the wall every morning, and I rub out the old marks and draw them again, because the chalk goes and the count has to stay right. 1,418. I keep the count because someone has to.
The papers come under the bucket on Tuesdays. Form 46-C. STANDING PATROL. RECOVER MARKED PROPERTY FROM CONVOY. NO REPORT REQUIRED. There’s never a name where the name goes. I stopped looking for one.
When the paper comes, I go. I don’t remember going. I remember the paper, and then I remember the crate in my arms and the buzzing in my knee going quiet like a hand over a mouth. Between those, nothing. A day gone. My boots dusty with a road I don’t remember walking.
Some mornings the cot is made and I don’t recall making it. Some mornings the crate is gone and a new one is there, and I feel strong as a girl. I tell myself the Bureau sends supply. That’s what it is. Supply.
My name was on a tag on my desk. The tag is on a desk in a corridor in a building I can’t find any more. I try to see the letters. They have the shape of letters, and that’s all I get. Four Six is what’s left. It’s a good name for a post.
Across the corridor from me there was a Four Seven. We never met. Opposite shifts. I came in and her chair would still be warm. Once, at the change, I saw her from behind, going down the hall with a coat over her arm, and something in the way she walked was tired in a way I understood. I knew that walk when it came round the hut with a rifle. I don’t know why I said her number. I think I wanted someone to know it was still mine.
Four people came to the tower once while I was away. I know because of the tea. There was a cup of it on the crate, gone cold, and it smelled like a kitchen. The shards don’t need tea. I held it a long time. I drank it in the end, and it was the best thing I’d put in my mouth in four years.
This Tuesday the paper was different.
MAINTENANCE SUSPENDED PENDING REVIEW.
I read it eleven times. Pending is a long word for something to be left holding.
My knee has started to click again. I put the paper up on the wall under the tally, and below it, in careful letters, I wrote NOTHING TO REPORT.
1,419.
Sara
I tore one page out of the ledger before we gave it to Miss V. I don’t know why. I didn’t tell anyone. It’s been folded in my jacket for six days, behind Gasket’s notebook.
Miss V said not to go back to the depot. She never said anything about the tower.
I’d been thinking about the cup. Four Six had a tin cup on a nail, washed and upside down, and I’d left a cup of tea on her crate. I wanted to know if she drank it. It’s a stupid reason to drive thirty miles. I told the others I wanted to see what Renova had done since the ledger went missing, and Deacon said “That’s a reason,” in the voice he uses when it isn’t. They all came. I hadn’t asked them to. Spank brought a pie nobody had asked for.
The Foundry Road gate was the same as it had been. Two towers, a rope across the road, and Tobin asleep in his chair under the awning with his hat over his face. I woke him with my boot.
“I don’t know anything,” he said. “That’s how I’m alive.”
“The east tower.”
“She’s in a mood,” he said, which was more than he’d ever said. “Two coins.”
“For what?”
“For me not knowing you’re here.” He took the coins and put his hat back over his face.
We went up. The stairs were dark. At the top, the door to the guard room stood open, and a voice came out of it, flat and gentle, like someone reading to a child.
“Halt. This is a restricted post.”
She stood in the middle of the room in her old guard’s coat, with her feet square and her hands at her sides. Her knee was locked straight and her right hand shook against her leg. The crate wasn’t at the head of the cot. She was standing guard over the place where it had been.
“Four Six,” I said.
“Four Seven.” She said it without any warmth at all. “You’re off your shift.”
“I’m not on shift.”
“Then you’re trespassing.”
Spank had come up behind me. “Hi!” he said, which was the worst thing he could have done.
She took him by the collar in one hand and put him against the wall, hard, without seeming to have moved. He made a noise like a kicked sack. The pie went across the floor.
“Let him go,” said Rook.
“You robbed a convoy on the Foundry Road.”
“We did,” I said.
“That was Renova property.”
“It was.”
“Then you’re thieves,” said Four Six, “and I’m a guard.”
Her voice hadn’t risen. That was the frightening part. She had Spank pinned with one hand, and I could see she’d do whatever came next the way she’d read a page. I thought of the long gun, and I knew I wasn’t going to use it.
I took the page out of my jacket instead.
“Who sends you the slips?” I said.
Something moved in her face. “That is not your business.”
“Look at the box.”
I held it up. It was a ledger page, blue stamp in the corner, a column of tiny boxes down the side. The last one said SUPERVISOR’S INITIALS. It was empty.
She looked at it for a long time. Then, without letting go of Spank, she reached under the cot with her other hand and drew out a tin. It was full of papers. She laid one on the floor beside my page and put her boot on it. FORM 46-C. STANDING PATROL. RECOVER MARKED PROPERTY FROM CONVOY. Down the side, the same boxes. The last one was empty.
“They get initialled in the morning,” she said.
“I sat across from you for three years,” I said. “I never saw one filled. Not mine. Not yours. Not ever. It’s a box. It’s there so a person who isn’t there can say they checked.”
She let go of Spank. He slid down the wall and said, “I’m fine,” to the pie, which is how I knew he wasn’t.
“I never looked,” said Four Six. Her hand was shaking harder. She pressed it flat against her leg. “I don’t remember going. When the paper comes. I remember the paper and then I remember the crate.”
“I know.”
“How do you know?”
“I think it’s been done to you for a very long time.”
“The post is never left.” She said it quickly, like a child saying a lesson. “The post is never left.”
“They closed it,” I said. “Nobody told you. I’m telling you.”
She looked at me. For a moment I thought she’d hit me, and I’d have let her.
Then her knee went.
It went with a snap, and she dropped, and Spank had her before she touched the floor. She hung in his arms. Her face had gone grey. Under her coat the plate on her forearm flickered violet, then dim, then violet.
“There’s been no crate,” she said into his shoulder. “Nine days. No crate. They stopped.”
“We know a place,” I said. “Somebody there who might help.”
“I can’t leave the post.”
“Then don’t leave it. Go on patrol. A patrol goes out, and comes back.”
She was silent a long time. Rook picked up the pie and set it on the cot. Deacon stood in the doorway with his hands in his pockets, looking for once like he had nothing to say.
“A patrol,” said Four Six at last.
“A patrol.”
“I’ll take the cup.”
“Take the cup.”
She reached up to the nail and lifted it down. She held it a moment, upside down, the way you’d hold something alive. Then she put it in her coat, and let Spank walk her down the stairs, and told him, quite clearly, that if he dropped her she’d have to kill him.
“Yes, ma’am,” said Spank.
I stayed at the top a moment after the others had gone. The cot was made. The wall was white where the chalk had been rubbed out and redrawn. I picked up the slip she’d left on the floor, FORM 46-C, and folded it into my jacket with the other page.
Deacon
We took her back to the shed. She wouldn’t come inside. She stood in the yard all night in her coat with her feet square and her hand shakin’, and told Rook it was a patrol and she’d be observin’ the perimeter. Rook gave her a chair. Four Six looked at it as if it had made a rude remark. I put a blanket on it anyway. In the mornin’ it was folded on the seat, square at the corners, which I counted as a yes.
“She needs parts,” says Sara, in the mornin’. “Not Miss V’s. Real ones. Renova hardware needs Renova parts.”
“She’s a soldier,” says Spank. “She’s got a soldier’s subscription.”
“She’s got nothing. She’s got a plate on her arm and a number on the plate. That’s all they left her.”
I put my hand up. I’d been waitin’ a long time to be useful in a way that didn’t involve a ditch. “I’ve got money,” I says. “More than I know what to do with. I’ll buy her one. A year, up front, same as anybody.”
Sara looked at me like I’d given her a bird. “You’d do that?”
“I’d do it twice. I’ve a gift for bein’ ignored by clerks.”
I wrote the number off her forearm plate on the back of my hand, and I put on my best jacket and went to Renova Subscriptions and Retention in the Market Belt.
It’s got plastic lilies. I want ya to know that. There’s a lobby full of plastic lilies, and a fountain that runs a thin pink water I’ll go to my grave swearin’ wasn’t water, and a girl at a desk in a violet blouse with a badge that said QUILL. “Welcome to Renova!” she says. “Are you looking to upgrade, renew or reactivate?”
“Reactivate.”
“Name of account holder?”
“Four Six.”
“Surname?”
“Six.”
“And first name?”
“Four.”
She typed that in without blinkin’. I’ll say this for Renova, they’ve got ya trained. The screen thought a long time. “I’m so sorry,” says Quill. “I can’t find anyone by that name.”
I read her the number off my hand. She typed it. The screen thought longer.
“That serial isn’t assigned to anyone.”
“It’s on her arm.”
“Then it’s on her arm in error.”
“She’s holdin’ up a tower.”
“I’m sure she is.” Her smile didn’t move. Her eyes did. “Sir, I’d like to help you, I would. But I can’t take payment on an account that doesn’t exist. It would create a record.”
“A record of what?”
“Of a person,” says Quill, quite softly, “who isn’t there.”
I laid a stack of money on her desk. A good one, enough to buy her a boat. She looked at it the way ya look at a snake that’s been left on yer chair. Then she looked at the door, and at the camera over the door, and at me.
“If you know where the property is, sir,” she says, “you should tell us. For its own safety.”
“Property.”
“Please take a seat. A Reclamation Associate will be right with you.”
There’s a thing I know about myself. I’ve got two instincts. One’s for money and one’s for bein’ out of a room, and the second one’s never once been wrong. I took my money, said thank ya very much, and was through the plastic lilies and halfway across the Belt before she’d finished sayin’ “right with you.”
Behind me the lobby speakers started to play a tune. It was cheerful. It’s the cheerful ones ya have to watch.
Spank
They come that same evening, at dusk, to the shed, in a van painted violet with the smilin’ hand on the side. Six fingers, same as the depot. They had speakers on the roof, and the speakers were playin’ a jingle.
We’ll make it right, we’ll make it right, whatever you’ve lost, we’ll make it right!
I’ll be dead before I forget that tune. There was a fella that sung it, and a lady who sung it back, and in between they had a little trumpet. I hummed it for two days after the whole thing was over and I never once meant to.
Four of ‘em got out. Violet blazers, name tags, clipboards. Trent, Brenda, Kyle, and a big smilin’ one called Mr. Dunmore, who had the biggest clipboard and a way of standin’ like the yard was his.
“Good evening!” says Dunmore. “We’re from Reclamation. We believe you have something of ours.”
We was all in the yard. Rook had the Biscuit across the gate. Sara was up on the shed roof with the long gun. Deacon stood next to me with a ladle he’d taken from Orrin’s for reasons he hadn’t explained. And Four Six stood at the end of the yard in her old guard’s coat, holdin’ perimeter, with her knee locked and her hand shakin’ and her face like a shut door.
“We ain’t got nothin’ of yours,” I says.
“Records indicate a Renova asset on these premises. Serial scrubbed. Condition poor. We’re here to collect it, with thanks.”
“She’s a person.”
“Records indicate otherwise.” He had a form. He held it out toward Four Six. “If you’d just sign here, to release the asset, I think we can all be home for supper.”
Four Six looked at it. Then she took one step forward. And I watched her read the top of it. FORM 46-C. The same blue stamp.
“That is my paper,” she said.
“It is,” said Dunmore pleasantly. “We issue those. Very reliable.”
“The Bureau issues those.”
“There’s no Bureau, dear.” He said it kind. That was the worst of it. “There’s us. There always was. You’ve been a wonderful asset. I want you to know we’re grateful.”
I seen her face. I’d like to say I didn’t.
“I was not an asset,” said Four Six. “I was a post.”
“Brenda,” says Dunmore.
Brenda was holdin’ a net. She threw it. It was a good throw, and it caught me and the chicken Rook had brung out for reasons of her own, and the two of us went down in a heap in the dirt, and the chicken said what I was thinkin’.
After that it was all noise.
Kyle come at Deacon with a cattle prod with a bow on it. Deacon hit him with the ladle. Deacon hit a man with a ladle and won, and I’ll be tellin’ it till I die. Trent went for the shed, and Sara’s first shot took the heel off his boot and her second took the jingle off the left speaker, and the jingle went on playin’ from the right.
We’ll make it right!
“I hate this song!” Sara shouted. It’s the first time I ever heard her yell.
I got out of the net with a lot of cussin’ and part of my shirt. Rook swung the Biscuit round and took the van’s front bumper off, and the van sat down like a dog. Dunmore stood in the yard holdin’ his clipboard. He’d stopped smilin’. He’s got a different face under it. It’s a face like a locked door.
And Four Six hit him.
I never seen anything move like that. It wasn’t fast. It was exact. She picked a spot on his jaw and put her fist there, and Dunmore took one step backward and sat down in the dirt with his eyes goin’ two ways. She stood over him with her fist still shut and read the form, which she’d taken out of his hand somehow, all the way down. Then she tore it in half, and put the halves in her pocket.
Then her knee went.
It went all at once, a sound like a bolt shearin’ off. She went down on the dirt and couldn’t get up. Trent had come round with the prod. I seen the bow on it. I seen the little blue spark on the end.
I don’t remember decidin’ nothin’. I was just on top of her, with my arms round her head and my back to him, and I thought well, that’s how it’ll be, and I waited for it.
Rook run over the van.
It’s the only way I can say it. She put the Biscuit on the van’s nose and she just kept goin’, and the roof speakers folded in half, and the jingle went up into a screech and stopped in the middle of we’ll make. In the quiet you could hear Trent drop the prod.
They left. Dunmore left on foot, holdin’ his jaw, and Brenda took him by the arm. Kyle looked at his clipboard like it had let him down. Nobody said nothin’. One of ‘em dropped a badge in the dirt. I picked it up later. It said HAPPY TO HELP.
I stayed where I was. Four Six lay under me, starin’ up at the sky, and she was shakin’ all over.
“Is it done?” she says.
“It’s done.”
“I didn’t ask the right questions.”
“You done fine.”
She turned her head. “Who are you?”
“Spank.”
“Spank,” she says, like she was fillin’ in a form. “I’m Four Six. I have nothing to report.”
I took her hand. Nobody else was gonna.
Sara
I knelt down in the dirt beside her. Her plate was hot. The violet slit in it was dim and flickering, and I thought, That’s a candle in a draught. There’s a particular way to hold someone’s hand when you can’t say a thing, and I know every way to do it.
“Tell me the time,” said Four Six.
“Dusk.”
“I missed the change.” She tried to sit up. “There’s no one on the post.”
“There’s no change.”
“There has to be a change. Somebody has to relieve me. It’s the rule.” She said it the way a child says a lesson, quickly, so it can’t fall apart. “A post is never left. A post is handed over. It is handed over at the post.”
I’d been carrying that sentence for four years. I looked at Spank, and Spank looked at me, and nobody said anything.
“Rook,” I said. “Is the Biscuit still running?”
We drove her thirty miles in the dark. Spank held her in the back seat with her head on his shoulder, and she kept murmuring state your business, state your business until Deacon took her other hand and said, “Business is we’re takin’ ya home, love,” which I’d never heard him say to anyone.
Tobin was asleep in his chair at the bottom of the east tower with his hat over his face. He didn’t stir when we carried her past. I didn’t expect him to.
We laid her on the cot. Deacon stood in the corner with the ladle, trying to look like he wasn’t there. I stood at the foot of the bed, the way I’d been taught, and I put my heels together.
“Post Four Six,” I said. “Four Seven relieves you.”
She looked at me. Her eyes did something I’d never seen a Lapsed’s do. They came back.
“Four Seven relieves Four Six,” she said. “Post state is quiet.”
“I have the post.”
“Nothing to report.” Her voice went. She said it again, smaller. “Nothing to report.”
“Then you’re relieved.”
She laid her head back. Her mouth opened and no sound came, and then she was crying, the way you cry when you’ve held something so long you’ve forgotten what it’s made of. I put my hand on her forehead. I didn’t say anything. I’d have said anything.
“Go and rest,” I said. “I have the line.”
There’s a bell on the east tower. An old iron one, on the landing, rusted green at the lip. The guards used it to say the gate was closing.
I went up. I put my hand on the rope. My hands shook on it. I made them stop.
I took the rope in both hands and pulled.
The bell is loud. I’d forgotten how loud a bell is. It rang out over the gate and the road and the whole black stretch of the Foundry flats, and it kept ringing, because I couldn’t make my arms stop. I rang it for her. I rang it for everyone it hadn’t been rung for. I rang until my palms were open and my shoulders burned and the whole town must have heard, and when I finally let go the rope swung on by itself.
Below me, Tobin sat up in his chair and watched the bell swing. He looked at it a long time. For once he didn’t put his hat back over his face.
Rook and Deacon took her to Varkatech that night. Miss V met them at the hatch in her shirtsleeves, looked at the plate, and went white. Then she said, “Bring her down,” and Rook told me afterward that Miss V had looked like she’d been waiting for it. They put new parts in her until morning. Miss V never presented a bill. “I’d like her alive,” she said. That’s all.
Spank
It was a clear night, so Sara and me stayed on the tower roof a while after.
Rook had took the Biscuit to Varkatech. Tobin had gone back to sleep in his chair like nothin’ had happened, which I was startin’ to think was the smartest thing anybody did.
Sara had her back to the wall and her knees up. She hadn’t said a word since the bell. Her hands were wrapped in rag and she was holdin’ them like they belonged to someone else.
“You rang it,” I said, because I couldn’t think of nothin’ better.
She laughed. It wasn’t a laugh.
“I mean it was good. It was real loud. I heard it from the road.”
“It was a long time coming,” said Sara. She was lookin’ at the stars like she hated ‘em. “I told you the rest wasn’t tonight. I think it is.”
I didn’t say nothin’. I’ve learned that part.
“At the Bureau,” she said. “At Skywatch. We had forty bells. Out along the edge of the Drift, one for every settlement the fall could reach. Renova ran them. Everyone thought it was a service. You pulled a lever at your desk and a bell rang in the town and people went down the hole. That was my job. Three years of it. I’d have been good at it if I’d been allowed.”
“You rung ‘em.”
“I rang every one. Nineteen falls. Never missed.” She wiped her face with the back of a wrapped hand and looked at the rag like she was surprised. “Then one morning there was a slip on my desk. Just a slip. HOLD.”
I felt it before she said it. I don’t know how.
“The screen said forty minutes. A big one. Coming down on a place called Dunmarrow. A mill town, about two hundred people. I sent up a query. Another slip came back. HOLD PENDING REVIEW.” Her voice was flat. She said it like she was readin’ it off a card. “I sat there. Forty minutes. I watched the number on the screen go down and I had my hand on the lever. I could have broken the glass. I could’ve walked out of the room and rung it myself. I had every chance.”
“Sara.”
“I held. I did what I was told. I was good at it.” She stopped. Her mouth shook, and she pressed her lips together to stop it. “I never found out why. There was a skiff overhead that day. I think they wanted the fall clean. I think someone wanted something I’ll never find out. I stopped wanting to know.”
The wind went across the tower. A long way off, somethin’ howled and thought better of it.
“Dunmarrow’s gone,” she said. “It’s a hole now. They put a sign on it. I went and read the sign.”
I’d taken her hand without noticin’. It was the rag one. I could feel her fingers under it.
“I had a brother. Dave. Seventeen. He’d taken a job at the mill that spring and he didn’t tell me. The letters went to my old place. I found three of them after.” She had one in her jacket. I could see the corner of it. She took it out. It was soft as cloth. “The last one says, You’d like it here. It’s quiet. They’ve got a bell.”
She stopped.
I’ve seen a lot of folks go. I seen Gasket go. I seen the sky come down on whole wards. I never seen Sara break, not in all the months, not when I thought she was gonna. She’d always been the one thing that held. And I watched it go, quiet, like a dam givin’ out in the dark. Her whole face come apart. Her shoulders shook. She couldn’t breathe right. She put the letter against her mouth and made a sound I’ve never heard a person make, and I thought, that’s what it sounds like when you’ve kept it in four years.
“I left that night,” she said, into the letter. “I put my badge face down on the desk. The guard said Night. That’s all. That’s my whole resignation. They never even noticed. It was weeks before anyone asked where Four Seven was. They thought I was sick.”
“Sara.”
“I killed them. I didn’t pull a lever.”
“No.”
“Two hundred people. Dave. I had my hand on it.”
“No.” I got my arms round her. I’m not a strong man. I don’t know much. I held on anyway, and she let me, and her whole body shook against mine like she was tryin’ to get out of it. “Sara, no. Listen. You ain’t a bell.”
She made a sound.
“They had a slip. They had a skiff. They had a whole building tellin’ you what to do and what not to, with a guard to say good night. That ain’t you. That’s them.” I was cryin’ too, by then. I didn’t mind. “I call ‘em early. Ever’ time. I got it wrong by a day once and they put it on a plaque. I’d rather be early a thousand times. If I’m wrong a thousand times, then I’m wrong a thousand times, and ever’body’s alive on the thousand and first.”
She went still against me.
“I’d never hold it, Sara. Never. I ain’t able. I ain’t got that in me.”
“I know.” It was almost nothing. “That’s why I said it to you.”
I didn’t say anything. She held on to my shirt with both hands, and we sat there under the stars while the tower went cold, and after a long time she said, in a small, wet voice, “Don’t ever stop being early.”
“I won’t.”
“Even if it’s wrong.”
“Especially.”
She laughed, a real one that cracked in the middle, and wiped her face on my sleeve. “That’s disgusting. You’ve got chicken on you.”
“It’s a requirement.”
“Shut up, Spank.”
I thought about what I’d said once. Renova don’t ring no bells. Renova just turns up, like a rash. I’d said it like a joke, and she’d been listenin’.
I put my chin on top of her head. She let me.
We stayed up there till the cold made us go down.

Rook came back for us a little before midnight, with the Biscuit and a chicken on the dash, and she didn’t say a word about our faces. Four Six was asleep in the cellar under a lot of violet light, she said, and Miss V had told her to go home and quit hoverin’. Deacon had stayed to watch.
We rode the thirty miles home with the windows down. Nobody talked. Sara kept her head against the glass, and I kept my eyes on the road so I wouldn’t look at her.
It was past midnight when we got to the shed. Everybody else had gone to bed or gone to the cellar. The one lamp was burnin’ in the yard, low, and Sara walked across the dirt like a woman on a deck. She didn’t go to the shed door. She went to the cot by the wall, sat down on the edge of it, and looked at the jar on the crate. She’d kept it there all this time, where she’d see it first thing.
I stood by the pump with my hands hangin’. I didn’t know what to do with ‘em. “I’ll let ya sleep,” I says.
“Spank.”
“Yeah?”
“Stay.”
I’d have walked into the Scar if she’d said it that way. I sat down on the crate by the jar, with my knees up round my ears like a grasshopper. She looked at me a while.
“That’s stupid. Sit on the cot.”
I sat on the end of it, stiff as a plank. She looked at me again, like I was a puzzle she’d decided to finish. Then she lay down and put her head in my lap.
I didn’t move. I don’t think I breathed. My hands went up in the air like somebody’d pointed a gun at me.
“Put them down,” she says, with her eyes shut.
I put one on the blanket. The other one I put, real careful, on her shoulder.
“Dave would’ve liked you,” she said, after a while.
“Yeah?” I says.
“He talked too much. He’d tell a stranger his whole life by the end of one bus ride. I used to want to hide.” She drew a breath. “I’d give a lot to be embarrassed by him one more time.”
I looked for somethin’ good to say and I didn’t find it. “I ain’t got nothin’ good,” I says.
“Then say the bad thing,” she says.
“I’m real glad I embarrass you. Ever’ day.”
She laughed, short and sweet. “You do,” she says. Then, quieter, “Thank you.”
I didn’t ask what for. She reached up and took hold of my arm, the one on her shoulder, and pulled it down across her and held it against her chest, the way you’d hold a pillow you meant to keep.
The lamp burned down. Out past the shed somethin’ rustled and went away. I stayed so still my leg started to go.
“Stay till I’m asleep,” she said.
“I’ll stay.”
“Don’t make it weird.”
“I ain’t.”
She was quiet. Her breath slowed, and her weight settled, and her grip on my arm went on a long while. Somewhere in there it loosened and let go. The jar on the crate caught what was left of the lamplight.
I sat there a long while after, to be sure.
Forty one days I’d sat in Gasket’s seat waitin’ for somebody to come and take it off me. Before that, years of standin’ out in the open callin’ falls for folks who never learned my name, and I liked it fine. I figured that was what I was for. A fella stands out front so ever’body else can get down the hole. Nobody ever turned round and stood in front of me.
Then a big man in a bar said my name like a joke, and she put him through a table. I’d spent days tryin’ to work out what I’d done to earn it, and I never found nothin’. That was the part I couldn’t get over. I hadn’t done a thing. She’d just decided.
I thought about the last line in Gasket’s notebook. Those two. Dear God. I’d laughed at it. He’d seen it comin’ before either of us had a word for it, and he’d left it in a glove box for whoever come next.
I’d never had somethin’ I was scared to break. I didn’t know that was a thing a man could be.
When I finally slid out from under her I did it a half inch at a time, and I put the rolled blanket under her head where my lap had been, and pulled the cover up and tugged it straight. I bent down and put my mouth to her hair, once, so light she’d never know. Then I said it, low, right by her ear, hardly a sound at all.
“I’ll be early for you. Ever’ time. Even if I’m wrong.”
She didn’t stir. She was gone, her breath goin’ slow and even. I stayed where I was a second longer, just lookin’.
Then I went across the yard, and I told the pump goodnight. It’s a habit now.
Sara
Four Six came out of Varkatech four days later in a new knee and a new hand, and she looked at the Biscuit like it had spoken to her.
“Where do I report?” she said.
“To me,” I said.
“What’s the post?”
“There isn’t one. There’s a truck.”
She looked at it for a long time. “There’s no room.”
Rook said, “Front bench has three, back row’s got Deacon. Roof’s got chickens.”
“I’ll stand.”
“You can’t stand in a moving vehicle.”
“I can,” said Four Six. She said it in the voice of someone reading to a child, and I knew we’d lost the argument.
She rode out of Varkatech on the running board with her new hand gripping the mirror and her face turned into the wind. She refused every offer of a seat. When Spank tried to lend her his coat she said, “I have a coat,” and she did, the old guard coat, patched, and the lantern on its button caught the sun.
Before we left, she took a piece of Rook’s chalk and went to the Biscuit’s door. Under the red paint that said FRESH MEAT SQUAD she drew a tally mark. One.
“Day one,” said Four Six.
“Of what?” said Deacon.
She considered it. “I don’t know yet.”
Spank started the engine. Four Six lifted her face. And the sky over the Foundry Road, which had been grey for a week, did something I can’t describe, and went the pale gold of the inside of a cup.
Rook honked at it. I leaned my head against the glass. And a hand, which wasn’t mine to ask for, slid across the bench and found mine, and I let it stay.
Nothing to report.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Aava
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Aava is a young woman of the old Molten Imperium who keeps a ledger and a lonely post on the Gate Road when the hunters find her in the dead city. She gives no family name.
What the story shows

Takes the party in after dark to a Gate-warden’s tower with a rope ladder and a hundred and twelve steps. The room at the top is swept, and she waters a patch of moss on the windowsill with a spoonful of water a week (Chapter 8: What the Stars Left).
Explains why the survivors of the city cannot simply leave: the Foundry holds the warmth, the Wellhouse holds the water, and no one is left who can build a hull (Chapter 8: What the Stars Left).
Says she lived inside the Imperium so long that she thought it was hers, and that she wishes its victims had been “a little less right about me” (Chapter 8: What the Stars Left).
Is fed by Varesa every ninth day in exchange for a count of who passes along the Gate Road. She names the Vigil and says she is not one of them (Chapter 8: What the Stars Left).
Walks Atver to the cistern road, then draws the road, the plaza and the Auditors’ Gallery in the dirt for Vael (Chapter 8: What the Stars Left).
Sends the party into the dead city with weighed rations, a candle stub and a tin lid (Chapter 9: What the Numbers Hide).
A year on, works as a handler at Ragnik’s inn with a brass pin on her collar, and the moss has outgrown its cup. She hears Vael’s father’s name and says she will gather some information first (Chapter 11: What the Ink Keeps).

Habits
Keeps a ledger and counts everything twice. Gives out food in measured portions.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Atver
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Atver is a short elf in burgundy robes with a brass monocle. He looks about thirty-five and has the eyes of someone much older. He reads while others panic.
What the story shows

Arrives in the Dracol plan to warn that the beast is intelligent and drawn to fear (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Catches Vael with flight magic after the fight. He has spent about two hundred and forty years, on and off, working on a lead about why the Dracol is the way it is (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Knows the old Molten Imperium and believes the Dracol went there. He joins the party and says only enough to keep them moving (Chapter 5: What We Carry).
Never seems to sleep. Calls the young “child” (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Speaks of a dear friend and student who led the Concord and tried to warn it (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Uses the monocle as an analyzer and cast “Let gravity forget” (Chapter 7: What Floats and What Falls).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Figo
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Figo is a huge, armored warrior with a gruff manner and a surprisingly big heart. His axe, Sheela, is his wife.
What the story shows

Takes Vael to the training grounds, and insists on the right way to speak about Sheela (Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past).
Survived a Dracol attack on his village years ago. The ballista malfunctioned and many died. He shivers whenever the word comes up (Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past).
Taken down by Framedious venom, saved by the tapilca honey (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
Shouts a tavern full of panic into silence, and throws James into the air in the Dracol fight with “Say less, drunkard” (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Sleeps flat on the bare ground, holding Sheela (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Discovers he is afraid of heights (Chapter 7: What Floats and What Falls).

Habits
Skins and loots every kill (“These will be useful for the guild”). Tells long, improbable fishing stories.
Relationships
Trista steadies him when he is afraid. Vael is the new recruit he claims not to care about.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Jade
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Jade rules Skygate, a thriving village with an elevator to the High Sky Islands. She wears storm-colored battle robes and a dark metal circlet, and she is James’s older sister.
What the story shows

Is surprised and delighted when James walks in (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Knew Saela and hunted with her. She gives Vael her ring (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Is a member of the Molten Vigil and tells Vael so in private. She believes the Vigil can be rebuilt as something that serves people (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Warns him not to trust Varesa fully (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Asks the party to find her missing soldier expedition (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

Family
She is the one who pulled a six-year-old James out of a tree. She has heard nothing from Mira, and only rumors of Finn.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: James
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
James is a lazy, loud and chaotic member of the Hunter’s Guild who seems to take nothing seriously. His gut, he insists, is never wrong.
What the story shows

Recruits Vael on a hunch (Chapter 1: The Ash and the Echo).
Reveals that he can see probabilities when he looks at a person, and that most of what he sees is bad. He drinks to take the edge off (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
Lets Loren go with a coin, a map to a magic school and a promise, over Trista’s anger (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Is the younger brother of Jade, one of about twenty children who grew up together in a home that has since closed (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

Powers
Dark magic: shadow dust, dark orbs, summoned swords and the spell “Endarken” (Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past, Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Habits
Gives people nicknames (“Jadey”, “Mr. Skyman”, “Burney”). Bows to Varesa and calls her “my love” (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark). In Skygate his cask goes untouched (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Relationships
Figo throws him into the air in battle. Trista heals him and loses patience with him. Jade is his sister. He has not heard from his other siblings since before the Starfall.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Laren
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Laren was Loren’s twin. The night before the Starfall they lay in the grass under the stars and promised to become traders, to lift their family out of debt.
He died under a fallen roof beam while Loren tried to free him (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Loren
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Loren is a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old boy who survived the Starfall and lost his twin, Laren, to it. Grief woke a fire magic he cannot control.
He killed a trader who grabbed him on the road, then took the man’s goods to keep a promise he and Laren made as boys. The party finds him on the road toward the High Sky Islands. James frees him, giving him a coin, a map to a school for magic and a promise to never kill an innocent again (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Ragnik
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Ragnik is the one-armed owner of the Hunter’s Guild Inn at Hunter’s Rest. He looks like a veteran mercenary and acts like a gentle host.
What the story shows

Gives Vael a bed and the name “V” (Chapter 1: The Ash and the Echo).
Keeps four rooms ready because something in him says danger is coming (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
His wife Zefra died in the Starfall. He has kept his door open ever since (Chapter 5: What We Carry).
Takes in Raul, leads the caravan south, and tells Vael: “My wife gave her life so yours could continue” (Chapter 5: What We Carry).

Relationships
Rebecca runs the front house. Raul is his adopted son.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Raul
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Raul is a quiet boy whose father died in the Dracol fight. Ragnik promised the man he would take his son in, and he keeps that promise (Chapter 5: What We Carry).
He sits apart from the others as the tavern empties until Vael sits beside him. He leaves with Rebecca and Ragnik (Chapter 5: What We Carry).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Rebecca
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Rebecca is the warm and unflappable woman who runs the front of Ragnik’s tavern. She welcomes every refugee and never flinches (Chapter 1: The Ash and the Echo, Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
She was already working for Ragnik on the day of the Starfall and was the one he trusted to help the wounded (Chapter 5: What We Carry). She leaves with the caravan, with Raul at her side (Chapter 5: What We Carry).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Saela
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Saela was a hunter and a Dragodor. She is a voice in Vael’s dreams and then in his memory: “You must defeat the Dracol… You are our only hope, my child… I love you, son” (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Jade remembers her in spotless white robes, a brilliant tactician who followed a plan even when she should have adapted. In the months before she left Jade’s hunting group, years before the Starfall, she kept saying the Pattern was fraying (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers). Vael’s father is unknown.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Sheela
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content: Sheela is Figo’s axe, and his wife. Insulting her is not recommended (Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past). He kisses her before a fight and sleeps with her in his arms.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Trista
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Trista is a healer in white robes with a staff and a lot of patience, most of it spent on James.
What the story shows

Her glitter bombs slow and stun, her light heals, and “May our wounds curse our enemies” turns a wound back on its giver (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
Tells Vael he is a Dragodor, and explains the Shadow Wolf is only the first of his powers (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Once belonged to a group that worshipped Lumia. She admired Lumia’s belief that everyone deserves a chance at life. She left when the group began extorting villages (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
Is furious when James lets Loren go (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
Her healing and calming light steadies Figo before the Dracol fight (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).

Relationships
She pretends to dislike James but relies on him. She is fond of Sheela and complains about Figo’s laziness.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Vael
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Vael is a young man, twenty-one at the Starfall, who woke in a tavern bed with no memory of who he was. He is the story’s point of view and the newest member of Ragnik’s hunting party.
What the story shows

Found alone and unconscious in the crater after the Starfall, and brought to Ragnik’s inn (Chapter 1: The Ash and the Echo).
Called “V” until his name came back to him on the road (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
His body knows things his mind does not: he dodges before he thinks, and he calls a shadow out of his own hand sign.

Powers

Hand signs call three summons: the Shadow Wolf (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers), the Spirit Bird and the Flesh Toad (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
The Ring of Eons, given to him by Jade, turns part of his own magic into a concentrated blast (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

Heritage

Trista names him a Dragodor (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark). A voice he hears in dreams is his mother, Saela.
Jade tells him about Saela, and that she knew no other Dragodor. His father is unknown (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).
He feels an unexplained hatred toward the old Celestial Concord (Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers).

Relationships
James, Figo, Trista and Atver are his party. Ragnik gave him his first home after the Starfall. Varesa watches him from the shadows.
See also
His champion kit is on Vael.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Zefra
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Zefra was Ragnik’s wife. On the day of the Starfall she told him the world was ending and walked out to fight, asking him to hold the bunker door (Chapter 5: What We Carry).
She did not come back. Three warriors carried an unharmed young man to Ragnik, and told him she had given herself to save people. Ragnik later tells Vael her life bought his (Chapter 5: What We Carry).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Champampa
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Champampas are small, rose-furred, tool-using creatures with long ears and lashing tails. They wear belts of braided grass hung with cord, flint and thorn. They speak in a soft chant of que, que, que, and they bow in rustling waves when their elder passes. They carry fire in cupped hands.
What the story shows

They are thieves in great numbers. A great many of them took Figo’s axe, and he was never able to stop them.
A colony is organised: terraces, shrines, bridges, and an elder whose fur has gone silver at the muzzle and who wears a woven circlet. Authority is hereditary.
They are not hostile. They carry Sheela in a slow procession, light a river of small flames for guests, and lead them on through a curtain of woven grass (Chapter 7: What Floats and What Falls).
Atver has wanted to see a Champampa court for as long as he can remember.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Aftermath/Creatures/Creatures of The Aftermath.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Creatures of The Aftermath
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Creatures of The Aftermath
The animals the hunters meet in the first months after the Starfall. Return to The Aftermath.
Hunted for the guild

Dagaruma: the pack hunters of the trade routes.
Framedious: the five-limbed beast with a mouth in its belly.
Dracol: the colossal winged hunter in obsidian plate.

Hunted for the cure

Davoura: the small climbers that guard the Tapil trees.
Tapilca: the honey-bearing flower that cures Framedious venom.

Of the High Sky

Varkador: the iron-feathered hunter of the islands.
Champampa: the small fire-bearing creatures of the hidden colonies.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Dagaruma
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
Dagaruma are scaled, low-slung hunters that move in packs with a patient, liquid grace. Their weapons are their claws and their tails, and the tail is the real danger: the bite is unpleasant, but the tail is worse. They are coordinated and opportunistic. They test a circle for a gap, send some of the pack wide to flank, and leave one waiting low in the grass.
Why they are dangerous

Since the Starfall, most of the prey they once hunted is dead, and the stardust on the vegetation has poisoned the plants. The packs are hungry and desperate, and they have taken to the trade routes.
The guild’s record has them killing more people each year than any other creature. Figo calls them small fry, and James tells Vael not to believe him.
Their meat is foul. James claims not to explain how he knows.

What the story shows
Trista explains them to Vael on the road, and the party meets its first pack where four traders have formed a ring of spears around an abandoned wagon (Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Davoura
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
A Davoura is a small, quick tree-climber with a flicking tail and a habit of stuffing its cheeks full. It lives for the Tapil trees, eats their fruit, and hunts for Tapilca in particular, and it is fiercely territorial about the ones it has found.
What the story shows

Because Davoura always return to the Tapil trees, a hunter can follow one to the plant he needs. James teaches Vael this, and following one through a winter forest turns out to need skills neither of them has trained for.
A Davoura that senses it is followed will stop and watch, then bolt straight up the nearest trunk and vanish into the canopy.
When Vael finally finds the right Tapilca, the Davoura he followed bites the stem through and is gone up the tree before he can stop it (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Dracol
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
The Dracol is the largest hunter on the guild’s record: a winged beast armoured in black obsidian plates, with seams of molten light running beneath them. The seams brighten when it is hurt, and the plates grow back over its wounds faster than a party of hunters can break them. The tip of its tail ends in a single faceted diamond.
What the story shows

A Dracol should sleep through winter. The one that comes for Ragnik’s tavern does not, and the hunters call it the Raging Dracol because no normal Dracol moves the way it does (Chapter 4: The Raging Dark).
It follows the scent of living things, and a crowd draws it more strongly than a few people do. The hunters plan their whole defence around that.
Its roar is felt in the chest before it is heard. It can fly, and it can gather light in its throat and loose it as a beam.
Arrows, bolts and spells skip off its healing plates. The wounds that last are the ones that reach the dark channels between its chest plates.

Hunters
Vael believes he is the only one who can stand against it, and he does not yet know how. Varesa fights beside the hunters, and Trista keeps her calm while the plan is made.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Framedious
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
The Framedious walks on five limbs rooted around a face set in the centre of its belly: a wide, wet, lipless mouth ringed with teeth that curve inward. It stands quietly at the tree line, then leaps, and shows its underside only as it rises. Its scream is a frequency that fills the skull.
What the story shows

It is strong enough to split frozen mud when it lands, and fast enough to follow its first leap with a short, deadly arc of the fifth limb.
A wound from that limb does not stay a wound. A grey tinge spreads under the skin from the cut, slowly and on purpose, and it needs a cure.
James knows it by name the moment it appears. Trista slows it, Figo opens its flank, and Vael calls the first Shadow Wolf against it (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
The cure for its poison grows in the same forest, in the Tapilca that the Davoura guard.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Tapilca
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
A tapilca is a tapil that has had a full summer of sun and good nutrition. It grows larger than the others, and a golden, honey-like fluid begins to run from its center. That fluid is antivenom for most of what lives in the region, Framedious venom included.
The tree
The Tapil tree is pink all through, bark included, and its branches are covered in clusters of small flowers called tapils. The petals are a deep midnight blue with pink edges. Even in a forest the Starfall has left grey and dying, it stands out in the light of a clearing. Davoura live in its branches, eat the tapils, and hunt the tapilcas in particular.
What the story shows

James sends Vael to find one when Figo goes down with Framedious venom, and tells him to follow a Davoura to the right tree (Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers).
Vael finds one by its size and the bead of gold at its center, but a Davoura bites through the stem before he can pick it. James takes another from the branch.
Fed to Figo from the flower, the honey draws the grey back from his collar and deepens his breathing.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.title: Varkador
lore-and-stories/stories/the-aftermath/c.content:
The Varkador is a great winged hunter with slate-grey feathers that run iron-bright along the wings, and a hooked beak as long as a man’s arm. A single deep red feather, striped in black, stands proud along its crown. It moves with the dull hunger of an animal that has eaten well for a long time and is now eating more.
What the story shows

It lands with the sound of a felled tree, and the whole clearing shudders.
A Varkador in season leaves a trail that only a fool could miss. Atver tracks it by the damage it leaves, and notes that it has not eaten everything on its island, only everything it could see.
It does not shake off a man on its back easily, but when both its wings fail it drops like a stone.
Figo, Vael, Trista, James and Atver all fight it in the same clearing (Chapter 7: What Floats and What Falls), in the High Sky Regions.

The Aftermath
The story of Vael and his hunting party in the first months after the Starfall. Read in this order.
For everyone in the story, see the Cast of The Aftermath.
For the animals the hunters meet, see Creatures of The Aftermath.
Chapters

Chapter 1: The Ash and the Echo
Vael wakes in Ragnik’s tavern with no memory and meets the hunters who will become his team.
Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past
Figo introduces Vael to Sheela, and the first Dagaruma hunt begins.
Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers
A Framedious attack, the first Shadow Wolf, and a name found. Part 1: The Framedious. Part 2: The Tapilca.
Chapter 4: The Raging Dark
The Raging Dracol closes in on the tavern. Part 1: The Dispatch / The Warning. Part 2: The Plan. Part 3: The Hunt.
Chapter 5: What We Carry
Ragnik’s loss, the graves, and the road east begins. Part 1: Zefra. Part 2: The Graves. Part 3: First Light.
Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers
The High Sky Islands, Loren, and Skygate. Part 1: The High Sky Islands. Part 2: What Fire Remembers. Part 3: What the Depths Remember.
Chapter 7: What Floats and What Falls
Skygate’s floating settlement, a voice in the forest, the Champampas who take Sheela, and a wounded Dracol coming home. Part 1: First Ground. Part 2: What Falls. Part 3: What Waits.
Chapter 8: What the Stars Left
Twenty-three years before the Starfall, Saela meets a stranger by a river. Then the road into the dead city, and a girl with a ledger. Part 1: The Sixth Star. Part 2: What the Ash Kept. Part 3: What the Ash Gave.
Chapter 9: What the Numbers Hide
The party makes its plan and walks into the dead city to face the Dracol. Part 1: The Zero. Part 2: The Four Seconds.

The end of the fight, and what it costs.

One year later, a stranger at Ragnik’s inn asks Vael for the whole story.
