His hands were already moving.
The second sign was different — both hands, a different fold, the fingers curved differently, the shape they made casting a shadow that was wrong in a different way, the wrong of a thing that belonged to a different register of existence. A bird shape. Wings spread.
The Spirit Bird came from behind him.
Where the Shadow Wolf had been darkness, the Spirit Bird was light — but not warm light, not firelight. The cold, exact light of something that exists at the boundary between the living world and whatever lives past it. It was translucent, its feathers the suggestion of feathers, its wingspan wider than its body had any right to support. It materialized with the sound of a breath held and then released, and its eyes — when they found the Dracol — were the particular calm of something that does not experience fear because it has a different relationship with death than the things death happens to.
It turned once in the air above Vael’s head.
Then its claws found his shoulders, and they went up together.
“VAEL—” Trista’s voice, from below, already shrinking.
The cold hit him differently this high — not the cold of winter but the cold of altitude, of moving through air that hadn’t been near the ground in a while. The Dracol was level with him, the new wings still hardening at their edges, lava cooling to obsidian in real time.
The Spirit Bird released him.
It folded its wings and flew through the Dracol’s left wing like the wing wasn’t there — like matter and spirit occupied adjacent spaces and the boundary between them was a courtesy that the Bird was choosing to waive. Where it passed, the wing’s structure failed. Not broke — failed, the lava that had hardened to obsidian returning briefly to lava and losing the structural integrity that had held the wing’s shape. The wing crumpled.
The Dracol screamed.
It was the first time it had screamed like that — not the territorial roar, not the hunting call, but the sound of something in real pain, the sound of something that has a threshold and has just found it.
It was still regenerating. The wing was already reforming. But it had turned its attention from the tavern and its attention was now on the floating human thirty feet away who was responsible for the current situation.
Vael floated there.
He had, in the intensity of the moment, briefly forgotten that the Spirit Bird had let go of him and he was not in possession of any natural ability to remain airborne.
Physics, which had been patient, began to reassert itself.
“HELP,” he noted, to anyone who was listening.
“I won’t let you steal the show alone.”
James’s voice, from somewhere below and then above as he rose past Vael at a trajectory that only made sense if someone had thrown him. Below, just audible over the chaos, Figo’s voice — warm, certain, entirely unbothered:
“Say less, drunkard.”
Figo’s arm was visible for one moment at the bottom of James’s arc, completing a follow-through that was more spin throw than any conventional launch. James rose past Vael with the easy, improbable grace of a man who has been thrown by a very large person before and has learned to lean into it.
He gave Vael a small, companionable smirk as he passed.
Then he opened his arms.
The sky changed.
The dark swords assembled themselves from James’s power and the available shadow and whatever James had in him that wasn’t precisely human and wasn’t precisely mortal — dozens of them, then more, arrayed across the air above the Dracol in a pattern that blocked the light from above and turned the space between them and the clouds into something that felt like standing under a held decision. They hung there, each one perfectly still, perfectly aimed.
“Look at this, Varesa,” James said, to the morning, to the ridge, to the woman with the shadow-colored coat who was somewhere below on the ground and who almost certainly could not hear him. “My love.”
“ENDARKEN,” he said.
The swords fell.
They fell slowly — too slowly, the way things in dreams move with a weight that has nothing to do with gravity. The Dracol saw them coming. Its head moved, tracking, finding the angle of escape.
Vael’s hands were already forming the third sign.
The Flesh Toad arrived below him from nowhere that made sense — a wide, heavy shape, all damp muscle and purpose, its skin the color of something that lives in the deep dark under the world and hasn’t seen light in a long time. It was not beautiful. It was not supposed to be. Its tongue was already extending, whip-fast, trailing a cord of saliva that was less like liquid and more like intention given physical form.
It caught the Dracol by the chest and held.
The Dracol pulled. The tongue held. The Dracol twisted. The tongue recalibrated. The dark swords, freed from the need to lead their target, fell straight.
The Dracol shot. A lava ball, point-blank, aimed directly at Vael’s floating, falling, entirely exposed position.
The arrow came from a direction there was no high ground for. It hit the lava ball from the side and deflected the trajectory five degrees — enough. The ball hit empty air twenty feet from Vael and bloomed into a brief, beautiful flower of orange light that cooled to black glass before it reached the ground.
Below, on the ridge, Varesa lowered her bow.
“My job,” she said quietly, “is done here.”
She stepped backward, into the shadow of the largest boulder on the ridge, and the shadow accepted her, and she was gone.
The dark swords hit.
All of them. Full contact, simultaneous, the sound of it arriving a half-second after the light — a deep, resonant impact that moved through the ground far below and through Vael’s chest where he hung in the air and through every hunter on the ridge who braced against it on instinct. The Dracol was still held by the Flesh Toad’s tongue when it hit, and the combination of the hold and the impact and the damage from the combined assault of the whole team arriving in sequence—
The Dracol shrieked.
A sound entirely unlike any it had made before. Not pain, not rage — recognition. The recognition of a thing that has a threshold for how much it can absorb and has, for the first time in this fight, been shown where that threshold is.
The lava veins across its body blazed white-hot as the regeneration surged — sealing the cracks, replacing the obsidian, rebuilding. Furiously, desperately, the regeneration running at a pace that visibly cost it. The Flesh Toad’s tongue released as the rebuilt chest surface changed composition under its grip. The dark swords dissolved.
The Dracol looked at them.
It looked at all of them — the hunters on the ridge, Vael in the air, the assembled wreckage of the ambush, the spent and breathing fighters who had given everything they had and left marks on it that would have ended anything else.
It looked at them.
Then it turned northeast and ran.
The wings — reformed, hardened, functional again — beat twice and lifted it clear of the ridgeline in a rising arc that shook frost from every dead branch within a hundred yards. It went up fast, faster than the ascent should have allowed, and it screamed once more as it went — not at them, not backward, but forward, into the sky it was escaping into, the sound of something furious about needing to leave.
The lava veins were already dimming as it rose, the regeneration throttling back to maintenance levels, the creature conserving what it had left. It crested the ridge to the northeast and dropped out of sight, and the sound of it faded, and the morning was very quiet.
Vael became aware, in the quiet, of several things in rapid succession.
He was still in the air.
The Spirit Bird was not, apparently, available for a second deployment today.
The ground was quite far below him and getting less far below him at an increasing rate.
He made a sound that reflected the situation accurately.
He tried the Bird sign. His hands completed it and nothing answered — not absent, just exhausted, the connection present but dry, a well that had given what it had and needed time. He tried the Wolf sign. Same result. He tried to think of something useful to do about the ground, which was now very close.
He covered his face.
Something caught him.
Not hands — a gentling of the force, a redirection, the falling converting itself from fast to present in the last ten feet, until he arrived at the ground at a speed that was embarrassing rather than fatal and sat down in the frost with an ungraceful ahh that he hoped nobody had heard.
“Apologies, young man.” The voice came from a few feet away. Small, dry, unbothered. “I don’t always stick the landing when catching others. Bit of an imprecise application of the discipline.”
Atver stood nearby, his book closed now, one hand still raised, the brass monocle catching the morning light. He looked at Vael the way someone looks at a mildly interesting phenomenon they’ve added to a running list of mildly interesting phenomena.
“Thanks,” Vael said, from the ground. “I’ll manage.”
“Atver,” the small elf said, and offered a slight bow that was both formal and entirely relaxed.
“Vael,” Vael said, and stood.
Then he heard the screaming from the direction of the carts, and he ran.

Trista was already there.
So were three other healers, and they were not enough. The second cart had taken the deflected lava ball on its right flank — the wood there had gone to nothing, the canvas above it still burning at the edges in a low, orange crawl that the cold was slowly winning against. People were helping people out of the wreckage, some moving under their own power, some not.
Vael helped where he could. He moved between people, following the healers’ direction, doing what hands could do when magic wasn’t available. Lifting, steadying, carrying.
He found Trista in the center of it, crouched over a man who was not moving, both hands full of healing light, the light very white and very bright and working very hard. Her face told him what the light was telling her.
She stood after a moment.
“Five,” she said.
The word sat in the morning air.
“We lost five.”
She didn’t cry. She looked like she wanted to. She looked like she had made a decision about that, and the decision was not yet, and the cost of the decision was visible in the set of her jaw and the stillness of her hands and the way she didn’t look at anything directly for a few seconds.
The hunters around them were quiet. Not the silence of shock — the silence of people who have been in enough hard situations to know that some silences need to be sat with before they can be spoken about.

They came back to the tavern in the late morning light, which had turned thin and pale and said nothing about what the day had been.
Ragnik was at the door before they were through the gate.
His face opened when he saw them coming — relief, the particular relief of a man who had spent an hour in a sealed shelter listening to things he couldn’t see and had not known, until this moment, which of the faces he was watching for would appear. He counted them. He saw who was there.
He saw who wasn’t.
His face did not close exactly. But something in it changed — settled into a different shape, heavier, the shape of a man adding something to a weight he already carried and making room for it.
He held the door.
He didn’t say anything. There wasn’t anything that needed saying that the open door didn’t already say.
Rebecca appeared behind him, and her eyes went immediately to the same count Ragnik’s had — who was there, who was missing, what the faces of the people who were there were telling her about the people who weren’t. Her hand went to her mouth briefly.
Then she straightened.
“Come in,” she said. “All of you. Come inside.”
Vael was last through the door. He stopped in the threshold and looked back at the northeast — the direction the Dracol had gone, the direction the sound of it had faded into, the direction the fight had ended but the thing hadn’t.
Atver appeared beside him, smaller than Vael’s shoulder, book back in hand, monocle glinting.
“It will rest,” the small elf said, conversationally. “Regeneration at that level is metabolically expensive. It will find somewhere dark and deep and it will sleep, and when it wakes it will resume.”
“You know where,” Vael said. It wasn’t a question.
“I know the region,” Atver said carefully. “I know the kind of place it would choose. And I have a lead — on why it is the way it is. Why it’s enraged, why it broke its cycle, why it is this and not what it should be.” He paused. “Developing that lead took me a considerable amount of time.”
“How much time?”
“Roughly two hundred and forty years,” Atver said, without particular emphasis. “On and off.”
Vael looked at him for a moment.
“You should come inside,” he said.
“Yes,” Atver agreed pleasantly. “I believe I should.”
Vael stepped inside.
The door closed behind them.
The northeast horizon was quiet, and empty, and was not going to stay that way.

Chapter 2: Sheela and the Shadows of the Past
Part 1 — Sheela
The following morning, the grey skies hung low over the ragged landscape, and the air had teeth. V’s breath came out in pale ribbons as Figo marched him across the tavern yard, one huge hand clamped around his upper arm. The big man had no intention of letting him idle.
“You’re not sitting around waiting for your memory to knock on the door,” Figo had announced at dawn, kicking open the door of room ten without bothering to knock himself. “Up. Boots. Training.”
The training grounds were a short walk from the tavern, a mud-slicked clearing enclosed by a rotting wooden fence. Frost clung to the rails and to the long stripes of the churned earth. A row of straw dummies stood at the far end, battered and patched, listing like drunks. Beside them leaned a weapon rack that had clearly been liberated from somewhere nicer. Half its pegs were empty, and the rest held a miscellany of steel and wood, gleaming dully in the weak light.
“Well,” Figo grunted, his armored boots sinking into the muck. “If you don’t know your specialty, I bet some practical training will refresh your memory. Every warrior loves his weapon, after all. It’s like a piece of your own soul.”
V glanced at the massive, terrifyingly sharp weapon strapped across Figo’s broad back. It was an axe with a head the size of a dinner platter and an edge that had been honed to a thin, bright line, kept so clean that V could see the pale sky in it. He tried to be friendly. He was fairly sure he had been the kind of person who tried to be friendly.
“I bet you’ve killed some feisty beasts with that axe.”
Figo froze in his tracks.
He turned slowly, and his eyes had gone wide with a mixture of offense and pure outrage.
“IT’S NOT JUST AN AXE!” Figo roared, and the sound shook the frost off the nearby pines. “IT’S MY WIFE, SHEELA!”
V blinked. He stood entirely paralyzed, his mouth slightly open, as his mind raced to catch up with the sheer absurdity of the sentence.
He named it what now? he thought. What exactly is that weapon to him?!
Before V could produce a single word, Figo unstrapped the massive cleaver and brought it gently to his face. He pressed his lips to the cold steel with a tenderness that made V’s ears go hot. “Don’t let what he said get to you, my sweet,” Figo murmured to the blade. “He doesn’t mean it.”
His gaze snapped back to V, fierce as a thrown spear. “SAY SORRY NOW!”
Not wanting to ruin his standing with the only heavily armored vanguard on the team before his first mission, V swallowed his pride and bowed his head. “I’m sorry, Sheela,” he said. “I didn’t mean to disrespect you.”
The silence stretched on for a long, long moment.
Figo grunted, apparently satisfied. He strapped his wife back onto his shoulders with a gentleness that, in a man his size, was almost unbearable to watch.

They resumed their walk toward the weapon racks, and for a while the only sound was the crunch of frozen mud. V thought back to the night before, to the raw panic he had glimpsed in the big man’s eyes during the argument at the table, a fear that had flashed there for an instant and been buried again. It had looked out of place on a man like this.
“Hey… if you don’t mind me asking,” V began softly, “you’ve actually seen a Dracol before, haven’t you? Would you mind describing it to me? Maybe it will spark something in my memory.”
The moment the word left V’s lips, Figo visibly shivered.
It was a small thing, a ripple in the shoulders, there and gone. But on a man built like a siege tower, it was impossible to miss. The tough, unyielding exterior of the veteran hunter seemed to crack down the middle.
“I… well, since you’re part of the team now, you ought to know,” Figo said at last. His voice dropped to a low, grim rumble. “Yes, I’ve seen one. It’s an ancient, catastrophic beast.” He kept his eyes on the horizon, as if the thing might be standing on it. “Luckily, the Hunter’s Guild is always prepared for them… or rather, we were prepared, before the starfall threw the entire order into chaos these past two weeks. You see, Dracols emerge in a specific season: mid-summer. They’re born from the bellies of dead volcanoes. They feast on destruction, eating and melting anything they cross. Normally the guild prepares special cryogenic weapons and specialized hunters to intercept them and minimize the fallout.”
V frowned. He looked around at the frost clinging to the mud, at the breath pluming from their mouths, at the iron-colored sky. “Wait… isn’t it the dead of winter right now?”
“You are indeed correct,” Figo said. His teeth were practically chattering, and it wasn’t from the cold, which was an unsettling sight from a man of his stature. “That’s where the ‘Raging’ part comes in. In incredibly rare, unknown occurrences, a Dracol becomes enraged. It breaks its hibernation cycle and stays active all year round.”
He fell silent. He stared blankly into the distance, and V waited, because it seemed like the thing to do.
“A normal Dracol attacked my village years ago,” Figo said finally. “The guild was there. We were all ready. But our main ballista malfunctioned, and the delay…” His jaw worked. “It caused a lot of losses. We weren’t prepared for the sheer heat. This beast is no joke, V. For the unprepared, it is a walking tomb.”
V’s chest tightened. He thought of a village he’d never seen and faces he’d never known. “I’m sorry,” he said, and his voice was quiet with genuine empathy.
“Not your fault,” Figo muttered, shaking his head hard, as if to clear a cloud of ghosts out of it. He forced a rough clap down on V’s shoulder that nearly drove him into the mud. “Hey, look, we’re at the racks! Let’s get you your fated weapon. From the looks of your build, I’d say you’re either a nimble mage or an assassin. Let’s try the daggers first!”
V felt a sudden surge of excitement, a spark of hope that maybe, just maybe, his muscle memory would take over where his mind had failed. His fingers closed around a pair of plain steel daggers, and they felt cool and strange and foreign in his hands.
“Yeah!” he said. “Daggers! Let’s do it!”

Two hours later, V was face-down in the dirt.
It had started with the daggers. He had dropped them a dozen times. He’d tripped over his own feet, nearly stabbed himself in the thigh, and failed to properly pierce a stationary straw dummy that, he was fairly sure, had been judging him the entire time. At Figo’s increasingly pained insistence he had tried a short sword, which went one direction while he went another, then a spear, which stuck uselessly in the frozen ground, and finally a shortbow, whose arrow had cleared the entire fence and vanished into the forest with a sad little whistle.
His muscles burned like fire. His lungs felt like they were filled with ash. His hands were raw and blistered.
“I’m done,” V groaned into the mud. His face was caked with it. “What is this… am I really this useless?”
Figo stood over him with his arms crossed, and the disappointment on his scarred face was painfully obvious. He didn’t say anything for a while. That was worse.
“I don’t get it,” he said at last. “What the hell did James see within you?” He rubbed his jaw, looking down at the lump of aching boy at his feet. “I guess… well, I guess you can be our backpack boy for the time being. Every party needs someone to carry the rations.”
V’s heart sank. A burden, he thought. That’s all I am.
He pushed himself up on shaking elbows, ready to say something, anything, to stop the feeling of the ground opening under him.
Part 2 — A Trouble Waiting to Happen
“HEY, YOU TWO!”
A sharp, echoing shout cut through the gloomy afternoon air.
V looked up. Two figures were sprinting toward the training grounds from the direction of the tavern, kicking up clods of frozen mud: James, one arm waving wildly over his head with a rolled-up piece of parchment clutched in his fist, and Trista, a few steps behind him, holding her robes out of the mud with her free hand.
“GET PACKED!” James yelled, a frantic grin on his face. “WE GOT A NEW QUEST!”
Figo’s eyes lit up the moment he saw the parchment, and every trace of the disappointed teacher fell away from him. He threw out his arms like a man greeting a long-lost friend.
“FINALLY!” he bellowed. “Some content!”
James and Trista skidded to a halt before him, both gasping for breath. Trista pressed a hand to her chest and forced the words out between ragged inhales.
“We have Dagaruma problems,” she managed, her voice tight with urgency. “A nearby trader sent word. His caravan is under attack. We need to move. Now.”
Figo was already turning to V, a wide grin splitting his scarred face. “Pack up, lad. It’s time we made some Dagaruma barbecue.”
James, still catching his breath, shot Figo a flat look. “Dagarumas are disgusting,” he said, wrinkling his nose. “They taste like rotten chicken rolled in pig droppings.” A beat of silence followed. His voice dropped to barely a whisper. ”…Don’t ask how I know.”
“Enough!” Trista grabbed both of them by the sleeve and dragged them toward the road with a strength that defied her slight frame. She threw a sharp look back over her shoulder. “You, V! Get the bags from the tavern and meet us at the entrance. Move!”
V nodded and broke into a run.

The tavern’s main hall was already stirring with the restless energy of another grey morning when V shouldered through the door. The hearth had been rebuilt to a roar. Refugees sat shoulder to shoulder over steaming bowls, and someone was trying to coax a tune out of a battered lute, badly, to the grudging approval of a few children. V had barely crossed the threshold when Ragnik’s graveled voice called to him from the service counter.
“Hey, V! Off on a mission already, are you?” The old innkeeper’s weathered face crinkled into a warm, knowing smile. “Trista told me everything! I hope the road’s good to you, and that memory of yours finds its way home.” He ducked beneath the counter, came up with something, and hurled it across the room with a practiced arm.
V caught it on instinct, a tightly wrapped bundle of dried meat, still faintly warm from the kitchen.
“Keep your energy up,” Ragnik said with a firm nod. “Good luck, lad.”
V tucked the pack under his arm, mumbled his thanks, and grabbed the party’s travel bags from the storeroom, four of them, heavy with rope and rations. He slung two over each shoulder, made for the door, and was across the yard in a handful of strides. It wasn’t until he was halfway there that it occurred to him he had covered the distance a little faster than his aching muscles had any right to allow. He frowned at his own legs, gave them a doubtful look, and kept running.

James was already leaning against the cart when V arrived, arms folded behind his head, looking like a man without a single concern in the world.
“Team Dracol Slayers, move out!” he announced grandly, and thrust a fist into the air.
Trista’s eye twitched. “We haven’t even beaten one.”
James turned to her with a patient, serene smile. “Not yet.”
Behind them, Figo said nothing. He simply pulled his coat a little tighter and stared at the middle distance with his jaw set, doing his level best not to visibly shiver.
V wisely said nothing either, and climbed into the cart.

The horses set off at a hard pace, wheels rattling and churning through the frost-stiffened mud of the road. Bare trees blurred past on either side, still scarred and grey from the aftermath of the starfall. Here and there the ground was cut with long, shallow scars where something had fallen from the sky and plowed a furrow through the earth, and the grass in the furrows grew a strange, silvery color.
“Saving a trader’s caravan,” Figo mused from his seat, with the unmistakable warmth of a man doing something he deeply enjoys. “Bet the pay is solid.” He settled back with a contented sigh and propped his boots against the side of the cart.
V studied him for a moment. He’s a remarkably simple man, he thought. In the best possible way.
He watched the road unspool ahead of them. The question he’d been carrying since the morning finally made its way out.
“So… what exactly is a Dagaruma?”
Trista turned from the road. The expression on her face was one V would come to recognize well in the weeks ahead: the look of someone quietly wondering how her life choices had led her to this precise moment. She sighed through her nose and answered anyway.
“Mid-sized monsters. They hunt in packs, and they’re aggressive, coordinated and opportunistic. Since the starfall, they’ve been hitting the trading routes hard.” She laced her fingers together in her lap. “Most of the prey animals they’d normally hunt are dead, and the stardust coating the vegetation has made the plant life toxic to most living creatures. They’re hungry, they’re desperate, and that makes them dangerous. Their primary weapons are their claws and their tails, the tails especially. The bite is unpleasant but manageable. The tail is not.”
“Small fry,” Figo added helpfully.
“They cause the most deaths per year of any creature on the guild’s record,” James said, without opening his eyes or adjusting his lounging posture. “Don’t take them lightly.”
A short, loaded silence followed. The cart bumped over a rut. Somewhere overhead, a single bird called twice and then fell quiet.
“We’re here,” said Trista.

V was the first to spot them.
About forty paces down the road, four traders stood back to back in a tight circle with their spears leveled outward, while a wagon heaped with sacks and crates sat abandoned behind them with its horses long gone. They were being slowly encircled by a writhing knot of scaled, low-slung shapes. The creatures moved with a liquid, unsettling patience, feinting left, retreating right, testing the circle for a gap.
“Fun fact,” James announced serenely, stretching his arms above his head as he stepped down from the cart. “The collective noun for a pack of Dagaruma is a trouble waiting to happen.”
Figo had already stopped listening. He unslung Sheela from his back, felt the familiar weight settle into his hands, and rolled his shoulders once.
“Come and get it,” he said quietly, and moved.
For a man sheathed from head to toe in armor, Figo covered the distance with startling, almost offensive speed. Sheela caught the nearest Dagaruma in mid-lunge, and the blow landed before the creature even had time to register the threat.
“HA!” Figo wheeled to face the rest, chest swelling. “Small fry! What did I say?”
Two of the remaining Dagaruma immediately peeled away from the traders and circled wide to flank him, tails whipping low through the frozen grass.
Nearby, a pale light had begun to bloom around Trista’s staff as she chanted under her breath, her focus locked entirely on James. Threads of white light unspooled from the staff’s crown and wound toward him, and he rocked on his heels with the bright, uncomplicated excitement of a child waiting for his turn at something.
His turn came. He spread his arms wide and spoke.
“Let the dark engulf them.”
The words seemed to press the air flat. A wave of deep shadow unspooled outward like smoke given weight, and everywhere it touched, a Dagaruma stiffened and faltered, shrouded in swirling, lightless dust, as though the world had momentarily forgotten they existed.
V stood at the edge of it all, taking in the controlled chaos. Something bright and unnameable rose in his chest.
So this is what real hunters look like.
A sharp instinct screamed along his spine.
He twisted left, just fast enough. Claws raked the air where his shoulder had been a half-second before. The Dagaruma that had been waiting for him, the hidden one, patient and low in the long grass, landed hard and spun to face him, coiled and ready.
V scrambled backward with his heart hammering, tracking the creature’s tail as it swept in a low, whipping arc toward his ankles.
A knife blurred past his ear and buried itself in the Dagaruma’s throat.
The creature crumpled.
V exhaled. He turned, still half-crouched. Across the road Figo stood with his arm still extended from the throw, his expression already cycling back to mild disinterest.
“Phew. …Thanks.”
Figo grunted. “Watch your flanks.”

When the dust settled, a handful of Dagaruma had cut their losses and bolted into the treeline with a stolen sack of provisions clutched between them. The traders stared after them, then, collectively, turned to look at the hunters.
“No casualties,” Trista said quietly. She was already moving toward the nearest injured trader, a healing light blooming soft and steady around her fingertips. She said it like a small, private prayer.
“Thank you.” The trader who spoke looked to be in his mid-thirties, road-worn and steady, the sort of man who had plainly handled bad situations before, though perhaps not quite this bad. He shifted the weight of an enormous pack, one hand still gripping his spear. “You genuinely saved us back there.”
In the background, Figo had found himself a clear patch of ground, dropped to one knee beside the nearest Dagaruma carcass, and was skinning it with the focused, reverent energy of a man who had found his calling.
“The pelts are guild material,” he announced to no one in particular, his voice warm with satisfaction. “These won’t go to waste.”
James returned from a brief, businesslike conversation with the traders’ leader, a heavy purse in his hand, looking perfectly content with the state of the universe.
“Another job,” Trista said, watching him, her hands still glowing softly as she worked. ”…Done well enough, I suppose.”
A second trader stepped forward and pressed his palms together. His eyes moved across all four of them with real feeling. “The goods, most of them, will make it to the villages ahead. People who need it badly.” He inclined his head. “May your paths be green, hunters.”
Figo stood up with the pelts bundled under one arm and began loading the cart with brisk efficiency.
“Right,” he said, entirely satisfied with himself and the world. “Let’s move.”
V climbed up after him. As the horses lurched into motion, he looked down at his hands, the hands that had not, as far as he knew, ever held a weapon properly in their lives. They were still trembling a little.
My body knew, he thought. It knew before I did.
He didn’t know what that meant. But for the first time since he had woken up in room ten, the thought didn’t frighten him.

Chapter 3: What the Shadow Remembers
Part 1 — The Framedious
The cart rolled back toward the guild at a comfortable pace, the horses finding their own rhythm on the familiar road. The afternoon light had gone thin and pale, filtering through the bare treeline in long, cold shafts.
Figo had been quiet for a while. For Figo, that never lasted.
“Hey.” He turned from the road, fixing V with the evaluating squint of a man who had spent decades reading fighters. “Your movement back there. Against that Dagaruma that came from hiding.” He gave a slow, approving nod. “It was natural. Instinctive. You’re a hunter, lad. Whatever else you’ve forgotten, that part of you remembers.”
V opened his mouth, closed it, then looked down at his hands. “It just… happened. My body moved before I thought about it.”
“That’s exactly what it means,” Figo said, turning back to the road with the satisfied air of a man whose point had been proven.
“See?” James hadn’t moved from his half-reclined position, arms folded behind his head, a smug grin stretching slowly across his face. “Told you all. My gut. Never. Wrong.” A private gleam crossed his eyes — there and gone in an instant. Right on time, he thought. Almost.  He cleared his throat with great ceremony. “I believe this calls for a drink. A reward for outstanding instinct.”
Trista turned to look at him with an expression so flat it could have been used as a table. “A drink,” she repeated. “Is not a reward, James.”
“It is if you’re me.”
V laughed — a real one, surprised out of him. “I feel… clearer,” he said, and he meant it. Something had shifted in the fog behind his eyes. Not a memory, not yet, but a shape where one might eventually be. “Like something’s starting to come back.”
“PROGRESS,” Figo announced, at a volume entirely unsuited to the size of the cart.
Then he stopped.
His head turned — slowly, the way a veteran’s head turns when something in the air changes. His eyes went to the west, to the dark line of trees beyond the ridge, and he said nothing for exactly three seconds.
The screech came from that direction.
It wasn’t loud in the way thunder is loud. It was loud in the way that made the ears feel wrong, like the sound was happening slightly inside the skull rather than outside it. The horses screamed. The yoke harness — old wood, dried out by weeks of cold — took the frequency like a hammer blow. A crack ran across the beam. Then another. Then the whole assembly splintered apart in a single sharp report, and the horses were gone, traces snapping behind them as they tore into the treeline and disappeared.
The cart, suddenly without anything pulling it, lurched hard to the left, tipped, and deposited all four of them onto the frost-hardened road.
V hit the ground and rolled, coming up onto one knee with his ears ringing. He looked up.
”…Framedious,” James said quietly. He was already on his feet, which was either impressive or suspicious. His face — for the first time since V had known him — had shifted. Not afraid. Not alarmed. Just… present. Alert in a way that sat strangely on features usually arranged into theatrical laziness.
“Time to lock in,” he added, glancing at V with a small smile. Your turn, kid. Right on schedule.
The Framedious stood at the tree line.
Seven feet tall at the shoulder — not counting the fifth limb, which was something between a leg and a spear, terminating in a rigid, glistening point that scraped the ground as the creature shifted its weight. It moved on the other four limbs with a horrible, fluid efficiency, and its body was armored in overlapping plates the color of old bone.
“Where’s its face?” V said.
“Look up,” Figo said, very quietly.
The Framedious answered the question by rearing back and leaping — a single, explosive movement that seemed to defy the weight of the thing — and as it rose, it showed its underside. The face was there, in the center of its belly, surrounded by the roots of all five limbs. A wide, wet, lipless mouth, ringed with teeth that curved inward.
“Fun fact,” James said pleasantly, “they eat and poop from the same place.”
“James,” said Trista, Figo, and V, in perfect unison.

The creature landed hard enough to split the frozen mud, and Trista was already moving. Her hands came up, fingers spreading wide, and she threw — not a weapon, exactly, but a compressed sphere of what looked like luminous powder that detonated against the Framedious’s chest in a cascading shower of iridescent light. The creature’s limbs seized. It staggered sideways, slowed, its movements suddenly laboring through an invisible resistance.
“Go!” Trista shouted.
Figo went.
Sheela came off his back in a single practiced arc, and he closed the distance at that startling, armor-defying speed, swinging into the Framedious’s flank with everything he had. The blade connected. The creature took one step back — actually moved, actually yielded — and then, while Figo was still in the long recovery of the swing, the fifth limb came around in a fast, short arc and opened a deep gash across his right shoulder.
Figo didn’t make a sound. He set his jaw and repositioned.
Trista threw the second bomb larger this time, and the burst staggered the Framedious backward far enough to buy a breath. She sprinted to Figo’s side, both hands already glowing, and spoke the chant low and fast beneath her breath.
“May our wounds curse our enemies.”
The light moved from her hands into Figo’s shoulder — and then, impossibly, the Framedious flinched. Its equivalent limb twitched and pulled inward, the same gash opening across its plating in a mirror of the wound it had just dealt.
“Woah,” V breathed.
The Framedious noticed. It screamed — that same skull-filling frequency — and charged.
It wasn’t slowed this time. It hit Figo full on, all the weight of it behind the impact, and sent him skidding back into the treeline. He struck a pine hard enough to crack the lower trunk, bark exploding outward, and dropped to one knee. He drove Sheela into the ground to stop himself falling further.
“Figo!” Trista was already running toward him. “The fifth limb — it’s venomous! He’s been hit, he needs—” She wheeled toward James. “James!”
James was lying with his back against the overturned cart, V’s pack arranged under his head like a pillow. His eyes were closed. His chest rose and fell with the slow, even rhythm of a man getting excellent sleep.
Trista made a sound that was not quite a word.

V watched Figo plant Sheela in the frozen ground and use the handle to haul himself upright, knuckles white, jaw locked. The big man’s right arm was hanging wrong. The shoulder wound was deep, and whatever was in the Framedious’s fifth limb had already started — there was a grey tinge spreading under the skin at the collar, slow and deliberate.
He’s still trying to fight, V realized. He’s going to try to fight it like that.
V’s feet were moving before he’d decided anything. He stepped past Trista, past the radius of relative safety she’d carved with her glitter bombs, and put himself between Figo and the Framedious, which had stopped its charge and was now tilting its belly-face toward him with a kind of cold, assessing curiosity.
“V.” Figo’s voice, behind him. Low. “You don’t have to do this.”
“I know.”
What am I doing? V thought, staring at the thing’s wet, inward-curving teeth, at the fifth limb dragging a pale groove through the mud as the creature shifted toward him. What in the actual hell am I doing right now? It has a poisoned leg-spear. It ate Figo’s shoulder. I don’t even know what I am.
The Framedious tilted its weight forward.
I am going to die in this road and I still don’t even know my name.
“I can’t keep being the backpack boy,” he said, mostly to himself.
Figo made a sound behind him — half protest, half something that might, in another context, have been pride. He heard the scrape of Sheela being lifted again, the old warrior refusing to stay down, using her as a third leg to push himself upright.
The Framedious charged.
All five limbs moved this time, the full terrible coordination of the thing unleashed at once, the belly-mouth screaming, poisoned saliva stringing from the fifth limb’s point in long, glittering threads. Trista screamed his name. Her hands were up, another bomb forming between her palms, but it wasn’t ready, it wasn’t going to be ready—
V’s right hand moved.
He didn’t decide to move it. It moved the way his feet had moved against the Dagaruma, the way his body had dodged before his mind caught up — pure muscle memory from a life he couldn’t see. His fingers folded inward, two knuckles raised, the shape his hand made casting a long, specific shadow on the ground before him even in the flat grey afternoon light.
The shadow rippled.
Something answered from beneath it.
A claw came first — enormous, dark as the space between stars, made of something that was not quite solid and not quite light. Then the shape of a wolf assembled itself from V’s shadow, rising without sound, without any of the drama the moment deserved. It simply was there, the way a thing is there when it has always been waiting.
It moved once.
The strike was surgical. A single sweep of one claw across the Framedious’s charging bulk — and the creature came apart. Not slowly. Not with a fight. The wound the shadow left didn’t bleed so much as open, and what had been a seven-foot apex predator folded into the mud with a sound like the world exhaling.
Silence.
The shadow wolf was gone. V’s hand was at his side. He was staring at the space where the Framedious had been, his own breathing loud in his ears, his fingers faintly tingling.
”…Well,” Figo said, from somewhere behind him. His voice was very quiet. “I’ll be damned.”
Trista hadn’t moved. The bomb she’d been building had dissipated between her palms, forgotten. She was looking at V — then at the shadow — then at the place the wolf had been — then, very slowly, at the cart where James was still apparently asleep.
Something connected behind her eyes.
Her expression went through several phases in quick succession, arriving finally at a particular kind of fury that was entirely too calm to be safe.
“Damn you, James,” she said, softly. “You could have just told us, you absolute rat.”
From behind the cart came the long, peaceful sound of someone snoring.
V turned around. He looked at his hand. He looked at Figo, who was still leaning on Sheela, grey-faced and bleeding but watching him with an expression that had moved well past surprise into something slower and more complicated.
“I don’t…” V started. Stopped. “I don’t know what that was.”
“I do,” Trista said. She was still staring at James. “Or at least — I know what it means.” She finally looked at V, and the fury in her face had made room for something else. Something almost like awe. “But that conversation can wait. Right now I need to stop Figo from dying.”
Figo, for his part, had the decency to look mildly embarrassed about the dying situation.
“I’m fine,” he said.
“You have venom in your shoulder.”
“I’ve had worse.”
“When?”
He paused. ”…Give me a moment, I’ll think of something.”
V looked between the two of them, then at the wreckage of the cart, then at the Framedious, then at his own hand one more time.
Somewhere in the fog of his memory, something had shifted. Not a face. Not a place. Just a word — rising from somewhere deeper than memory, from whatever part of him had just moved his hand without asking permission.
A name.
Vael.
He held it in his mind for a moment, testing it, the way you test ice before putting your weight on it. It held. It felt like his.
“Hey,” he said quietly, interrupting nothing in particular.
Trista looked up from where she was already kneeling beside Figo, hands glowing.
“My name,” V said. “I think… I think it’s Vael.”
A beat of silence.
“FINALLY!” James shouted from behind the cart, in the wide-awake voice of a man who had not been asleep at all. “I WAS WONDERING WHEN YOU’D FIGURE THAT OUT!”
Trista closed her eyes.
“I’m going to kill him,” she said, with great serenity, “after I finish healing Figo.”

Part 2 — The Tapilca
James’s response to Trista’s threat arrived with the unruffled calm of a man who had already seen how this conversation ended.
“You knew that I knew that you knew that this outcome is entirely to our benefit, Trista.” He said it the way someone reads a sentence they’ve already memorized, then pivoted without drawing breath. “Okay! Here is the plan—”
Nobody noticed Figo quietly losing the battle to stay upright. His grip on Sheela loosened by degrees, the great axe serving its second purpose of the day as a leaning post, and then even that wasn’t enough.
“I’ll just…” he murmured, to no one in particular. “…rest for a while.”
He went down slowly, which was somehow more alarming than if he’d simply collapsed.
“Tapilcas!” James announced, spinning on his heel with the energy of a man presenting a solution he’d had in his pocket the entire time. “That’ll get him back to new. Vael — with me. Trista, stay here, keep him breathing. We won’t be long.” He turned and offered her a wink of such specific confidence that it stopped just short of infuriating.
Trista looked at Figo’s grey face. Then at James. Then at the middle distance, communing silently with whatever reserve of patience she had left.
“Fine,” she said. “Don’t take long. And Vael—” her eyes moved to him, sharp and serious, “—we’re talking about your powers when you get back.”
“Understood.” Vael grabbed James by the sleeve and pulled him toward the treeline. “Let’s go.”
“This way!” James pointed confidently in the wrong direction.
Vael looked at the direction. Looked at James. Turned them both around and walked the correct way without comment.

Thirty minutes into the forest, the world grew quiet in a way that felt deliberate.
It was the kind of quiet that took a moment to identify — not peaceful, exactly, but emptied. The Starfall had been weeks ago and the forest had not forgotten. Half the trees they moved through were dead on their feet, bark split and grey, branches bare not from winter but from something more permanent. The stardust had settled into the soil and the roots had drawn it up like poison through a straw. Some trees had fallen already, their trunks collapsed inward, soft and blackened. Others still stood, holding the shape of living things while being nothing of the sort.
What birds remained moved in small, nervous clusters rather than the easy scatter of a healthy wood. No undergrowth rustled. No distant calls answered each other across the canopy. The forest existed, but quietly, and carefully, as though it understood it was operating on reduced numbers and didn’t want to draw attention to the fact.
Vael walked through it and felt the absence like a pressure behind the eyes.
“Figo’s going to be fine,” he said, mostly to fill the silence. “Right?”
“Mm.” James had his hands in his pockets, moving through the dead wood with the relaxed familiarity of someone on an evening stroll. “Probably.”
“Probably.”
“Relax. Trista’s bought him time. We just need to move.” He glanced sideways. “Speaking of which — congratulations, by the way. On the name.”
Vael blinked. In the chaos of the Framedious and Figo going down, he’d almost forgotten the moment had happened. Vael. It still felt like pressing a bruise — tender, but real. “Thanks. I think.”
“We’ll celebrate properly when we’re back.” James said it with the warm finality of someone marking something off a list. “Now. Tapilcas. You want to know what you’re looking for?”
“That would help, yes.”
James tilted his head back, apparently organizing information he found mildly tedious to explain. “Right, the memory. Okay. Tapilcas grow from a specific tree — you’ll know the tree when you see it, it’s pink. Entirely pink, bark included, because the flowers cover the whole thing. The flowers themselves are called tapils — small, blue and pink, they grow in clusters all over the branches. Pretty enough.” He waved a hand. “But what you want is a tapilca. That’s a tapil that’s had a full summer of sun and good nutrition. It grows larger than the others and it starts producing a honey-like fluid from its center — you’ll see it dripping if you look closely. That fluid is what we need. Antivenom for most of what lives in this region, Framedious included.”
Vael turned this over. “And if they’re rare — how do we find one without searching the entire forest?”
“Hah.” James grabbed his arm and pulled him sideways into a low bush in one smooth motion, crouching without any apparent urgency. “Easy. We cheat.” He pointed through the branches. “Look.”
Vael looked. He scanned the undergrowth for something large, something dangerous, something proportionate to the problem they were trying to solve—
And then he found it. Barely twenty feet away, half-hidden in the shadow of a collapsed trunk: a creature no larger than his fist, round and absurdly fluffy, with a tail that seemed to account for half its total volume. Two enormous cheeks bulged on either side of its face. Green stripes ran along its back in uneven lines, the color close enough to the dead moss that Vael had looked directly at it twice without seeing it.
It was, objectively, very cute.
Aww, Vael thought, and immediately felt strange about thinking it given the circumstances.
“Davoura,” James murmured. “They live for Tapil trees. Follow it, it leads us right to one. Simple.”
“Simple,” Vael agreed, watching the small creature stuff something into its cheeks with dedicated efficiency. “Let’s go.”

Following a Davoura through a winter forest turned out to require a specific skill set that neither of them had formally trained for.
The creature moved in short, decisive bursts — several feet, then stillness, then several more feet in a direction that seemed to bear no relation to the previous one. It paused to investigate things. It doubled back. At one point it sat entirely motionless for ninety seconds for no discernible reason before abruptly sprinting sideways into a thicket.
James and Vael followed it through all of this in a low, shuffling crouch that was doing neither of them any favors, communicating in gestures that grew increasingly frantic as the Davoura began, unmistakably, to sense something was wrong.
It stopped. Sat up straight. Its enormous eyes swept the treeline behind it.
“That cheeky little thing,” James murmured.
“What?” Vael breathed.
“It’s stressed. It feels us.” James didn’t move a muscle. “If we spook it here we lose the trail entirely.”
The Davoura sat a moment longer, cheeks bulging, tail flicking in slow arcs. Then it bolted — straight up the nearest tree trunk, claws finding purchase in the dead bark, and vanished into the upper branches.
“We lost it—”
“We’re already here,” James said, and walked calmly around the other side of the tree.
Vael followed, and stopped.
The Tapil tree stood in a small natural clearing where two fallen trunks had opened a gap in the canopy. In the pale winter light filtering through, it glowed. There was no other word for it — the pink of the bark, the dense clusters of blue-and-pink tapils covering every branch from root to crown, the whole thing so saturated with color in a forest this grey and dead that it looked like something from a different world bleeding through. Several Davoura moved in its upper branches, unhurried and proprietary, stuffing tapils into their cheeks with professional focus.
“Davouras eat the tapils,” James said, coming to stand beside him. “And hunt for the tapilcas specifically. Territorial about them too.” He looked satisfied. “Now find one that’s dripping. Larger than the others, honey coming from the center.”
Vael moved around the base of the tree, scanning the lower branches, crouching to check the clusters within reach. The tapils were beautiful up close — petals the deep blue of a midnight sky with pink edges, clustered so thickly that the branches beneath were invisible. He moved along one low branch, checking each flower, and then—
There. Bigger than its neighbors by half, the petals slightly separated, a slow golden bead forming at its center and running down the outside of the petal in a thin, gleaming line.
Vael reached up carefully and closed his fingers around the stem.
Something landed on his hand.
The Davoura that had felt followed — their original quarry, cheeks still full — sat on his knuckles, looked him directly in the eye, bit the tapilca stem clean through, and was gone up the tree trunk before Vael had processed what had happened.
He stared at his empty hand.
“Hey!!” He was moving before the indignation had finished arriving, sprinting after the creature to the base of the tree, craning upward as the Davoura disappeared into the canopy. He stood there for a moment, breathing hard, one hand on the bark, the small creature nowhere to be seen.
“This is going to be impossible,” he said.
“Patience,” said James, from somewhere behind him. A short pause. “And — there we are.” The sound of a stem being carefully separated from a branch. “Got one. Let’s head back.”
Vael turned to find James holding the tapilca with the careful, two-fingered grip of someone handling something fragile, the honey already beading at its center, golden and slow. He looked entirely unbothered. He also looked, Vael noticed, just slightly more focused on moving quickly than his usual performance of ease would suggest.
They turned back toward the road.

The forest was quieter on the return walk, or maybe Vael was just more aware of it now. The dead trees stood in rows on either side, patient and still. Somewhere above them a single bird called twice and went silent.
The question had been sitting in Vael’s chest since the fight. He let it out.
“James.” He kept his eyes on the path. “When we were fighting the Framedious. You knew, didn’t you. You knew I’d step up. You knew what would happen.” A beat. “When you looked at me — right before the charge. You knew.”
James walked a few steps without answering. Then:
“I don’t know you,” he said. “Not personally. No.” He looked up at the canopy, at the dead branches crosshatched against the pale sky. He took a slow breath, the kind that comes before something true. “I have a curse. Others might call it a gift, I suppose, but I’ve had it longer than them, so I get to name it.” He paused. “I can see probabilities. When I look at someone — really look — I see the likelihood of outcomes. Good ones. Bad ones. Every shape a moment could take and how likely each one is to happen.”
Vael processed this quietly. “So you saw a probability that I would step up. That my power would emerge.” He thought about it. “It was a gamble. You just… took your chances with Figo’s life.”
“Yup!” James said, and did a small, inexplicable celebratory shuffle without breaking stride.
Vael stared at him. “That’s insane.”
“Probably.” The shuffle stopped. James was quiet for a moment, and something in his posture shifted — barely perceptible, but there, like a door opened a crack onto a darker room. “Most of the time… the probabilities I see are bad. Awful, sometimes. I see outcomes people don’t know are coming and can’t be warned about. I see the weight of what’s likely, and what’s likely is often—” He stopped. Reached into his coat. Produced a small, battered flask of ale and took a long pull from it. Exhaled. “This helps. Takes the edge off the numbers.”
Vael said nothing. There didn’t seem to be anything useful to say.
“But you, Vael.” James looked at him sideways, and for a moment — just a moment — the lazy theatrical mask was entirely gone, and what was underneath it was something older and more tired and completely sincere. “Your probabilities are interesting. I haven’t seen a spread like yours in a long time. Maybe ever.” The corner of his mouth pulled up. “I want to see how it all unfolds. That’s why I wanted you on the team. That’s why I’ll see it through.”
Vael turned this over in the silence of the dead wood around them.
“And Trista and Figo,” he said finally. “They trust your judgment because of this. Because they know what you can see.”
“Bingo.” James tucked the flask away. Hiccupped, once, with dignity. “Lesh go,” he announced, switching registers without warning. “Shave Figo!!”

They found Trista exactly where they’d left her, kneeling beside Figo in the grey afternoon light, both hands pressed to his chest, the healing glow coming from her fingers dimmer now than it had been — the particular dimness of something running on fumes. Her shoulders were tight. Her jaw was set. She looked up when she heard them coming and the expression on her face did about four things in quick succession, ending somewhere between relief and the specific fury of someone who has been holding everything together alone and has feelings about that.
James held up the tapilca.
The death stare she leveled at him was magnificent. It communicated, without words, a detailed record of every grievance she had accumulated since meeting him, organized chronologically and cross-referenced by category.
“Feed him,” she said. “Vael. You do it.”
“Me?”
She was already moving back to give him room, and Figo’s condition answered the question of whether there was time to discuss it. Vael knelt, took the tapilca carefully in both hands, and tilted the flower over Figo’s parted lips. The honey came slowly at first — a single gold thread — then steadier, catching the last of the afternoon light as it fell.
They waited.
The grey at Figo’s collar began, very slowly, to recede. The tight, shallow rhythm of his breathing deepened by degrees. Color returned to his face in the gradual, stubborn way that color returns to things that aren’t ready to give up.
Trista made a sound that was not quite a word — something between a sigh and a prayer — and her hands finally went still. Then, without ceremony or warning, she sat down where she was standing and did not get up.
Vael moved fast enough to catch her before she hit the ground, lowering her gently into the frost-stiff grass.
She was already asleep before she was fully horizontal.
He sat back on his heels and looked at the three of them — Figo breathing slow and even, Trista folded into the exhausted sleep of someone who had simply run out of self — and felt something settle in his chest. Not peace, exactly. Something quieter than that.
“James,” he said, standing. “Watch duty.”
“Aww—”
“Watch. Duty.”
James looked at him for a moment, then at the treeline, then produced his flask again with a philosophical shrug. “Fine.”
Vael collected what dry wood he could find within a short radius — harder work than it should have been, the starfall having robbed the forest of most of its good tinder — and built the fire low and practical, the kind that lasts rather than the kind that impresses. He set the camp with quiet efficiency, moving between his sleeping teammates with the ease of someone doing something their body understood even when their mind was still catching up.
When he finally straightened and turned to gather the last of the wood, he stopped.
The treeline was dark. The fire behind him threw his shadow long across the frost, and beyond its reach the forest was simply black — the compressed black of a winter night with no moon yet and too many dead trees to let in what stars there were.
But between two of those trees — thirty feet out, maybe forty, right at the edge of where the firelight gave up — there was a shape.
Still. Upright. Watching.
Not an animal. The proportions were wrong for that, too deliberate in their stillness, too vertical. A figure. He could make out almost nothing — a silhouette only, and within the silhouette a quality of shadow that seemed somehow denser than the dark around it, as though the darkness there had been gathered rather than simply fallen.
He blinked.
The space between the trees was empty.
No sound. No movement. Nothing to suggest anything had ever been there — except that the frost on the ground between those two trees was undisturbed, and something about the shape of the dark there still felt occupied in a way the rest of the treeline didn’t.
Vael stood very still for a long moment, firewood in his arms, heart doing something careful and measured in his chest.
Then James spoke from behind him, entirely casual.
“Better get that fire built, Vael. It’s going to be a cold one.”
Vael looked at him. James was looking at the flask in his hands, turning it slowly, his expression unreadable.
He knew. Of course he knew.
Vael turned back to the treeline one more time. Empty. Just trees.
He added the wood to the fire and said nothing.

Chapter 6: What the Sky Remembers
Part 1 — The High Sky Islands
The cold changed shape somewhere around the fourth day.
It didn’t leave — the mornings still bit at exposed skin, the nights still demanded every blanket and every body pressed close to the fire — but the snow thinned with each mile east, giving way first to frost-hardened mud, then to simple, dry, biting cold with nothing white left to show for it. The forests changed too. The dead grey trees of the tavern’s outskirts gave way, gradually, to stretches of hardier growth that had weathered the Starfall’s touch more lightly — pines that still held their needles, undergrowth that hadn’t entirely given up.
They walked through all of it in the particular rhythm that long travel creates — quiet stretches where only footsteps and wind filled the air, and looser stretches where conversation wandered wherever it wanted to.
Figo told a long, meandering story about a fishing trip that had gone wrong in three separate and increasingly improbable ways, and somehow made it funnier each time a new complication appeared. James contributed color commentary that made the story worse and better at the same time. Trista corrected several of Figo’s exaggerations with the patient exhaustion of someone who had apparently heard this story before, in a different and equally implausible form. Atver walked slightly apart from all of it, hands folded behind his back, wearing the small, contented expression of a man enjoying a play he’d already read the ending to.
Vael listened more than he spoke. He was starting to learn the shape of them — not through revelation, not through crisis, but through the accumulation of small, ordinary things. The way Figo hummed under his breath when the road was flat and easy. The way Trista’s hands never quite stopped moving even at rest, as though some part of her was permanently ready to heal something. The way James’s jokes got sharper when he was tired, as though humor were a muscle he reached for reflexively under strain.
He was starting, without quite noticing it happening, to care about all of them.

He couldn’t sleep.
It was well before sunrise, the sky still holding onto its deepest dark, and Vael had spent the last twenty minutes attempting increasingly hopeless configurations against the hard ground, his rolled jacket doing very little in its role as a pillow. He finally gave up and lay still, looking at the dying coals of the fire and the shapes of his companions around it.
Trista slept curled around her staff like it was something precious rather than a weapon, her robe folded under her head, a strip of unidentifiable but clearly warm fur draped over her shoulders as a blanket. Even asleep, her face held a kind of watchfulness — the sleep of someone who had learned, somewhere, not to sleep too deeply.
Figo slept flat on the bare ground, no bedroll, no blanket, nothing beneath him but frost-hardened earth — and Sheela cradled against his chest with both arms, held the way a man holds the person he loves most in the world, which, as far as Figo was concerned, she was. He seemed entirely unbothered by the cold that had Vael shivering under two layers.
James, a short distance away, slept sitting upright against a tree trunk, his rum cask still clutched loosely in one hand. He was muttering — soft, disjointed fragments of speech, the unmistakable cadence of a man deep in a dream about something he clearly missed very much. Vael caught the word “ale” twice and something that might have been “one more round” and left it at that.
Atver was nowhere.
Vael sat up properly and looked around the small camp. No sign of the small elf — not curled anywhere, not standing watch, not visible at all.
Does he even sleep? Vael thought. It occurred to him, turning the question over, that in nearly a week of travel he had never once seen Atver asleep. Never seen him tired. Never seen him do much of anything except read, walk, and occasionally offer information with the calm of someone who had all the time in the world, which — Vael supposed — he essentially did.
He got up quietly, careful not to wake the others, and found a line of footprints leading away from camp — spaced, deliberate, almost too neat, as though someone had left them specifically to be followed.
The prints led him to the base of a tall outcrop of rock, rising black against the pre-dawn sky.
He looked up. Atver was already at the top, a small silhouette against stars that hadn’t yet given way to morning.
“Ah. Hello, child.” The voice drifted down, warm and unhurried. “You’ve come at the right time. Join me.”
Vael eyed the climb. It looked steep, and he was tired, and he had not entirely forgiven his body for the last week of walking. “Can’t you just fly me up with that magic of yours?” he called, only half joking. “Old man privileges.”
Atver’s laugh carried down, dry and genuinely delighted. “Ha! You’re a young lad — surely you can manage a rock. In my day I climbed mountains without stopping to catch my breath.”
“Oh, here I come,” Vael muttered, already reaching for the first handhold.
It was not easy. His arms complained. His fingers found purchase in cracks that seemed designed to discourage exactly this kind of activity. But he was not, whatever else remained uncertain about him, a weak man, and he made it to the top, hauling himself over the final ledge with a graceless scramble and sitting there a moment just to breathe.
Then he looked up.
The sunrise had just begun — the first pale gold breaking the horizon’s edge — and it was breaking across something that stole every word Vael had been planning to say.
Islands. Vast slabs of stone floating in open sky with nothing beneath them, no support, no explanation, drifting in slow formation against a sky still holding the last of its stars. From this distance they looked impossibly delicate — dark silhouettes rimmed in the coming gold, trailing thin mist from their undersides like clouds that had forgotten how to fall.
“This,” Atver said quietly, beside him, “is new.”
“This is—” Vael’s voice had abandoned him somewhere in his chest. He tried again. “This is new to you too?”
“Our first landmark.” Atver’s eyes reflected the growing light, calm and pleased. “Nobody has named it officially. Everyone simply calls it the High Sky Islands, because that’s what it plainly is, and no one has felt moved to improve on the description.”
He raised a hand and pointed toward one island in particular, further out, where something glowed — faint at first, then brighter, a point of light that moved with purpose against the dark stone.
“That,” Atver said, his voice sharpening with interest, “feels similar to the Starfall. I wonder what’s found that kind of power up there.”
The light arced suddenly — a streak, brilliant and fast, launching from the island’s surface in a trail that briefly outshone the coming sunrise, curving up and out over the open drop between islands like something that had decided gravity was a suggestion rather than a rule. It vanished behind a further island a moment later, and the sky held its breath, and then, faintly, impossibly, something like laughter carried across the vast empty distance — distorted by wind and altitude into something closer to an echo of a sound than the sound itself.
Vael stared. “This is—” He laughed, disbelieving. “This is gorgeous. Is this what’s left? Of our world after the Starfall?”
“It’s what remains,” Atver said, “and remaining, as it turns out, isn’t the same as ending. Humans adapt. Lands adapt.” He smiled faintly, looking out at the drifting shapes. “This is not the first hardship this world has faced, and it will not be the last. It has always recovered. Always adapted, given time.”
Vael looked at the islands a while longer, the light climbing steadily now, gilding the undersides of the floating stone in gold.
“What caused it?” he asked finally. “Did the Starfall reach even here?”
Atver’s eyes closed briefly, and when he spoke, something had shifted in his voice — old grief worn smooth by centuries of carrying it.
“The Starfall’s primary target was the capital. The Concord.” He said the name carefully, like something handled with tongs. “They sat at the center of this region. Grew powerful — too powerful, in the end, for any one steward to hold responsibly. A dear friend of mine led them, once. A student, if you’d like the honest word for it. He tried to warn them. Tried, for a long time, to hold back what the institution was becoming.” He opened his eyes. “But greed doesn’t listen to warnings. It consumed them, and when the Starfall came, it came for them fully. What was the Concord is a scar now. A reminder of exactly where pride and greed lead — nearly to extinction. Nearly.”
Vael sat with that. Something in his chest tightened without permission — a hot, unfamiliar pressure, sudden and specific.
“For some reason,” he said slowly, “my body feels nothing but hatred toward the — the Concord, was it?”
Atver looked at him for a long moment. He nodded, unsurprised.
“Nothing stays the same,” he said. “The Concord was only ever a nation in its prime, and nations have lifespans like anything else. What comes at the very end of a lifespan is, sadly, almost always the worst version of the thing that came before.” He gestured out at the islands. “These floated free when the debris struck this region. The Starfall was powerful enough to lift mountains, Vael. Don’t ever mistake it for a small thing.”
A voice reached them from below, faint at first, then rapidly less faint.
“You guys — where ARE you?! Vael! Old man! HELLOOO?!”
Vael leaned over the ledge. Trista stood at the base of the outcrop, hands on her hips, radiating a very specific and very familiar kind of fury.
“We’re here! Sorry, Trista!” he called down, in the tone of a man trying to defuse a situation before it fully arrived.
“There you are.” She did not look mollified. “Come on, we need to move. That Dracol isn’t waiting for anyone.” She glanced back toward camp, where — presumably — Figo and James remained exactly as unconscious as Vael had left them, and sighed with real feeling. “Those two get slower every single morning. They need their princess mornings, apparently.”
Vael grinned. He looked at Atver.
“Old man,” he said, “your flight magic is about to become very useful. I have a plan.”
He punctuated this with the worst, most theatrically evil laugh he could manage, which needed some work.

Down at camp, Figo was working through a sandwich of indeterminate origin with the slow, grumpy dedication of a man who resented being awake but respected the sandwich too much to eat it quickly. Sheela lay across his knees. James sat nearby with his morning cup in one hand, humming something tuneless and cheerful to himself, apparently unbothered by anything the universe had to offer him at this hour.
In the treeline behind them, three figures crouched in a low bush, doing an admirable job of not laughing yet.
A minute passed. Figo chewed. The forest held its usual morning quiet.
Then Figo went still.
”…Not to alarm you,” he said slowly, “but I don’t hear Trista anymore, James.”
James took a sip of his drink, entirely unconcerned. “Probably found an interesting plant.” He didn’t look up. He did not, in fact, see any obvious danger, and had long ago decided that most mornings that didn’t obviously contain danger could be trusted not to.
“Now,” Vael whispered.
Figo looked up at the exact moment something bright detached itself from the canopy above — a compressed ball of pure white light, falling with the deliberate accuracy of a woman who’d had a full week to perfect her aim. It detonated a few feet above both men in a silent, blinding flash.
“WAHH—” Figo’s voice hit a register that no man his size had any business producing.
James’s cup went flying. Both men froze, hands over their eyes, entirely and comprehensively stunned.
“WE’RE UNDER ATTACK!” James managed, his voice cracking with the effort of forming words through the aftershock of the flash.
“TRISTA!” Figo bellowed. “VAEL! OLD MAN! ANYONE!”
That was when the tongue found them.
It arrived from the shadows at ground level, long and glistening, trailing a cord of thick, sticky saliva that connected both stunned men in a single unfortunate strand before either of them registered what had happened. The Flesh Toad’s tongue withdrew as quickly as it had come, leaving both warriors dripping and abruptly, violently awake.
“AAAAAA—” James’s shriek, when it finally arrived, came out in a register that could charitably be described as unmanly. He did not care.
Vael hit the ground laughing, unable to hold himself upright, tears actually forming. Trista landed a moment later — a perfect, graceful three-point landing directly from the tree above, entirely composed, entirely delighted with herself.
“Wakey wakey,” she said sweetly.
“That’s not fair,” Figo said, wiping toad saliva from his face with an expression of profound betrayal.
“At least our teamwork’s improving,” James said, trying very hard to sound unbothered and mostly succeeding, aside from the residual dampness on his sleeve. “Also, that scream. That was the bird. Not me.”
“Sure it was, buddy,” Trista said.
“It was.”
“I won’t tell the shadow lady about it,” Trista said, entirely too sweetly, “if you’re ready in five minutes.”
James threw his cask into his pack with the speed of a man suddenly and completely motivated. Figo, muttering something about dignity and toad saliva, wiped Sheela down carefully and strapped her back into place, and within the promised five minutes the whole camp was packed and moving, the morning’s indignity already folding itself into the growing pile of stories the team would apparently never let each other forget.

The path east ran through a stretch of hardy, wind-bent trees, the ground rising in low, rolling shelves of stone that suggested the land here had once been much more violently rearranged than it currently appeared. The air smelled of cold stone and pine resin, clean in a way that made the destruction elsewhere feel briefly distant.
Then the path curved sharply around an outcrop, and Vael, walking point, stopped.
“Look!”
Ahead, half-swallowed by undergrowth at the path’s edge, a caravan lay tipped on its side. Abandoned. One wheel had come free entirely and lay several feet from the wreckage, and the canvas covering had torn along one long seam, flapping faintly in the cold wind.
“I smell trouble,” Figo said immediately, scanning the treeline on both sides, Sheela already coming off his back.
“We should check for survivors.” Trista was already moving, quick and low, circling toward the wreck.
There were none. The caravan was entirely empty — no bodies, no belongings left behind that suggested a controlled departure. Just abandonment, sudden and total.
“There are signs of a struggle here.” James crouched near the overturned frame, his usual looseness gone, his attention narrow and focused. He touched a dark patch on the splintered wood, careful not to press too hard. “Recent. This blood isn’t dry yet.”
He looked up. His eyes followed a trail — dark spots, spaced with the irregular rhythm of something dragged or something fleeing, leading away from the wreck and deeper into the trees ahead.
Nobody said anything for a moment.
“Well,” Atver said, mildly, into the silence. “That’s a promising start to the day.”
