“Those people asked for terms three times, and were answered with a fourth engine.” He said it without heat, as one reads out a date. “It is in your own archives. I have read the copies. I can recite the dates, if you wish. I would greatly prefer not to.”
Nobody moved. Even James had found something interesting about his boots.
“And third.” For the first time he turned from the window. “Provided for. Who carried the water, Miss Aava? Who swept the avenues you were so proud of? Who scraped the vents?”
“The maintenance,” said Aava. “The craftsfolk. They were—” And she stopped, because she did not know the rest of the sentence.
“Quite,” said Atver, and his voice, for the first time all evening, was almost gentle. “I do not say it to wound you. I say it because you are asking why it ended so badly, and the answer is not the sky. The sky only cut the rope.”
For a long moment she looked at the ledger on her knee, at the tidy columns, at the neat pencil that hung from her neck on its string.
“I was taught otherwise,” she said at last, very quietly. “By people I trusted.”
“Most of us were. That is how it works.” He inclined his head, and the monocle caught the lamp. “You are asking a better question than you know. Hold on to it.”
“I think that is the cruelest part,” said Aava. “Not that it ended. That I lived inside it so long, and thought it was mine.”
The lamp burned low and blue in its hood. Far to the north, a long dark shine lay across the roofs like a spill of ink that had set, and at the heart of the bowl the thread of smoke glowed a small, steady red.
“We came to kill that,” said Vael.
He had not planned to say it. It came out of him because the room had gone still, and because the girl had given them water and a floor and the truth, and he had nothing to give her but his own.
“The Dracol,” said Aava.
“You know it?”
“I watched it arrive.” She rose and went to the window, and stood with her arms folded, looking out. “Nine days ago, over the north-western rim, on a wind like an oven door being opened. I have never seen anything so large. It was bleeding fire from the shoulder, from a seam in its plates, and one of its channels had gone dark, and it flew like something that was ashamed to be seen flying.” Her voice had dropped. “It did not come straight to the Seat. It fed first. Do you see that long dark shine to the north, where the roofs have run like wax? That was its table. It crept in a district at a time, eating the foundries, drinking the slag, sleeping in what was left, and I watched the glow of it from this window for four nights. And then, three nights before you came down, the whole bowl began to shake. It rose. It circled the Seat three times. Then it went down on the throne plaza and coiled itself around the throne as if it were a stove, and it hasn’t stirred since. Except to roar.”
“We know,” said Trista.
“Then you know why I shiver.” Aava’s arms tightened. “The Foundry sent twelve people to the Seat in the second week. They wanted the vents beneath the plaza, because they stay warm. That was before the beast. Two came back. Neither could tell me what they’d seen. One of them has not spoken since.”
“Do you think we can kill it?” said Vael.
She did not turn.
“No,” she said.
Nobody breathed.
“I’m sorry. You asked. I have lived six weeks by being honest about numbers.” She turned from the window then, and looked at them, one at a time, at the cracked-lipped, ash-grey five of them, and something in her face softened. “But I think you are on the right road. Because nobody else is going at all.”

The hum began a little after midnight.
By then the others had settled, wrapped in the blankets she had pulled from a chest, laid in a row along the curve of the wall like seeds in a furrow. Trista had insisted on checking Aava’s chest after she’d heard her cough, a small dry hack, three times in an hour, and Aava had submitted with the grim politeness of someone who had never been looked after in her life. Trista’s palm had glowed against her ribs, white and gentle, and when the light faded, Aava had stood in the middle of the room with her hand half raised and her mouth a little open.
“It’s quiet,” she said, in a very small voice. “My chest is quiet. I haven’t breathed all the way in since the Stopping.”
“It was the ash,” said Trista. “It’ll come back if you stay in it, but not so fast.”
Aava had not said anything to that. She had gone and sat on the stool with her back to them, for rather a long time.
Now Vael lay awake and listened to something that was not a sound.
It was a vibration. It came up through the floor, through the bones of his back, a note so low that the ear could not hold it, only the chest. It rose and held, and fell, like the note a very large man might hum with his mouth closed.
“It’s been doing that since the night of the Stopping,” said Aava’s voice from the dark.
She was sitting up in her cot. She had not slept either. “At first I thought it was my own pulse. Then I put a cup of water on the sill, and it shook. Look.”
On the sill, beside the moss, a tin cup trembled. Rings ran across the water inside it, small and perfect, in time with the note.
Beside the window, Atver stood in the dark with his back to the room. He had not lain down. He had not touched his broth. He had been standing there for an hour, with his palm laid flat against the wall, and the lens of his monocle burned a strange deep gold.
“It began the night the thread snapped,” he said quietly. “Not before.”
“The night after the Stopping,” said Aava, surprised. “Yes.”
“And it rises, a hair a week. And since the beast came, it has been steadier.” He did not say it as a question. “The beast did not choose the plaza by chance. It went to the warm place, and the warm place is warm because of what lies beneath it.”
“The Seat has a lower city.” Aava’s voice dropped. “My father went down to it every morning of my life, by a stair I was never to use, and came back smelling of hot oil, and never once said a word about what he did there. I used to watch from the gallery. The Provost’s Stair, they called it. A red arch on the east wall, with an iron door.” She hesitated. “In the week after the Stopping, I went to the door. I wanted to know what he had been doing down there. It was sealed. I put my ear to the iron, and something on the other side was breathing. Not like a person. Like a bellows as big as a house.”
Atver had turned. In the light of the blue lamp his face was unreadable, but behind the lens his eyes had begun to glow, faintly, with something Vael had never seen in them: a deep, quiet, very old hunger. The light of the monocle spilled over his cheekbone like gold.
“You were taught,” he said, “that the Seat spoke.”
“The Voice,” said Aava. “We had whisper-stones on every street, black pillars, one at every corner. When the Seat spoke, every stone spoke, and every engine in earshot listened. It was how the whole Imperium thought one thought. It went silent the morning of the Stopping.” She tilted her head. “But they hum now. All of them. Very faintly. The same note as this.”
“The Seat never said a word, child. It is a chair. What spoke was the thread beneath the world, and the stones were only its ears.” He took his palm from the wall and looked at it. “I have wondered for six weeks what else the Voice did. I think I know. I think it did more than give orders. I think it also said not yet.”
“Not yet to what?” said Trista, from the dark.
“The old workers had a saying,” said Aava slowly. “I heard it as a child, from the kitchen. I thought it was a joke. Never wake the one that moves mountains.”
Something went through Atver. It was not a flinch. It was quieter and stranger than that, the look of a man hearing the first bar of a song he had feared he’d forgotten. The gold in his lens flared to white.
“It is not a joke,” he said. “I will tell you what it is, once, and then I should like never to say it again.”
Nobody spoke.
“Beneath the Seat, behind doors that closed themselves, there is an engine that was never made to carry, or dig, or serve. The Imperium built it for the day a mountain stood between its armies and something it wanted. It does not hunt. It does not chase. It sends small things ahead of it, little flying eyes that walk the ground and drop marks, and it looks at what it has marked from beyond the horizon, and it begins to fire. It fires in lines. It fires in domes. It does not stop. When it has finished with a mountain, there is a hole where the mountain was, and when it has finished with a city, the ground itself, at the end, falls in.”
Vael found that he was sitting up. He did not remember doing it.
“Its makers gave it one instruction,” said Atver. “Continue until nothing stands. And then, being careful people, they built a voice that could tell it to stop.”
“And the Voice is silent,” said Vael.
“And the Voice is silent, and the engine is warm, and a Dracol has lain down on top of it. Twice a night it roars. Every roar is a hand on the sleeper’s shoulder.” He looked at the wall. “I should very much like for the vaults to stay sealed. I said so. I meant it.” A pause. “I did not say I had no wish to see what was inside them.”
“You knew,” said Vael.
“I suspected.”
“You said you’d tell me enough to get us moving in the right direction.”
“And have I?”
Vael thought of the tavern, and of the neutral, careful expression on the old elf’s face when he’d said that civilization was engaged in work it should not have been. “You have,” he admitted.
“Then I have kept my word.” Atver turned away again, toward the window. “I will tell you the rest in the morning, child. Sleep. You are going to need it.”

Vael did not know how long he slept. When he woke, the room was dark and the lamp turned so low that its blue core was a seed of light in the hood. The hum was in the floor. Along the curved wall the others lay in their blankets: Figo on his back with Sheela on his chest, Trista curled on her side, James with one arm flung across the cask. Atver’s place by the wall was empty, and a faint creak below told him the old elf was walking the ridge, as he did when he thought nobody was watching.
Aava was at the window.
She sat on the sill with her knees drawn up, looking out at the bowl, and did not turn when he came to stand beside her. At the far center of the plain a red glow lay along the rooftops of the capital, steady as a banked fire, and against it stood the dark crown of towers and three round domes, green with age, clustered like eggs in a nest.
“You should sleep,” said Vael.
“So should you.”
“I tried.”
“So did I.” She did not look at him. “That ring. Hold it up.”
He did, puzzled. In the dark the stone in it gave off a dull deep red, like a coal at the bottom of a banked fire, and now that he looked, it was brighter than it had been at noon, a little, in time with the hum.
“It does that near the beast,” he said. “Or near whatever is under it. It started a few days ago.”
“A ring that glows like a coal,” said Aava, to the window. “A wolf made of shadow. A boy who says the word Dracol like a man naming someone who owes him money.” She turned, then, and for the first time there was nothing careful in her face. It was only tired, and very watchful. “Where did you get it?”
“I don’t know.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It’s the only one I have.”
He had meant to say something short. But she waited, the way no one had waited for him in six weeks, without filling the silence, and it came out of him in a rush. He told her about waking in a tavern bed with nothing, no name, no face in the mirror he recognized, and a stranger kind enough to let him stay. He told her about the shadow that came out of his hand before his mind knew how, and the hand sign, and the other two summons, and the word Trista had said to him one morning, in the rising light: Dragodor. He told her about his mother. Saela. A woman in white, a hunter and a mage, whom he could only reach in dreams, and who had said, once, You must defeat the Dracol. You are our only hope, and who had said, I love you, son, and he had no face to put to the voice.
“I’ve been collecting her,” he said. “From other people. A woman who knew her told me she wore spotless white robes and kept to a plan even when she should have adapted. I’ve never met her. Not that I remember. I carry her around in pieces.” He rubbed his face. “And every day I wake up and I think, today it’ll come back. Today I’ll just know. And it doesn’t. And I feel like I’m running out of time, and I’m so—” He stopped. “I’m tired of being furious at a hole.”
Aava was silent a while. When she spoke, her voice had changed. It was not softer, exactly. It had simply stopped being a wall.
“My mother’s voice,” she said. “Do you know, I could not remember it. For weeks after. I’d close my eyes and try, and there was only the silence where it should have been. I made myself ill with trying.” She turned the ledger-pencil that hung from her neck on its string. “And one afternoon I was scrubbing a pot. In the second month. A common iron pot, with a rag. And without any warning, she was there, saying my name from the next room the way she used to, a little impatient, a little fond. As clear as a bell. I dropped the pot.”
“What did you do?”
“I finished the pot.” She smiled. “It had to be finished. But I remembered, afterward, that I’d stopped looking for her an hour before.”
“So I should stop trying.”
“I think the past is rather like a road,” said Aava. “You can stare at the horizon all day, and it will not come any closer. It only comes when you are walking.” She tilted her head, not looking at him. “You are already walking, Vael. I wouldn’t worry about the rest. It knows where to find you.”
He found he had nothing to say to that. It sat in his chest and was warm there, like something swallowed very hot.
“Then I owe you something true,” said Aava. “I find I cannot spend the whole night being clever.”
He waited.
“I was told to look for you.”
The hum rose in the stones. Vael did not move.
“Not by name. A woman came to this tower in the first week after the Stopping, when I had been four days in a cistern and had begun to talk to the water. She came in through a door I had barred, and put a tin on the table, and sat down as if she had been invited. She had a bow, and a coat that drank the lamplight, and a way of crossing the ash without leaving a mark. She never gave me a name.”
“Varesa,” said Vael.
Aava’s head turned. “You know her.”
“She fought beside us once.” He considered it. “I don’t trust her. I don’t think she means me harm. I don’t think she would tell me if she did.”
“That is exactly my position,” said Aava, dryly, and for a moment something that was almost fellow-feeling crossed her face. “She has fed me since. A tin, a brick, a jar of salt, every ninth day, left at the foot of the ladder. In exchange I watch the Gate Road and keep a count of who comes through it. That is all. A column of names and dates. I have never been told whom it goes to, and I have never been foolish enough to ask.” She drew her knees in. “I know the word for people who do that sort of work. Everyone in the Imperium knew the word and nobody knew a face. The Vigil. I am not one of them, Vael. I am a woman with a pencil who has to eat.”
She had said it fast, the way one pulls a splinter. Now she sat rigid on the sill with her chin up and her hands knotted around her knees, braced for whatever came next: the flinch, the cold look, the hand drifting to a weapon. She had plainly decided which of them she could bear.
Vael gave her none of them. He turned it over slowly. A tin on a table. A girl four days in a cistern, so hungry and so alone that she had begun to talk to the water, and a stranger walking in out of the dark with a bow, a quiet voice, and the only food in the bowl. He thought of the tavern, and of waking with no name, and of a stranger’s kindness being the one thing between him and the street. He knew what it was to take what was offered because there was nothing else to take, and to hate yourself a little for how grateful you were.
She didn’t choose a side, he thought. She chose a meal.
And the room looked different to him then. The squared corners on the cot. The ledger, kept so carefully. The water measured out level in five cups to five strangers, when she could have drunk it alone. It had never been a hiding place. It was a debt, kept in perfect order by someone who was terrified of defaulting on it.
Something in his chest eased and ached at the same moment.
“I know,” said Vael. He said it gently, and he meant all of it.
“Four days ago she came at dusk and said that five would walk the Gate Road, out of the sky. That one of them would carry a ring that burned like a coal. She said: Feed them. Tell me what they do.” Her mouth twisted. “Then the light came down, and I thought I had imagined it. And then you came out of the Gatecut looking like a dropped basket of laundry, and I thought: well. Not very impressive. But it fits.”
“You’re right about the laundry,” said James, from the dark. Nobody had known he was awake.
“James,” said Trista, from elsewhere in the dark.
“I’m asleep.”
Aava did not smile. “Tonight I am supposed to write that you are five hungry fools and that one of you wears a ring. I am telling you instead, because you told me something true, and I find I cannot write the lie. I will write something, Vael. I have to. There is no other tin.”
“Then write it,” said Vael.
She stared at him. “I beg your pardon?”
“Write what you need to. You have to eat.” He turned the ring on his finger. It was quiet now, a coal going dull. “I know some of them. Vigil. Not the ones who sent her. A few who want to change the sound of that name. And right now they want what we want, which is the beast dead. I would rather you ate and told them that than starved and told them nothing.”
“They want it dead,” said Aava slowly. “And so do you.”
“That is all I know of what they want.”
“For now,” she said, “is a phrase I have learned to listen for.”
“So have I.”
She looked at him for a long moment. Then, quite suddenly, she laughed, one short, startled breath, the sound of a person who has been braced against a door for weeks and found that it opened outward. “You are a very strange person to be saving anything.”
“I’m not saving it. I keep walking into it.”
She turned back to the window. The red glow lay along the rooftops, steady as a banked fire.
“Do you see the three domes? The middle one.”
“I see them.”
“I grew up under that one.” She said it flatly, the way one reads out an address. “The one with the broken finial. That was my father’s house. You can see the roof of my bedroom from here, if you know where to look, which I do, and which is why I’m up here at this hour every night, being foolish.”
He did not say anything. After a moment she went on.
“My father was an important man, Vael. I’m not going to tell you what he was, because I don’t know. I was twenty-one years old and I did not know what my own father did for a living.” She laughed, very shortly, and it was not a good sound. “I knew he went down the Provost’s Stair every morning. I knew he was respected. I knew that people stood up when he came into a room. I knew we had a cook, and a cellar, and a garden in the atrium with a tree in it that was older than the house. I knew that I was going to work beside him one day, in his work, and that it was something important and clean and very much needed, and I was proud of that. I never once asked what it was.”
The red light slid across her face. She did not seem to notice.
“The morning of the Stopping was his birthday. There was a cake. I was on the gallery over the plaza, because the family sat there for the Seat’s ceremonies, and I was holding the ribbon for him to cut. And the engines stopped.” She said it very evenly. “Not slowly. All at once, all of them, mid-step. Do you know what it is like to live your whole life on the back of something that carries everything, and have it let go? The haulers fell on the crowds that were under them. The pipes burst along the avenues. The vault doors came down, and some people were still standing in them.” She drew a breath. “My father was on the steps of the Seat. He wasn’t quick enough. I’m not going to tell you more than that. They weren’t quick deaths, and I saw every one.”
“Aava—”
“No, let me finish. I’ve never said it out loud. It’s very strange, to find that one can.” Her hands had tightened around her knees. “That was the first thing. Nobody tells you about the second.”
“The second?”
“The people who carried the water,” she said. “The ones who swept the avenues and scraped the vents and carried the ash out of the foundries in baskets on their backs. They had been waiting. Not for the sky to fall. For the first morning there was nobody left to stop them. They went up the hill with whatever they had in their hands, and they were not looking for a cause, they were looking for a house.” Her voice shook, and steadied. “I hid in a cistern for four days. I cut my hair with a kitchen knife. I learned to say pass in their accent, and to stand the way they stand, and not to say thank you too nicely. And I learned that I had been living for twenty-one years in a house built over a pit, and that the people at the bottom of the pit had been making the house the whole time, and that in all my life I had not once asked a single one of them their name. The old elf asked me tonight who carried the water, and I have lain here counting. In a house with ninety servants, I know the names of four.”
Vael stood very still.
“They were right to hate us,” said Aava. “I think about that every night. I wish they’d been a little less right about me.”
She was crying. She was doing it quite silently, without any sound at all, with her chin up and her eyes fixed on the red glow on the horizon, the way a child cries who has been taught that it is rude to be seen. It was the most dignified and terrible thing he had ever watched, and he found that he had no words for it at all.
“I thought every morning would be my last,” she said. “For weeks. I still wake sometimes and I’m surprised.”
“It wasn’t your fault,” Vael said.
“It wasn’t me who built it.” She wiped her face with the back of a grey-scrubbed hand. “But I ate from it.”
For a long moment neither of them spoke. The hum rose and held in the stones.
“After the beast is dead,” Vael said, “I’m going to find a way to get you out.”
She turned her head.
“All of you. The whole bowl. Back across the sea, to the mainland. There’s a world on the other side of it, and it’s alive, and it has fields and trees and people who’ll take you in. Nobody should have to live like this. Nobody deserves to.”
“That is a very large promise.”
“I know.”
“You can’t build a boat out of a promise.”
“No.” He found, to his surprise, that he was smiling, a small, tired, unsteady smile. “But I know people who might know how. A woman who built an elevator to the sky. A man who kept a whole town alive in a bunker through the worst day of its life. I don’t know how yet. I’m not going to tell you I do.” He met her eyes. “But I’ll find a way. And Dorrek goes first.”
“Dorrek.”
“He’s the one who asked for a boat.”
She stared at him. Then something unexpected happened in her face. It cracked, softly, at the corners, and out of the crack came a smile, small and startled and entirely real, the first she had let him see. It changed her whole face. It took years off her.
“That is the most honest promise anyone has ever made me,” said Aava. “You’ve no idea how to do it, and you’ve said so.” She wiped her eyes again, and this time she was laughing, just a little. “Very well. I’ll hold you to it. And in return, I’ll make mine. Whatever I have, you may have. It is lent to me by a woman I do not trust, but it is mine to lend. The cistern. The way down to the Seat.” She hesitated. “I mean, it is the party’s.”
“Thank you,” said Vael.
“Don’t mention it.” She seemed to find the sill extremely interesting for a moment. She tucked a strand of hair behind her ear, discovered that it was too short to tuck, and put her hand down quickly.
“I’m afraid I’m no help with the Dracol,” she said. “I only know the road.”
“The road is a great deal,” said Vael.
“Go to sleep,” said Aava. “You’ve a beast to kill, and I’ve a ledger to balance.” And then, a moment later, to the dark and the red light on the horizon, not turning her head: “Thank you for saying it.”
“I haven’t done it yet.”
“I know,” said Aava. “But nobody had said it before.”

The morning meal was a brick each and half a cup of broth, and it was the most pleasant breakfast any of them could remember.
Trista had woken early and washed her face in a spoonful of cistern water. Figo had slept so deeply that Sheela had slid off his chest in the night and he had woken clutching a corner of the blanket and had to be reassured. James had spent a quarter of an hour examining Aava’s shelf of tins with the frank interest of a connoisseur, until she took one out of his hand and put it back without a word.
It was James who noticed.
He noticed it the way he noticed most things, in the middle of a mouthful, and he went on chewing for some time with his eyes sliding from Aava to Vael and back, like a man watching a very small and interesting card game. Vael was telling Figo about the wolf. Aava was refilling his cup. She had refilled it twice already, to the brim, and the other cups only to the level mark.
“Our host,” James observed, to the room in general, “has a very generous ladle.”
“I beg your pardon?” said Aava.
“Oh, nothing. Just that she’s been looking at Vael since sunrise like he’s the last tin on the shelf.”
There was a small silence.
“I look at tins,” said Aava, with great dignity, “with considerably more suspicion.”
Trista choked on her broth. Figo, who had not understood any of it, looked from face to face with the pleasantly bewildered expression of a large dog at a wedding. Aava’s cheeks had gone the color of the stove’s coals, but her chin was up, and her voice, when it came, was crisp and cool as a ledger.
“If you would like to inspect the cistern, Mr. James, I would be glad to push you into it.”
“I’m just saying,” said James happily, “if there’s a spare room in this tower, I have never been so well placed to deliver a toast.”
“James,” said Trista.
“What are you talking about?” said Vael, genuinely puzzled, and the whole room burst out laughing, Figo a beat late and mostly because everyone else was. Even Aava did, behind her hand. Vael looked around at them with a baffled, good-natured frown, and went on eating his brick, the only one at the table neither laughing nor in on it.

Atver was waiting for them at the foot of the tower.
They came down the rope ladder one by one into a grey dawn, with the wind coming warm and slow from the east. He stood on the road with his pack at his feet, the same pack he had carried since the tavern. He had cleaned his monocle and brushed the ash from his burgundy robe. He looked, for the first time in all the weeks Vael had known him, like a man dressed for a journey that was not theirs.
“You are going,” said Vael.
“I am going.”
He had known it since the night. He had known it, perhaps, since the tavern. It did not make it any easier.
“I told you I came to learn why the Dracol is what it is,” said Atver. “That is true, as far as it goes. This is the rest of it.” He folded his hands. “The beast lies on a warm plate above a thing that was built to take mountains apart. The thing is waking, a hair a week, and the one voice that could tell it not yet has been silent since the Stopping. You will fight the beast. That is right, and I would not ask you to do otherwise. But you will fight it on top of the sleeper, and I do not think the sleeper will care which of you is winning.” He drew a short breath. “I cannot prevent the one. I can try to see that the other does not become the end of this bowl, and then of the road beyond it. Someone must be below, with a hand on the door. I have read what its makers wrote about it, and none of you have. If it can be told not yet a second time, I am the only one here who knows how to ask.”
“You’re going to the Provost’s Stair,” said Aava.
“If Miss Aava will be so kind as to show me where it begins.”
“And the Dracol?” said Trista. “You were going to fight beside us.”
“I have walked you to its door.” Atver smiled, very faintly. “I believe this is the door. Beyond it you do not need an old man with a monocle. You need each other.” He glanced at Vael. “And if the beast lies where I think it lies, directly above the sleeper, then every moment it holds your attention is a moment nothing below will stir. I shall be grateful for the noise. I should be a great deal less grateful for the blows. Fight it on the road, on the roofs, in the air, wherever you like. Pray do not fight it upon the iron.”
James whistled softly. “So we’re the distraction.”
“You are the reason I will get in,” said Atver. “It is a different thing.”
“Will you write to us?” said James. “Let us know you’re alive?”
“I do not write, James. I annotate.”
Figo, who had been standing with his lip trembling for a full minute, could bear it no longer. He crossed the ash in two strides and caught the old elf up off the ground in both arms. Atver’s feet dangled. The monocle swung on its chain. His face, over Figo’s shoulder, wore an expression of mild and philosophical resignation.
“Please put me down,” he said.
“I can’t,” said Figo, wetly. “I’ve only just got you.”
“Figo.”
“Sorry. Sorry.” He set him down, sniffing, and patted the robe flat with a hand the size of a spade. Atver straightened it and cleared his throat, and for a moment he looked, behind the lens, almost unbearably touched, and then he looked at Figo and said, with perfect gravity, “Mind that she does the thinking. She is the better strategist.”
“I always do,” said Figo.
“I know.” He turned. “Trista.”
She had already stepped forward, and she gave him the dip of her head, grave and gracious. “I’ll miss your lectures.”
“You will not. But you are kind to say so.” He regarded her a moment. “Keep them alive. You have a talent for it.”
“I’ll do my best.”
“You always do,” said Atver. “That is rather the point.” He looked at James. “You see a great deal more than you tell them. I understand why. I would only ask that, when it matters, you tell them the one thing that counts.” And to Vael, last, he turned fully, and for a long moment he only looked at him.
It was a look Vael could not read. The old elf’s face was composed, as it always was, courteous and dry and difficult, but something moved far back in it and was folded away again before he could name it.
“This is your battle,” said Atver, to all of them, in a quiet voice. “It was never mine. I have walked beside you long enough to say a thing I did not expect to say: I believe the world is in good hands. They are loud, and hungry, and prone to embracing, but they are good.” He drew a breath, and when he spoke again it was only to Vael.
“Do what is right for this world,” he said. “And trust yourself, child.”
Vael found that he could not speak. He nodded.
“That’s all,” said Atver, briskly, shouldering his pack. “That is the whole of my wisdom. I should hate to be thought to have more.”
He went with Aava, in the end, the two of them small against the haze, the old elf in his burgundy robe and the girl in her patchwork, walking east along a path that went by the cisterns and was not the Processional. He walked with his hands behind his back and his head a little bowed, listening, Vael thought, to the hum.
She came back alone, an hour later, climbing the road with her arms wrapped around herself. Her face had the closed, careful look of someone who has done a difficult thing and wishes to say so to no one.
“He’s gone,” she said. “I walked him to the head of the cistern road and told him how to find the red arch. He made me say it back to him three times, as though I might change my mind. Then he thanked me, quite gravely, and told me to go home.” She sat down on a milestone. “He seems to be a very odd man.”
“He’s all right,” said Vael. “He’s the best of us.”
“I’m inclined to agree.”
She got up. She found a length of pipe in the ash and knelt in the dirt and drew with it, a long line, straight, and a circle at the end of it.
“This is the Gate Road,” she said. “It joins the Processional at the Fourth Ring. After that, it is three miles of avenue, dead straight, with the engines on both sides. You’ll be seen from the plaza for the last mile. There’s no help for that. But the engines are tall, and if you keep close to the ranks, you’ll have cover almost to the end.” She tapped the circle. “This is the plaza. At the center is the throne. At the foot of the throne is a circle of iron plates, each as wide as a barn. They’re warm. I don’t know why. Stay off them if you can. It lies there.”
“What about this?” said Trista, pointing to a little mark at the east wall.
“The Auditors’ Gallery. It overlooks the whole plaza. The ceremonies were held below it. If one of you were to stand on that ledge, she could see everything on the iron circle without being seen.” Aava paused. “I’d wager that’s not nothing.”
“It isn’t,” said Vael. He was looking at the line in the dirt, at the long straight road to the Seat. “Aava, thank you.”
“Do not thank me. Do what you promised.”
“I will.”
“Then go.” She stood, and dropped the pipe, and wiped her hands on her patchwork skirt. “Be careful. All of you. Please.” And then she did something she hadn’t done before. She stepped close, and for a single moment she took his hand in both of hers, quickly, like a woman signing a paper, and let it go.
It was brief. It was almost nothing. Behind him, James opened his mouth, and Trista, without turning her head, trod hard on his foot.
They went down the Gate Road in a loose line, four of them now, with Figo’s great shoulders at the front and Sheela’s blade catching the first of the sun. Vael looked back once. She was standing on the milestone with her arms wrapped around herself, small and grey and straight-backed against the black cone, and she raised one hand. He raised his.
The ash took their footprints, one after another, and kept them. By the time they passed the Fourth Ring there was a long line of them stretching back along the road, four sets, wide and narrow, quick and slow. And beside the first milestone, where the road met the tower, a much smaller set stood a long while in the dust before they turned and went back the way they had come.

At the heart of the bowl, on the iron circle, in the red dark under the throne, something old opened one eye.
It had been lying quite still for six nights. It had listened to the machines hum, and to the thing beneath the machines, and to the long cold silence of a dead world. It had licked its wounds, which did not close. And now, on the wind that came across the bowl from the west, it caught a scent it knew. Warm blood. Salt on the skin. Iron and shadow, and a small, stubborn flame.
The black glass of its eyelid slid back.
Come, it thought, in the old tongue, in the slow burning dialect of volcanoes. Come, little ones. I am waiting.

Chapter 5: What We Carry
Part 1 — Zefra
Year 0. The Starfall.
The sky had been wrong for three hours before the screaming started.
Ragnik would remember it that way for the rest of his life — not the moment the first star came down, not the light that turned night into a color the world had no name for, but the screaming, because the screaming was the moment it stopped being something happening far away and became something happening here.
The tavern shook. Somewhere outside, a support beam that had held for two generations gave way with a sound like the earth clearing its throat, and a cloud of grey dust rolled past the windows where blue sky had been that morning.
Zefra was already at the door.
“Zefra, please—” Ragnik had her hand in his, and he was holding it the way you hold something you already suspect you’re about to lose. “We go to the bunker. It’s safer there. We wait it out, we—”
“Look outside.” She didn’t raise her voice. She never needed to. “Look at it, my love. Can’t you see.” Her eyes found his, and there was no fear in them — only the terrible clarity of someone who had already made her decision and was simply waiting for him to catch up to it. “This is the end of the world. If we let it be.”
She pulled her hand free.
“Anyone who can fight — with me.” Her voice carried now, filling the tavern’s main hall, cutting through the noise of falling plaster and frightened voices. “Ragnik. You stay. I’ll bring as many as I can find back to this door. Get them into the bunker. Keep it safe.”
He didn’t stop her the second time. He wanted to. His hand reached and found only air where hers had been.
Three men were already moving toward her — warriors he recognized, regulars, men who drank at his bar and complained about small things and had apparently decided, in the space of one terrible morning, that they were willing to die for strangers. A healer joined them, young, her satchel already open, checking supplies with hands that shook and didn’t stop moving anyway.
Outside, something enormous came down half a mile distant, and the sound of it arrived a full second after the light did, and the light was the color of the inside of a furnace.
Zefra walked out into it without looking back.

The bunker filled through that day the way a wound fills with blood — steadily, terribly, more than the space was built to hold. Children first, herded by whoever could spare the moment. Then the old, the injured, the ones who couldn’t run anymore and had stopped trying. Ragnik counted them as they came, and stopped counting when the number became a shape too large to hold, and simply kept the door open and kept them moving through it.
He caught glimpses of outside every time the door swung — brief, terrible frames of a world rearranging itself into something worse. A street he’d walked a thousand times, unrecognizable. A building that had stood since before his father’s father, gone. And once, just once, far down the road through a gap in the smoke, a figure in familiar robes standing between a fallen wall and a group of huddled survivors, one arm raised, something bright and defiant burning at her palm.
He didn’t get to watch longer than that. The door swung shut. More people needed to come through.
A day passed in the compressed, formless way that terrible days pass — not measured in hours but in the number of people who came through the door and the number who stopped coming.

The three men returned as the light outside was finally starting to fade from wrong to merely dim.
They were carrying someone.
Ragnik’s chest did something complicated and hopeful before he registered the details — the body slung between them was not Zefra’s. It was a young man, unfamiliar, and strangely, impossibly, he looked fine. No burns. No wounds. His face had the soft, untroubled quality of someone deeply asleep rather than someone who had just survived whatever these three men had clearly not survived unscathed.
They set him down carefully near the fire. Then they stood there, all three of them wounded, all three of them not looking at Ragnik.
The healer’s tears had already started.
“Zefra?” Ragnik heard his own voice from somewhere outside himself. “Where is she?”
Nobody answered right away. That was the answer.
“She sacrificed herself for us,” the healer finally managed, her voice breaking apart on the last word. “She—” She couldn’t finish it.
“I’m sorry,” one of the men said. The other two couldn’t lift their eyes from the floor.
Ragnik stood very still. He was holding a box of bread — he would remember that detail forever, the absurd, mundane weight of it in his arms, bread meant for people who were still alive to eat it. He looked down at it as though seeing it for the first time.
He set it down.
He took a breath that cost him more than any breath had ever cost him before.
“Rebecca.” His voice came out steadier than he expected, though it carried a weight underneath the steadiness that would never fully lift. “Help these lads. I need a moment.”
Rebecca — younger then, but already the person she would grow into — looked at him with an expression caught between concern and the understanding that some moments cannot be shared, only permitted. She nodded. “Come on,” she said to the warriors and the healer. “Let’s get you seen to.”
Ragnik walked to the door.

He sat on the porch steps in a world that no longer resembled the one he’d grown up in. The sky still held that wrong color at its edges, fading slowly toward something that might, eventually, become night again. The smell reached him in full now, unfiltered by walls — smoke, and stone dust, and underneath both of those, the specific, unmistakable smell of a world that had lost too much too fast to properly grieve any of it yet.
He sat there and looked at the horizon where he had last seen her.
Then he let out a sound that the world around him absorbed without comment, because the world around him had heard a great many sounds like it that day and had stopped being able to distinguish one grief from another.
It was not a short sound. It carried in it a marriage, and a promise made in a bunker doorway that he was only now understanding the true cost of, and a woman who had walked toward the end of the world because she couldn’t do anything else and still call herself who she was.
When it finally ended, Ragnik sat for a long time in the settling quiet.
Then he stood.
His face, when he turned back toward the door, had changed. The grief was still there — it would always be there, folded somewhere under everything else he would ever do — but something had been built on top of it. A decision. Simple, and total, and entirely without drama.
I will help them. All of them. However many there are, however long it takes.
This will not be the end. Not while I have a door to hold open.
He walked back inside.

Part 2 — The Graves
The current timeline. Present day.
The morning was cold and clean in the way mornings are after something terrible has finished happening. Frost lay thick on the ground behind the tavern, in the small cleared plot where five new mounds of dark earth sat in an uneven row, each one marked with a plain wooden stake.
Ragnik stood at the head of the row with a shovel in his hands, the blade still dark with the last of the turned soil. Three warriors stood behind him with their own shovels, breath fogging in the cold air. Vael. Figo. A third hunter who had ridden the long path and made it home.
“I couldn’t keep my promise,” Ragnik said, to the graves, to no one, to the memory of a bunker doorway and a hand pulling free of his. His voice held, barely, on the last word. A single tear traced down through the lines of his weathered face and he didn’t move to wipe it away.
Vael put a hand on his shoulder.
“I’m sorry,” Vael said. “My plan wasn’t good enough. There should have been a better way. I should have—”
He stopped. The weight of it sat behind his sternum like something physically lodged there — five people, five names he hadn’t learned in time to properly mourn, five families that existed now only in the past tense because of a route he had chosen on a hand-drawn map in a panicked morning. He looked at the graves and felt the particular, hollow devastation of someone measuring the exact size of a mistake against the exact size of the cost, and finding that the two numbers didn’t comfort each other at all.
Ragnik turned to look at him. Whatever was in his face wasn’t blame. It was something closer to the opposite of blame.
“Without your plan,” Ragnik said, “and without every fighter who stood on that ridge — we would be burying more than five.” He looked past Vael to Figo, whose scarred face carried its own version of the same grief. “You’ve all done well. Grief doesn’t mean you failed. It means the cost was real.”
He looked back at the graves. His eyes settled on the third one from the left.
“This one had a family,” he said quietly. “Wife died a month back — injuries from a Dagaruma raid, nothing that could be fixed. His son survived. Made it into the bunker. Raul, the boy’s called. He’s seven.” He was quiet a moment. “I told the father, before he rode out yesterday, that if anything happened to him, I’d take the boy in as my own.” He straightened. “I intend to keep that promise. At least that one.”
He turned and walked toward the tavern door.

Inside, the hall held the particular mixture of a place processing two truths at once — relief at having survived, and grief at the price of it. People moved quietly. Someone was crying softly near the hearth. Someone else was laughing, once, briefly, at something a friend had said, and then looking guilty about the laugh.
Ragnik pushed the door open and raised his voice — not loud, but carrying.
“Everyone.” The hall turned toward him. “I know we’ve just survived death. I know we’re grieving. But we have to prepare — we’re low on supplies, and we need to move before that becomes a second crisis on top of the first.”
Atver, who had been sitting near the hearth with his book closed on one finger to mark his place, rose and produced a folded map from inside his robes. He unfolded it across the nearest table — old, detailed, clearly drawn before the world had rearranged itself into its current shape.
“Your best option is here.” He tapped a point on the map.
“The volcano?” Figo said, eyebrows climbing.
“Yes.” Atver didn’t look up. “There will almost certainly be a village at its base. If there is, it survived the Starfall — that region has held stable since Year 0. Volcanic regions are resource-rich besides. You’ll be welcomed.”
James, seated nearby with his boots up on a second chair and an expression of profound unconcern, glanced at Ragnik and gave a single confirming nod. “Your best bet,” he agreed.
In the corner, Trista moved between three injured hunters, her hands glowing faint and steady, her focus entirely on the work in front of her.

The packing began in earnest — the particular controlled chaos of an entire community preparing to move at once. Boxes stacked by the door. Blankets rolled and tied. Rebecca moving through it all with a list in her head and an answer for every question thrown at her.
Vael found Atver at the edge of it, still bent over his map.
“You said you know where it went,” Vael said. “The Dracol.”
“A lead,” Atver corrected, without looking up. “Here.” His finger moved to a wide stretch of territory east of the tavern, marked in old ink with a name that had clearly once meant something grander. “The Molten Imperium. Whatever remains of it will be Machine Wastes now, after the Starfall did what it did.” He finally looked up, and something in his expression was carefully, deliberately neutral. “That civilization was engaged in work it should not have been engaged in. Its absence is not, on the whole, a loss to mourn.”
“You’re not telling me everything,” Vael said.
“No,” Atver agreed pleasantly. “I am telling you enough to get us moving in the correct direction.” He rolled the map with brisk, precise movements. “I’ll join your party. There’s more to uncover about this variant — why it’s raging, why now, why this one — and I intend to uncover it. The Wastes are roughly a month’s ride from here.”
“We can’t spare the horses,” Ragnik said, passing with an armful of boxes, not slowing. “Every animal we have goes to the caravan. The people need them more than the road does.”
Atver considered this without visible distress. “Two months, then. On foot.”
Vael looked around at his team. James, still reclined, radiating the specific unbothered calm of a man who had already seen this conversation happen and approved of the outcome. Figo, fully recovered now, Sheela steady on his back, ready in the particular way of a man who processes grief by preparing to act on it. Trista, still working, her hands never quite stopping even as she listened.
“We go to the Molten Imperium,” Vael said. His hand closed into a fist. “We end this. Whatever it costs.”
Atver nodded once, satisfied.
“Then we help however we can today,” Vael continued. “And leave at first light tomorrow.”

The rest of the day dissolved into work.
Figo carried what Figo could carry, which was considerably more than most, hauling crates and furniture toward the waiting carts with Sheela strapped across his back the entire time, refusing every offer of help with the specific stubbornness of a man who needed his hands full of something. Trista moved between the injured and the packing in equal measure, splitting her attention and her strength across both without complaint, though the exhaustion showed in the set of her shoulders by midafternoon. James, surprisingly, turned out to be genuinely useful at logistics — directing traffic, sorting priority from clutter, occasionally producing a piece of information about probable weather or road conditions that he had no obvious way of knowing and declining to explain how he knew it.
Vael threw himself into the work wherever the line was thinnest: lashing crates onto the carts, hauling water, taking the weight of loads that were too heavy for the people carrying them. It was easier than thinking. Somewhere in the middle of it, he noticed Raul, the boy Ragnik had named at the graves, sitting apart from the others near the wagon wheels, small and quiet, watching everyone else move with a stillness that didn’t belong on a child his age.
Vael sat down next to him. He didn’t say anything at first. Neither did Raul.
“Your dad,” Vael finally said, carefully, “did something that mattered. All of them did.” He looked at the wagons, the packed boxes, the people preparing to survive another day because of choices made on a battlefield. “It doesn’t make it hurt less. I know that.”
Raul didn’t answer. But he leaned, very slightly, against Vael’s side, and Vael let him.

Evening came, and with it, the last of the light Ragnik would see from this porch as its owner.
He walked the tavern’s ground floor alone after most had gone to sleep, running his hand along the bar he’d built with his own two arms — one of them, now, the only one he had — and the shelves, and the door frame that had held a thousand comings and goings since the day the world ended and he’d decided to keep it open anyway.
He stopped at the window that faced the horizon Zefra had walked toward, that terrible morning not so long ago.
“We made it,” he said quietly, to no one, to the glass, to the memory behind it. “Longer than I thought we would. I kept the door open, Zefra. Like I promised.” He was quiet for a moment. “I’m taking the boy. Raul. I told his father I would, and I’m keeping that one too.” He touched the window frame once, lightly. “I don’t know where this next part takes any of us. But I think you’d have liked them. The ones I’m sending out to finish what you couldn’t.”
He stood there a while longer.
Then he went to bed, because morning was coming whether he was ready for it or not.

Part 3 — First Light
The yard outside the tavern was full of the particular energy of a departure that has been dreaded and prepared for in equal measure.
Two directions. Ragnik’s caravan, loaded and ready, would head south toward safer, more populated ground — the people, the children, Raul small and solemn at Rebecca’s side, already looking like he belonged there. And east, on foot, with packs and weapons and whatever they could carry, the five who were going the other way.
Ragnik found Vael last, when most of the goodbyes had already been said and the yard had thinned to its final moments.
Vael took his hand. He held it, and found, as he suspected he would, that he had absolutely no idea what to say. Every sentence that arrived in his head seemed too small for what it was trying to hold.
“Thank you, Ragnik,” he settled on, finally. “For everything.”
Ragnik’s grip was firm despite the missing arm, despite the years, despite everything the morning was asking of him.
“It’s not me you should thank.” He looked at Vael’s face for a long moment — really looked, the way he had that first morning in room ten. “My wife gave her life so yours could continue. Whatever that was worth to her, it’s yours to spend now. So spend it.” His mouth twitched, almost a smile. “Go and beat that oversized orange rock.”
Somewhere behind them, James made a sound that was unmistakably a laugh, quickly and unsuccessfully disguised as a cough.
Ragnik released Vael’s hand. He looked at the rest of them — Figo, Trista, James, Atver — and gave a single nod that held in it everything a man like Ragnik allowed himself to say out loud.
Then the caravan moved south, and the five of them turned east, and the tavern that had been the first solid ground under Vael’s feet since he woke up with no memory at all grew smaller behind them, and then smaller still, until it was only a shape on the horizon, and then it wasn’t anything at all.
The road ahead ran east, toward the place where sky broke into floating stone, and beyond that, toward wastes that had once been an empire, and somewhere past all of it, an enraged and wounded thing that was, even now, healing in the dark and waiting to be found.
The journey had begun.

← Chapter 4 · The Aftermath · Chapter 6 →

lore-and-stories/stories/the-eleven-year.title: The Eleven Years
lore-and-stories/stories/the-eleven-year.content:
What follows is a reconstruction from several sources: personal correspondence recovered from the outer archive, internal Vigil records recovered separately, and two accounts from individuals who served under Kael Sorveth during his tenure as First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate. The accounts were given to different people at different times and agree on the events while disagreeing on what the events meant.
Kael Sorveth is the only leader in the Imperium’s recorded history who the Witness Body never formally assessed. The trial record for his selection cycle is missing from the outer archive. The body’s private files have not been recovered. Whether the gap is administrative accident or something else is not established.
— The Archivist

I. The Man Who Won
Kael Sorveth passed the trials at thirty-one, which was young — most candidates who reached the final examination were closer to forty, carrying the accumulated weight of two decades of administrative experience and strategic positioning. He carried eleven years of frontier posting and a reputation, among the people who had worked under him, for being difficult to lie to.
He was not magnetic in the way that leaders in the records tend to be described. He was attentive. He remembered things people had said months earlier and referenced them accurately, which unsettled people who were used to being managed rather than heard. He asked questions that had obvious answers and waited to see if you gave the obvious answer or the true one, and he remembered which you had given.
He passed the Physical Trial with competence rather than distinction. He passed the Strategic Trial with something the examining records describe, in the only surviving notation, as an approach not previously observed. The Witness Examination is not on record.
He was appointed First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate at thirty-two and spent the next several years doing his job with the same attentiveness he had brought to everything else — listening to the district reports, walking the supply routes himself, learning the names of the forge workers in each complex he visited. Not because it was good for morale, though it was. Because he was interested. He had always been interested in how things actually worked rather than how they were described as working, and the gap between those two things, in the Eastern Directorate, was considerable.
He did not, in those early years, think much about the Witness Body. It was an institution. It had administered the trials for longer than anyone could remember and produced the leadership the Imperium required. He had passed through it and come out the other side and that was, as far as he understood, the extent of their relationship.
He was wrong about this, but it took him years to understand how wrong.

II. The First Thing He Noticed
It was a small thing, and he almost missed it.
He was reviewing the previous administrator’s resource allocation records — standard practice for a new posting — and found a pattern in the forge complex assignments that didn’t follow the stated logic. Certain production runs were allocated to specific complexes for reasons the paperwork described as efficiency, but the efficiency calculation didn’t hold up when he worked through it himself. Complex Seventeen, specifically, appeared in the records more than its production capacity warranted, and in the years where it appeared most frequently, its output records were either absent or unusually brief.
He made a note. He did not file a report. He had learned, in eleven years on the frontier, that filing reports about things you didn’t yet understand was how you ended up in conversations you weren’t ready for.
Over the following months he found three more things that didn’t follow the stated logic. Each was small. Each was deniable. Together they suggested that some portion of the Directorate’s resources were being allocated to purposes that the standard administrative record didn’t describe, authorized by an office whose documentation he could find referenced but whose actual files he could not locate.
He mentioned this to his deputy administrator, Eryn Voss, over a working dinner. Not as a formal concern — as a puzzle. He framed it as an administrative inefficiency he was trying to trace. She was a careful woman, twelve years his senior, and she listened without expression and said she would look into it.
She came back to him three days later and said she hadn’t been able to find anything either, and changed the subject, and he noted the way she changed the subject — a fraction too smoothly, a fraction too quickly — and filed that away alongside everything else.
He didn’t push. He had time.

III. Varek
The Witness Body member who broke first was not who anyone would have predicted.
His name was Varek — a quiet man, slight, who had been on the inner body for twenty-two years and was known among his colleagues, to the extent that anything personal was known among them, for the precision of his thinking and the absence of anything resembling doubt. He had been the one, in three separate deliberations, to articulate the third position — the argument that risk must be assessed not by what a person has done but by what they might do, the logic that had closed Beth’s variable and a dozen others before her. He had made the argument calmly and been agreed with and moved on.
He encountered Sorveth at a district review in the second year of the administrator’s tenure. These reviews were standard — the body maintained observers at significant administrative postings, a practice so embedded in the institution’s structure that it had stopped requiring justification. Varek was not the observer; he was there in an official capacity, representing the body at the quarterly resource assessment. Sorveth was running the meeting.
What happened at the meeting was unremarkable. What happened afterward, when Sorveth detained him briefly on his way out to ask about a resource allocation discrepancy he had noticed — the same discrepancy, Varek realized with a cold feeling, that the body had been quietly managing for eighteen months — was less unremarkable.
Sorveth didn’t know who Varek was, not really. He knew him as a body representative, a proceduralist, a man who had come to observe the quarterly review and was now being asked about a number that didn’t add up. He asked the question the way he asked all questions: directly, without apparent suspicion, as if the answer were simply something he needed to know.
Varek gave the standard deflection. The administrator nodded, thanked him, and let him go.
On the journey back, Varek thought about the way Sorveth had nodded. It was the nod of a man who had been given a deflection and had noted that it was a deflection and had decided, for now, to accept it. The man knew something was there. He didn’t know what. He was patient.
Varek had sat in judgment on a dozen people over twenty-two years. He knew what it looked like when someone was going to become a problem, and he knew what the body did about problems, and for the first time in twenty-two years he sat with that knowledge and felt something that was not the body’s assessment of a risk variable.
He felt something closer to dread.

IV. The Argument
It took Sorveth four more years to accumulate enough that he was certain something was there, and another year after that to find a thread he could pull without alerting whoever was on the other end.
The thread was a man named Dorath, a forge supervisor at Complex Seventeen, who had been transferred out of the complex seven years earlier and was now running a small operation on the eastern frontier. Sorveth found him through the transfer records — one of many anomalies in the Complex Seventeen documentation — and visited him under the pretext of a routine frontier inspection.
Dorath was fifty-three and careful and had been careful for seven years, which is to say he had been living with something he had decided not to talk about for seven years and was very tired of it. Sorveth had a gift for finding people who were tired of their own silence, and he sat with Dorath for an evening and let the silence do most of the work, and by the end of it he had a partial picture of what Complex Seventeen had been producing and for whom and where it had gone.
It was not the full picture. It was enough.
He went home and sat with it for three days and then wrote a letter to Varek. Not to the Witness Body — to Varek specifically, at the address he had found through administrative records that the body hadn’t thought to obscure because nobody was supposed to be looking.
The letter was three paragraphs. The first described what he knew. The second described what he suspected. The third said: I am not writing to you because I think you will help me. I am writing to you because I think you are the kind of person who, when you sit alone with what I have just described, will find it difficult to continue as you have been continuing. I may be wrong. If I am wrong, I expect I will know about it shortly.
He sealed the letter and sent it and then waited, and while he waited he worked, and he told no one what he had sent or why.

V. Varek Alone
The letter arrived on a Tuesday. Varek read it twice, burned it, and did not sleep.
He had been in the body for twenty-two years. He had joined because he believed what the body believed — that something was coming, that the work mattered, that the cost of the work was not greater than the cost of inaction. He still believed this. He had read the astronomical records. He had seen the models. He understood, with the same precision he brought to everything, what the sky was showing them and how much time remained.
What he had not done, in twenty-two years, was sit alone with the body’s decisions and ask whether the decisions were what the original purpose required or what the institution had become comfortable requiring. These were not the same question. He had treated them as the same question. He had been very good at treating them as the same question.
He thought about Beth, though he didn’t know her name. He thought about the case — Depot-14-South-Logistics-F, which he had been present for, which he had articulated the third position for, which had been decided unanimously and closed. He thought about the reasoning and found he could not fault it. The reasoning was still correct. The variable could not be left open. He had meant every word.
He thought about what it meant that the reasoning was correct and that he could not sleep.
He did not write back to Sorveth. He went to the next body meeting and sat in his usual place and said nothing about the letter, and afterward he went home and sat with the question for another two weeks, and at the end of two weeks he had not resolved it but he had decided that sitting with an unresolved question was not the same as acting on it, and the body needed him, and the work was real, and he went back to the work.
He went back to the work for eight more months. Then something happened that he had not anticipated.
The body assessed Sorveth.

VI. The Assessment
The risk assessment for Sorveth was twelve pages, which was longer than any the body had produced. This was because Sorveth was not a depot administrator or a trade liaison. He was the First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate, selected by the body’s own trial system, and closing his variable required a level of care that closing Beth’s had not.
Varek read the twelve pages and felt the reasoning close around him like something he had built himself and could no longer leave.
The assessment was thorough. It documented Sorveth’s movements, his contacts, his correspondences. It documented the meeting with Dorath. It documented, with a specificity that meant the body had known about the letter before Varek had burned it, the letter Sorveth had sent. It noted that Varek had not disclosed the letter to the body, which the assessment described as a monitoring anomaly requiring separate review.
The assessment’s conclusion was the same conclusion it always was. The variable could not be left open.
Varek read the final page twice, and then he did something he had never done in twenty-two years of body membership. He asked for a deliberation.

VII. The Deliberation
He made the argument carefully. He had always been careful.
He said: Sorveth was selected by our own system. If our system produces men who notice what he noticed and ask what he asked, then closing his variable does not solve our problem. It confirms that the problem is us.
He said: we have been managing the world for three thousand years on the basis that we know what is coming and nobody else does. We have killed people who noticed the edges of what we do. We have bent institutions that were working toward the same end we are working toward. At some point the question is not whether we are right about the threat. The question is whether what we have become is capable of addressing it, or whether we have spent so long managing variables that we have forgotten what the variables are for.
He said: Sorveth does not know what we are. He knows something is there. If we close his variable, we lose a leader the system correctly identified as extraordinary, and we confirm to ourselves that we can do this indefinitely. If we bring him in — not to the body, not fully, but enough — we gain someone who has already proven he can see what we do not want seen, which is exactly the capacity we need.
The body listened. The body deliberated. The body’s response was patient and thorough and engaged with every point he made, and at the end of it the body’s position was unchanged, and the reasoning — which Varek could not fault, which he had helped build over twenty-two years — closed around the question the same way it always had.
The variable could not be left open.
Varek was asked, at the end of the deliberation, whether his own variable required assessment.
He said no. He said he understood the body’s position and would continue his work.
He went home. He sat for a long time. Then he wrote a letter to a woman named Sela, who had been on the body for eleven years and whom Varek had recruited personally and who was, as far as Varek knew, the only other member who had ever shown anything resembling doubt in a closed session.
The letter was two sentences. They are going to close Sorveth. I think we both know what that means for the work.

VIII. Sela
Sela was younger than Varek by fifteen years and had joined the body for different reasons. She had not joined because of the astronomical data — she had joined because Varek had recruited her, and Varek had recruited her because she was brilliant and because her particular brilliance was the ability to hold two contradictory things simultaneously without resolving them prematurely, which was a capacity the body needed and rarely found.
She had been holding two contradictory things for eleven years. The body’s purpose, which she believed in, and the body’s methods, which she had been accommodating rather than believing in. She had told herself the accommodation was temporary — that she was new, that she would understand better when she had more context, that the cases that troubled her would trouble her less once she had the full picture. She had been waiting for the full picture for eleven years.
She read Varek’s letter and understood it was not about Sorveth. It was about whether she was still waiting.
She wrote back: What are you asking me to do?
He wrote back: Nothing yet. I am asking you to know.
She knew. She had known for a long time. She went to the next body meeting and said nothing, and she went to the meeting after that and said nothing, and she went home each time and sat with the two contradictory things and felt the weight of them differently now — less like a condition she was living with and more like a decision she was not yet making.

IX. Sorveth at the End
Sorveth was fifty-one when he understood what he had been dealing with.
He understood it not through a revelation but through an accumulation — a pattern that resolved, one evening in his study, from a collection of separate observations into a single coherent picture. The hidden allocations. The body’s unrecorded deliberations. The personnel transfers that had no administrative logic. The people who had asked too much and disappeared into postings that didn’t exist. He had been assembling the picture for years without seeing it whole, and then one evening he saw it whole.
He sat with it for a long time.
He was not afraid, exactly. He had been afraid before — on the frontier, in situations that had a logic to them, where the danger was external and the response was knowable. This was different. This was the understanding that the institution he had served for twenty years, that had selected him and trusted him with the Eastern Directorate, had been watching him for the entire duration of that service, had read his mail, had assessed his risk, and had — he understood this clearly — decided something about him that had not yet been carried out.
He thought about writing to Varek again. He decided against it. If Varek had received the first letter and not acted against him, something had shifted there, and pulling on that thread might resolve it in the wrong direction.
He thought about what he could do with what he knew, and concluded the answer was almost nothing. He had no proof of anything that would survive outside his own understanding. He had a pattern, a picture assembled from gaps and anomalies, and the people who would need to be convinced were the same people the body had been managing for centuries.
He wrote in his journal that evening — he had always kept a journal, openly, which in retrospect he understood was the reason he was still alive, because a man who writes openly is less dangerous than a man who hides things — and he wrote: I have been fighting something I couldn’t name for twenty years. I know its name now. I don’t think the name changes anything except how I feel about what I have been part of.
He went to work the next morning. He kept doing his job. He kept being extraordinary at it, which was the only defense he had left — a man doing his job so well that closing his variable carried a cost the body had to keep weighing.
He died eight years later of a fever. The body’s records note his death without assessment. Whether this was because he was no longer considered a risk, or because the fever was the assessment, is not established.

X. The Suspension
The trial system was suspended two years after Sorveth’s death.
The official record gives no reason. The inner body’s private deliberation files for this period have not been recovered. What is known from the outer archive is that three members of the body did not appear in records after the suspension, and four members who appear afterward had no prior documented history.
Varek is among the three who disappeared.
Sela is not among the four replacements.
Whether she survived the suspension in some form — reassigned, managed, accommodated in a way the record doesn’t show — is not established. Her name appears once in a document postdating the suspension: a resource allocation request for the observatory expansion, co-signed by an administrator whose posting matches the district where Sela had been stationed. The signature is not identified as hers. The handwriting has not been analyzed. It is a single co-signature on an unremarkable document.
It may mean nothing.

The suspension lasted eleven years. When the trial system resumed, the body was different in ways the outer record cannot fully describe. The Imperium continued. The mandate continued. The work continued.
What changed, in those eleven years, is something the body’s private records would show if they had been recovered. They have not been recovered. What the outer record shows is that in the two centuries following the suspension, the Imperium did not expand. Its administrative records are the most carefully maintained in the entire archive. Nothing appears to go wrong. Nothing appears to happen at all.
A body that had spent three thousand years managing the world had spent eleven years managing itself. What it found there, and what it decided about what it found, produced either a purified institution or a broken one — and the difference between those two outcomes is exactly the kind of thing that would only be visible from inside the private archive.
Kael Sorveth spent twenty years fighting something he couldn’t name. He named it eight years before he died and spent those eight years doing his job in the knowledge of what was watching. I find this harder to read about than almost anything else in this record. I am not certain what that says about me, or about the record.
— The Archivist

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The night air was a sharp blade. Asterion stood in a courtyard where the sea spray hovered in mid-air, caught in a local gravity loop. He was teaching Maren, his apprentice, how to bleed color into the gaps of reality.
“It looks… fragile,” Maren said, her brush trembling.
“Fragile things endure longest,” Asterion said. “The Capital was made of stone and iron, and it is now dust. This lattice is made of attention.” He reached out, his fingers brushing a silver line of magic. It shivered, bending around his touch in a perfect curve. “Magic is no longer a tool, Maren. It is an honest conversation. If you forget that it is not yours to own, it will vanish.”
A tremor ran through the earth, the sea-loop collapsing in a roar of salt water. Maren stumbled, but Asterion remained a fixed point. “Do not fear the shift,” he said. “The sky is testing us. It wants to see if we’ve finally learned how to listen.”

See also: Asterion, Starfall Magic, The Shattered Seas
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Architecture of Preservation
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
Garvak stood atop a pylon, his cloak snapping in the wind. Below him, his engineers winched a massive bulkhead out of the dunes. The Siegeborn knew that a wall was only as strong as its rarest component, and he needed this steel for his people’s salvation.
A subterranean hum vibrated through the sand. From the shadow emerged CR-9 — a massive, six-legged brass tank. It emitted a pulse of sound that made teeth ache.
IDENTIFIED: BIOLOGICAL UNAUTHORIZED EXCAVATION. STATUS: PRESERVATION BREACH.
Garvak hopped down, hammer ready. “My people need that steel to survive the winter. Stand aside.” CR-9’s turret clicked; it cared only for the integrity of the site.
As the titans clashed, Bogrund crouched nearby in his bulky power-suit, clutching his mace, Bonk.
“Look at the plating on that crab, Bonk,” Bogrund whispered. “If we peel off one fin while the Siegeborn has its attention, we power the forge for a decade.” A stray bolt pulverized the rock next to his head. “Or we die. Dying is also an option. Don’t look at me like that, you’re a mace.”
No further record of this encounter exists. The fin in question is unaccounted for.

See also: Garvak, CR-9, Bogrund, Bonk, Machine Wastes, The Ashen Seat
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The City of the Unmoving Reflection
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
In the Capital, the wind was a curated melody. The city was a marvel of white stone, silver banners, and grand, orderly spires. The Celestial Concord had refined the Silent Veils until the weather itself was a matter of administrative decree. Asterion walked the Plaza of Constant Light, where the architecture was so precise that shadows seemed like a breach of protocol. He stopped by the Great Fountain, where the water fell in elegant, rhythmic sheets.
“The world is finally in its proper place, Asterion,” the High Prelate said. “No chaos. We have perfected the Reflection.”
Asterion reached out, his brush hovering near the water. It felt hard, resisting his touch with a dull, vibrating tension. “You haven’t perfected the world, Prelate,” Asterion said. “You’ve silenced it. This water wants to be a river, not a monument. You are building a debt of friction that this city cannot pay. Eventually, the reflection will shatter, and the dark will claim the pieces.”

See also: Asterion, The Celestial Concord, The Great Concord, The Starfall Crater
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
