lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Day the Earth Lost its Weight
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony, Year 0.
(The phrase “the gravity has lost its resolve” appears verbatim in Asterion’s private field notes from the same date. I did not take it from his notes. I do not know why we used the same words.)
The Starfall began with the paint. Asterion was in the high vaults, finishing a map of the Western Reach. He watched as a droplet of crimson on his brush hovered, then drifted upward, joining a thousand other spheres of ink rising toward the ceiling.
“Gravity has lost its resolve,” he whispered.
Then, the impact hit. From the balcony, Asterion watched as the Great Spire shattered into massive, clean-edged blocks that drifted into the air, pulled upward by the meteor’s gravitational wake. Below, the ground opened like a jagged, glowing mouth. The World Scar was born in a flash of violet light, swallowing the center of the world.
“Master! We’re falling!” an acolyte screamed.
“No, boy,” Asterion said, standing tall against the roaring wind. “The earth is falling. We are merely being left behind.”
He watched his life’s work ascend into the clouds to become the High Sky, memorizing every fracture of the world he once knew.

See also: Asterion, The Starfall Crater, High Sky Regions, The Celestial Concord, The Cosmic Devourer
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The Edge of the Circle.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Edge of the Circle
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The air in the council chamber was thick with the scent of old parchment and arrogance. Asterion sat at the periphery, his fingers tracing the rim of a chromatic sphere.
“The northern deviations are unacceptable,” a Governor stated. “If the tides do not align with our trade schedules, we must re-anchor the coastal stars. We have the right.”
Asterion rose slowly, his robes of shifting pigments catching the light. The room went silent. “I am neither malice nor mercy,” he said. “I am the Witness. And I tell you now: the sky does not recognize your schedules. You speak of ‘rights’ as if the stars are your cattle.”
“We are the Concord!” the Governor snapped.
“Then you shall define reality without me,” Asterion replied. “I will go where the sky remembers its own colors. When the friction finally breaks you, do not look to the stars for pity. They gave you a masterpiece, and you tried to edit the ink.”

See also: Asterion, The Celestial Concord, What the Sky Remembers
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The First Anomaly.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The First Anomaly
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The funeral was a silent affair of white silk and heavy incense. Asterion stood at the edge of the terrace, his fingers stained with the deep blues and violets of a mourning palette. He watched them lower Elara into the earth — his finest student, a woman who had mapped the tidal pulls of the inner moons with the stroke of a brush. Now she was dust, and he remained a static canvas, unchanged since he first taught her to see the soul in a sunrise eighty years prior.
“The Master is a painting that refuses to dry,” a deacon whispered.
Asterion did not turn. His eyes were fixed on the Southern Belt. A star there was shivering — a rhythmic pulse, like a heartbeat forced through a narrow throat. He felt a cold, sharp loneliness settle over him. He realized then that his immortality was a requirement of the Pattern; the universe was beginning to stutter, and it needed a witness who wouldn’t die before the sentence was finished.

See also: Asterion, Constellation Lines & Star Points, The Cosmic Devourer
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Friction of Being
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The tent smelled of ozone and damp fur. A young fragment-seeker was huddled over a shard of Starfall glass, trying to force it to emit warmth. The air around her was turning brittle, and frost began to spiderweb across her fingers — the world’s natural resistance pushing back.
“Stop,” Asterion said, stepping from the shadows, his brush trailing a line of warm amber light through the air. “You are shouting at a mountain and wondering why the echo is deafening.”
“I have to make it work!” she gasped.
“The world does not owe you its fire,” Asterion said. He relaxed his posture, letting his awareness of the shard soften. “The harder you define the heat, the more the cold must exist to balance it. This is the friction of being. You call it a curse. I call it the world’s way of saying ‘No’.” He moved his hand near the shard, and the frost vanished. “If you want to survive this age, learn to be a shadow. The sky does not answer those who try to rewrite its paints.”

See also: Asterion, Starfall Fragments, Starfall Magic
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The air at the lip of the World Scar felt unfinished. Serathiel stood at the precipice, wings of fractured light tucked tight. Her beam-bow was drawn, pointing into the violet mists. Her head moved in sharp, bird-like snaps, checking her arrows with obsessive, trembling fingers.
“The light must be absolute,” she whispered. “If the darkness moves, it is a confession.”
“You’re arguing with a hole in the dirt, Serathiel,” Asterion called out, limping up the slope with his brush and palette in hand.
“The hole swallowed the Law, Witness,” Serathiel said. “I saw a ripple in the fog near the Meridian foundations. It was unaligned with the vertical.”
Asterion looked into the Scar. He saw the ruins of the Capital — white stone now shattered and floating. “You cannot execute the wind, Serathiel. You are guarding a graveyard. The ‘Sin’ happened thirty years ago. You’re holding a grudge against a memory.”
Serathiel’s bow hand trembled. For a second, she looked like a veteran who had forgotten how to go home. Then, her eyes hardened. “The Law does not have a sunset. Something is coming up from the dark. I will be the last thing it sees.”
Asterion sat on a rock and opened his ledger.
Asterion’s ledger from this period has never been recovered.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The Treaty of the Melting World.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Treaty of the Melting World
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The meeting was held on The Great Shelf — a tongue of ice groaning under a rising sea. Thorall stood at the center, his tusks draped in iron chains. He was a straightforward man; he could smell the scent of a dying season. Across from him stood Aaron, the Tiderest chieftain, skin pulsing with blue light.
“The glaciers are bleeding, Aaron,” Thorall said. “The paths are turning to rivers.”
“And those rivers carry sickness to my reefs,” Aaron replied. “The water is losing its breath.”
Thorall looked at the source: a jagged Starfall shard embedded in the mountain peak, glowing violet. “I can crush that mountain, Fish-man. But the avalanche will bury your shoals. Or, I let it melt, and you swim over the ruins of my home. Neither is victory.”
Aaron stepped forward. “I can use the Ocean’s Curtain to draw the heat away, but I need your mammoths to haul the resonance-stones. We break the mountain together, or we drown in silence.”
Thorall looked at his lead mammoth. “Get your stones. But if a current trips a mammoth, I’m using your reefs as a bridge.”

See also: Thorall, Aaron, The Great Shelf, Tiderest Shoals, The Tundra Confederation
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The Whisper in the Ash.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Whisper in the Ash
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The slopes were covered in a grey shroud of ash. Asterion watched Krysta training, her movements jagged and powerful. Rhaegor stood beside him, smelling of deep earth and cooling iron.
“She is strong, Cartographer,” Rhaegor grunted. “But her focus is brittle. The trials are weighing on her.”
“You are looking for a vessel, Rhaegor,” Asterion said, his eyes narrowing. “But for what? You treat that secret like a holy burden.”
“The sky needs an anchor,” Rhaegor said, his voice like grinding tectonic plates. “A power like that needs a bearer who cannot be moved. If she cannot find her center, she will never be worthy to touch what I guard. A weak vessel would only let the fire consume the world.”
Asterion watched Krysta strike, but she stumbled, her eyes darting toward the empty air beside her. For a moment, she looked terrified — not of the volcano, but of a shadow only she could see. Asterion felt the shiver in the Pattern, a subtle subversion he mistook for the girl’s own internal resistance.
(Asterion’s field notes from this period were later revised. The original reads differently.)

See also: Asterion, Krysta, Rhaegor, Ashenvale Pyrehold, The Eternis Core, Varesa
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The Will of the Survivor.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.title: The Will of the Survivor
lore-and-stories/stories/the-long-accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The black iron of the glaive was hot, but the sweat on Krysta’s brow was cold. She was ten again in her mind, standing in the mud of her village. She remembered the vibration in her grandfather’s rusted scythe as it met the bone of a scavenger. She hadn’t been “chosen” then; she had survived because she refused to be helpless.
He’s testing your obedience, Krysta, not your strength, a soft, melodic voice drifted through the sulfur.
Krysta didn’t look at Rhaegor on the ridge. She looked at Varesa, sitting on a jagged rock — a tall, elegant presence with eyes like a moonless night. To anyone else, the rocks were empty.
“He says if I don’t master the stance, the power will break me,” Krysta muttered.
“He wants to turn you into a pillar,” Varesa said, her touch icy against the heat. “But you survived the Starfall with a rusted scythe. You were already worthy before he ever looked at you. Why be a pillar for a world that already broke?”
Krysta raised her glaive, caught between Rhaegor’s demand for a Warden and Varesa’s promise of freedom.

See also: Asterion, Krysta, Varesa, Rhaegor, Ashenvale Pyrehold, Cinderhearth
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/A Light for the Lost.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: A Light for the Lost
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Lumia knelt beside the dying traveler, hands trembling as she channeled a gentle glow into his wound.
The man coughed weakly. “You should… flee. The Starfall changed the forest. The beasts —”
“I know,” Lumia whispered. “That’s why I’m here.”
Fireflies gathered around her, drawn to her magic. They swirled in a gentle cluster, illuminating the darkness.
She focused harder, letting her light pulse with warmth.
Somewhere far off, the ground shook. A roar echoed through the trees.
Lumia looked up toward the tremor, eyes wide.
“That wasn’t an animal.”

See also: Lumia, Verdant Rupture, The Green Seat
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Ascension
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
In the midst of a siege, Serathiel stood atop a crumbled wall. CR-9’s bombardment thundered in the distance; Ka’Ruun’s starlance carved streaks across the sky.
Serathiel drew her string.
One condemned target below glowed with runes.
As her verdict struck, dawn erupted —
And Serathiel rose on incandescent wings.
The battlefield froze.
Judgment had come.

See also: Serathiel, CR-9, Ka’Ruun
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Beneath the Molten Throne.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Beneath the Molten Throne
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Deep within the volcanic labyrinth, Rhaegor felt the tremor before it hit.
The magma river rose, pulsing like a heartbeat. The cavern’s walls glowed bright red.
“Again?” Rhaegor snarled. “The Starfall stone dances restlessly.”
The lava beneath him churned. Beneath the molten lake, something old stirred.
He drove his flaming glaive into the magma bed. The lake stilled instantly.
“Who dares rattle my dominion?”
A pulse answered him. A rhythm. A cosmic resonance that did not belong to fire.
Rhaegor’s jaw tightened. An intruder.
He lifted his weapon and marched toward the surface, dragging molten stone behind him.
“Whatever crawled from that crater… I will return it to ash.”

Filed alongside — oral account, source unknown, collected ~30 AD. Provenance unverified. Included because the details are too specific to be invention.
The children sat cross-legged on the scorched earth outside Ashenvale Pyrehold, their wide eyes reflecting the glow of the ever-churning lava river nearby. The elder’s voice rose above the crackle of embers, soft but firm, carrying centuries of stories and warning.
“Long ago,” he began, “before your grandparents were born, before even the oldest stones cooled, the mountain was restless. Flames climbed higher than the sky, rivers of fire flowing unchecked. The villagers prayed, but no prayer could calm the volcano.
“Then came Rhaegor, the Lava Warden. Some say he was born from the mountain itself, others say he was a man who dared to wrest power from the magma. Wherever he walked, the earth bent to his will. Lava obeyed him.
“Sometimes he saves, sometimes he punishes. He serves the mountain. If you disturb its balance, it is his fury you will face. That is why we call him the Warden — because he watches, judges, and tempers the flames.
“And they say he knows things the mountain hides… secrets older than fire itself. There is a crystal deep inside the volcano, glowing with a light that can shape destinies. Some say Rhaegor has seen it, guarding it quietly in his own way. Some say he waits for the right moment… or the wrong one.”
*The children exchanged nervous glances, eyes wide with wonder and fear.

See also: Rhaegor, Rhaegor’s Peak, The Eternis Core, Cinderhearth
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Condemned
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Garvak raised his war-cannon toward a village.
Serathiel’s voice cut through the smoke.
“You were warned.”
Golden seals closed around him like a cage.
Garvak laughed. “I have judged myself worthy.”
“Then dawn will disagree.”
A single beam pierced the battlefield.

See also: Serathiel, Garvak
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Embers of Sanity.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Embers of Sanity
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Velrisa’s candle flickered.
She’d lit it to calm herself, but the flame danced unnaturally, stretched thin as if trying to escape its wick.
A whisper echoed behind her.
You could burn so much brighter.
Velrisa froze. “No… not again.”
The whisper circled her mind like smoke in a glass jar.
You used to heal. You begged for peace. But look how they cast you aside…
Her hands trembled. She remembered the last time she held back. The last time mercy cost lives.
A second voice joined the first — her voice, speaking from somewhere deeper.
Ignite them. Heal yourself.
Velrisa grabbed the candle and crushed it in her fist. Hot wax burned her palm, and something inside her laughed.
Fire flickered from her fingertips.
The enchantress stood slowly, eyes glowing violet.
“I will soothe nothing,” she whispered. “Tonight, I set the world free.”
Behind her, the room lit with spectral embers — her sanity cracking like porcelain.
The candle was found still burning three days later. No wax had melted.

See also: Velrisa
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Neutralization Protocol.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Neutralization Protocol
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
A sandstorm howled as CR-9 trudged through the desert.
The machine scanned the horizon.
THREAT LEVEL: MODERATE
THREAT TYPE: UNKNOWN METEORIC INCIDENT
PRIMARY PROTOCOL: INVESTIGATE. NEUTRALIZE.
Its internal core pulsed — Starfall energy warping its logic so subtly it almost seemed like emotion.
The machine detected distant tremors. Unknown entities. Unknown weapons signatures.
MISSION UPDATE:
TARGETS OF INTEREST DETECTED.
ENGAGING INVESTIGATIVE ORDNANCE.
It fired a shell.
Something screamed.
CR-9’s lens flickered.
THREAT RESPONSE: SUCCESSFUL.
MOVING TO NEXT TARGET.
The horizon does not scan back.
Probably.

See also: CR-9, Machine Wastes, Molten Imperium
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Siegeborn Awakening.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Siegeborn Awakening
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
The runes inside Garvak’s chest flickered. For the first time in centuries, he heard his gears grind.
Memory cores rebooted. Shields recalibrated. Weapons locked and loaded.
Across the cavern, a blue-white Starfall shard pulsed like a second sun.
Purpose identified.
Garvak rose to his full colossal height and marched toward the surface, carving a trench through stone.
The world above would soon witness the return of the Siegeborn.

See also: Garvak, Machine Wastes, Starfall Fragments
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Starfire Trajectory.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Starfire Trajectory
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Ka’Ruun balanced on a floating basalt chunk, surveying the molten horizon.
“My trajectory was off,” he muttered, adjusting the dials on his gauntlet.
Teostra groaned. “Boy, you nearly vaporized the mountain’s spine.”
“That means it worked!”
The Starfall shard pulsed again, humming like a star’s heartbeat.
Ka’Ruun looked at it, eyes gleaming.
“You’re calling to something… and I’m gonna find out what.”
He fired a blast downward, launching himself into the sky, laughing like a mad comet.
Teostra watched him go.
“One day, you’ll explode,” he muttered.
Then, a tiny smile crossed his face.
“But until then… burn bright.”
He never came back down from that ridge.

See also: Ka’Ruun, Teostra, High Sky Regions, Starfall Fragments
Filed separately at subject’s insistence. See also: The Dragon’s Temper.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The Current That Chose to Move.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The Current That Chose to Move
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
When the first whisper of Starfall reached Tiderest Shoals, the waters trembled. Waves rolled in unnatural patterns, and sea creatures fled deeper than the trenches dared allow. As chieftain, Aaron felt the disturbance like a bruise pressed against his spirit. Starfall had touched the land above… and soon it would gnaw its way into the sea.
So he rose.
From the heart of the Shoals, where tide-crystals shimmered around the sacred pool, Aaron emerged in full form — water sharpened by purpose. He gazed toward the horizon with a current’s steady resolve.
He remembered an old friend then: Thorall, the frost-tusked chieftain who once traveled beside him, tide and tundra united in a bond forged by storms. If Starfall threatened the land and sea alike, then the currents of fate were pulling them together once more.
“I will return,” Aaron vowed to his people. “But first, I must meet the storm before it meets us.”
With a sweeping surge, he left Tiderest Shoals behind — becoming a streak of shimmering blue racing across the world, determined to break the Starfall before it breaks everything he swore to protect.

See also: Aaron, Tiderest Shoals, Thorall, The Shattered Seas
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The Dragon's Temper.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The Dragon's Temper
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Teostra sat atop a smoldering ridge, staring into the crater’s glow.
The Starfall shard pulsed with cosmic fire, its heat warping the air.
He snorted smoke. “An ember not of this world.”
A creature moved behind him.
Teostra didn’t turn. “It’s you, Ka’Ruun. You always step like a thunderbolt in a bottle.”
The boy skidded to a stop. “Teostra! You have to see what I found —”
The shard flared, and Ka’Ruun’s gauntlet blazed. Starfire danced wildly, out of control.
Teostra growled. “That rock will burn you from the inside.”
Ka’Ruun’s grin widened. “Then I’ll burn brighter.”
Teostra closed his eyes.
Foolish, brilliant child.

See also: Teostra, Ka’Ruun, High Sky Regions, Starfall Fragments
Filed separately at Ka’Ruun’s insistence. See also: Starfire Trajectory.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The First Light.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The First Light
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Serathiel walked through the ruins of the Concord’s Sanctuary, her steps silent on marble broken by centuries.
Where once a thousand adjudicators trained beneath dawnlight, only dust remained.
A flicker — twilight, not dawn — pooled behind her.
“Still mourning ruins?” Varesa’s voice, soft as silk.
“No.” Serathiel raised her bow. “Hunting what destroyed them.”
The arrow glowed. The shadow smiled.

See also: Serathiel, Varesa, Celestial Concord HQ, The Celestial Concord
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The Fractured Heart.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The Fractured Heart
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
The volcano groaned like a living god.
Deep beneath Ashenvale Pyrehold, the Eternis Core pulsed with fractured memory, its radiant facets casting broken light across the molten walls. For centuries it had kept the village alive — a guardian and a cage all at once.
From the Core’s wound, a shard broke free. She emerged humanoid, crystalline, facets glowing with raw magic. Her first breath resonated with the Core’s ancient voice:
Preserve. Control. Maintain order.
But another voice, softer and darker, slipped from the cracks of the mountain:
Break… unravel… let silence bloom.
The two voices collided in her mind. Her body trembled, shards grinding against themselves, and she screamed.
Above the tunnels, Varesa heard the sound and smiled. A ghost of twilight, she drifted like frost across fire, watching the corruption creep through the Core.
“Light fears me,” she whispered. “For even it casts a shadow.”
Elsewhere, lava dripping from his fists, Rhaegor felt the tremor. The mountain itself obeyed his fury.
“The ground’s waking angry.” He rose, molten stone trailing him, following the Core’s call.
Krysta stumbled through the volcanic tunnels, two voices clawing for dominance.
She entered a chamber where flame met shadow — and saw them: Varesa, a silhouette of darkness. Rhaegor, molten and towering.
Not allies. Not enemies. Just two forces drawn to the same fracture.
Varesa’s voice cut softly: “What a beautiful shard you are… breaking yourself to stay whole.”
Rhaegor’s voice rumbled like a quake: “She ain’t breaking. She’s choosing.”
Krysta’s chest burned with conflicting wills. Finally she whispered:
“I am here for a purpose… to protect the many.”
The Core flared in approval. The shadow recoiled in mockery. And the shard chose her path — between two entities, she would walk alone.
(The record here is incomplete. — )

See also: Krysta, Rhaegor, Varesa, The Eternis Core, Ashenvale Pyrehold
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The Mammoth's Burden.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The Mammoth's Burden
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
The wind howled like a wounded animal, whipping around Thorall’s furred shoulders.
He marched toward the Starfall breach, tusks heavy with frost. Behind him trudged his herd — warriors, shamans, and the last children of his dwindling people.
The sky shimmered with unnatural light. Purple cracks spread across the tundra.
“Velrisa’s curse,” Thorall muttered. “The land grows restless.”
A child beside him shivered. “Chief… will the Starfall hurt us?”
Thorall placed a massive hand on the boy’s head.
“No force can break us if we remain together.”
But as they neared the crater, the ground rumbled —
And something enormous awakened beneath the ice.

See also: Thorall, Frozen Fracture Tundras, Velrisa, The Starfall Crater
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/The Suit With an Attitude.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: The Suit With an Attitude
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
Bogrund’s workshop was always loud, but tonight it roared.
Steam hissed from pressure valves. Sparks showered the floor. A metal suit stomped in circles, swaying side to side like a frustrated toddler.
“Hold still, Bonk!” Bogrund shouted, tightening a bolt with both hands.
The suit ignored him, shaking like an angry kettle ready to blow.
Bogrund yanked his wrench free. “You want your ankle servos fixed or not?”
The suit slumped, groaning. Bogrund nodded. “Thought so.”
Outside the workshop, a red glow lit the night — the glow of the Starfall’s shards drifting from the crater far to the north. Everyone in the city felt the pull… everyone except Bogrund.
He had enough problems with the entity inside his suit.
Bonk tapped Bogrund’s shoulder, metal fingers clanking. It pointed to the distant crater.
“You want to go toward the giant sky-rock that’s making half the continent crazy?”
The suit nodded.
Bogrund sighed. “Bonk, buddy… if that thing wakes up again, we’re both in trouble.”
The suit thumped its chest with pride. Bogrund blinked. “Oh. You wanna punch whatever comes out of it.”
The suit nodded harder.
The engineer scratched his mustache. ”…Alright. We’ll go look. But if we die, I’m haunting you.”
The suit saluted with perfect military precision.
They left the workshop arm in arm — man and machine — marching toward the sound of distant explosions.

See also: Bogrund, Bonk, Bogrund’s Workshop, Machine Wastes
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Short Accounts/Xero & Rita.md
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.title: Xero & Rita
lore-and-stories/stories/the-short-accou.content:
This page is a placeholder. Xero and Rita’s full story has not yet been written.
Xero is a survivor of the Starfall — not because he was strong, but because something chose him. Rita is the presence that answered when he refused to accept what was taken. No one else can see her. No one else can feel the weight pressing against their spine, until Xero lets her through.
She does not comfort him. She does not guide him. She promises one thing.
For the full account, see The Starfall Anthology — filed as [untitled], not yet received.
Connections

The Starfall Anthology — their story is listed but absent from the official record.
The Starfall Crater — Xero’s connection to the Starfall is personal and unresolved.

lore-and-stories/stories/the-variable.title: The Variable
lore-and-stories/stories/the-variable.content:
The following account was reconstructed from two sources: a partial personal journal recovered from the outer archive’s miscellaneous correspondence division, and an internal Vigil deliberation record recovered separately, by means not established. Neither source references the other. They have been arranged here because, placed together, they describe the same event from two directions.
The journal’s author is identified in the outer archive only by a district posting code. The deliberation record refers to the same individual by a risk designation. Neither source uses a name.
— The Archivist

I.
Beth had been in Border District Fourteen for eleven years, and in that time she had learned to process what she saw the way she processed supply manifests — methodically, without attaching to the details, moving on.
The advance had reached the valley three weeks ago. She had watched it from the depot roof because the depot faced east and there was nowhere else to look. The constructs came over the ridge in the early morning, and they kept coming, and the valley — which she had seen on survey maps as three settlements, marked in the standard notation, medium density, agricultural — was by afternoon something the maps would re-annotate as a transit corridor. She had processed that paperwork herself. Four minutes. She was good at her job.
What the paperwork did not contain was the smell that reached the depot on the second day. Nobody discussed it. She didn’t discuss it either. She went home and wrote about it in her journal, because writing things down had always been how she confirmed to herself that something had actually happened. She was not planning anything. She understood that clearly. She had watched from a roof and smelled what was left behind and written four pages, and that was the whole of it.
She had lived alongside the advance for years without writing anything down. The notation system was not ambiguous if you could read it, and she had been reading it for nine years. She had made a quiet decision early on — she could not have said exactly when — not to look too closely at what the numbers described. It was not cowardice, or not only that. It was the understanding that she had built something here, a life that worked, and the life required a particular kind of attention that excluded certain questions.
She had read V. Sorath’s treatise when it circulated. Most of the administrative class had. She had found it persuasive in the way arguments are persuasive when they confirm something you have already decided. The line that stayed with her was the one about the mandate not being chosen by individuals, only inherited by peoples. She had found it comforting at the time. She was less sure about it now, which was why she had written four pages instead of none.
She kept the journal under a false bottom in her desk drawer. She had built it herself, about eighteen months ago, for no particular reason she could name at the time. It had seemed prudent.
She replaced the false bottom and went to make dinner. Outside, the constructs moved along what the maps now called a transit corridor, and the evening settled over the district the way evenings always had, indifferent to what the afternoon had been.

[Internal record. Permanent Witness Body, deliberation files, ~3,500 BCE. Recovered separately from the outer archive. Classification at time of filing: body records only.]

RISK ASSESSMENT — DESIGNATION: DEPOT-14-SOUTH-LOGISTICS-F
Convened: full inner body. Matter: passive observation, frontier district. Status: under assessment.

Summary of matter:
Subject is a logistics administrator, Border District Fourteen, nine years in post. No prior flags. Performance assessments consistently satisfactory. No documented contacts of interest.
Subject was observed on the depot roof during the valley clearance operation, approximately dawn to mid-morning, Day One of the clearance. Subject’s position gave unobstructed sightlines to the eastern ridge approach. Duration of observation: estimated three hours.
Subject has not filed any report referencing the clearance. Subject has not discussed the clearance with any monitored contact. Subject has made no documented attempt to access restricted survey records beyond her standard remit.
Subject’s personal quarters were assessed on Day Four. A journal was located beneath a false panel in a desk drawer. Contents are attached. The journal predates the valley clearance by approximately two years and contains routine personal material. The four most recent entries reference the clearance directly. They are observational in character. They contain no plans, contacts, or intent to report. They contain accurate descriptions of what the subject observed, and a record of the subject’s decision not to report it.
The false panel is of note. It was constructed by the subject and predates the clearance by at least eighteen months, suggesting habitual concealment practice rather than a response to this specific event.

Body deliberation:
First position: The subject has done nothing actionable. Nine years of satisfactory service. No contacts of interest. No report filed. The journal contains no actionable content. The appropriate response is continued monitoring.
Second position: The subject witnessed a clearance operation at close range, documented her observations accurately, and made a deliberate decision to conceal those observations. The concealment was not reactive — the false panel predates the event by eighteen months. We do not know what she concealed before the valley clearance. We know only what we found.
Third position: The subject’s journal records a decision not to report. Decisions can be revisited. She is stable now. She may not be stable in three years, or ten. She may encounter someone worth speaking to. The entry that concerns this body most is not the four pages about the clearance. It is the single line referencing the Sorath treatise: I have made a decision not to examine the foundations. A person who has decided not to examine the foundations has acknowledged the foundations exist. That acknowledgment does not expire.
Response to third position: Acknowledged.
On monitoring as sufficient: Monitoring produces information. It does not produce certainty. The body’s purpose is the production of certainty. The subject’s risk profile will not change in a direction that reduces risk. She has seen what she has seen. She has written what she has written. Time does not remove these facts.
On the subject’s service record: Noted and set aside. The subject’s service record is not under assessment.
On proportionality: The body does not assess proportionality. The body assesses risk. The question is not whether the subject deserves what follows. The question is whether the variable can be left open. The body’s unanimous position is that it cannot.
Decision: closure authorized. Designation passed to field operations. Standard protocol. No further documentation will be issued on this matter.

II.
Three days later, Beth’s supervisor noted her absence at morning roll.
The depot log had her signing out the previous evening at the standard time. Her quarters showed no disturbance. Her desk was in order. The false panel in the bottom drawer was open and empty, which he noticed and did not know what to make of and did not record.
He filed a missing persons report. The Office of Administrative Oversight responded within the day: the subject had been reassigned to another posting, effective immediately, transfer order mislaid in transit, apologies for the confusion.
He accepted this. He closed the desk drawer. He did not mention the false panel in any subsequent document, because mentioning it would have required explaining how he knew it was there, and explaining that would have required him to say that he had gone through her desk, and going through her desk would require a reason, and he did not have a reason except that something felt wrong and he had been in Border District Fourteen long enough to know that feeling wrong and saying so were two different things with two different outcomes.
He had been here for six years. He was good at his job.

The journal was not in the drawer. The body’s field record notes, in its final line: personal effects secured and destroyed per standard protocol.
What the field record does not note — because the body already knew, and the body’s records are for the body — is that three members of the field operations team had been in Beth’s quarters before she came home that evening. They had opened the desk. They had read the four pages. They had replaced the false bottom and left, and she had come home and made dinner and gone to bed and the variable had been open for one more night before it was closed.
She had decided not to examine the foundations. She had been careful. She had built a false panel and kept her head down and done her job for nine years and it was not enough, and it was never going to be enough, because the body was not asking whether she had done anything. The body was asking what she might do. The answer, as far as the body was concerned, was the same for everyone who had seen what she saw and written what she wrote.
I have compiled worse things than this. I am not certain why this one is harder to set down.
— The Archivist

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

The pages, drawn

lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.title: Time, Entry I: What Was on the Table
lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.content:
Approximately 3,490 BCE. The Keeper’s earliest surviving pages.
Four winters in this tower, and I still talk to the stairs.
I didn’t plan it. It started in the first month, when I was too tired to hold a thought without hearing it, and it stuck. I tell the stairs when I’m going up. I tell the kettle it’s taking too long. If anyone had seen me they’d have thought I’d gone a little strange, and they might have been right.
I wasn’t always like this. I used to keep my mouth shut and my figures straight. Nine years of it. I worked for people who believed that anything left open had to be closed, and I believed in them. That is the part I still can’t forgive myself for. I read their treatises and nodded along. I sat at dinners and said the right things. When I saw what they did in the valley, I wrote it down at night where no one could read it, and in the morning I went in and did my work as though I hadn’t seen it, and I told myself that was the same as being decent.
They had read it. Of course they had. I found that out later, from the three who walked me out. They’d been in my rooms while I was still at work. They’d sat in my chair and turned my own pages. Then I came home and made dinner, and I stood at the stove stirring something while strangers’ fingerprints were on everything I owned.
I think about the dinner more than anything. I made soup. I remember tasting it for salt.
They came before dawn. A lamp lit that I hadn’t lit, and a man’s voice telling me to dress. I asked what I’d done. Nobody answered. I asked again at the gate, and again on the road, and the one who finally spoke said the question was a courtesy I wasn’t owed. They gave me a coat that wasn’t mine and a loaf of bread, and they told me I was no longer a person on record. They said it kindly. That was the worst of it. They could have been telling me the weather.
I walked all day because I didn’t know what else to do. By evening I knew I was going to turn around, and I did. I walked back and stood at the gate of the district where I’d lived for nine years, and I said my name to the guard.
He looked at me. I knew him. He’d waved me through that gate nearly every morning of my working life, and we’d talk about the weather, and he’d once given me a pear. He looked right through me and said, “There’s no one by that name here.”
I think I laughed. I know I sat down. I sat in the dirt outside the gate with my back against the wall, and I stayed there until someone told me to move on, and then I moved on.
I can’t tell you the next stretch in order. There were barns and ditches. I wasn’t sane for a while. I talked to myself the way I talk to the stairs now, but louder, and I said terrible things about the people I’d served and about myself and, for some reason, about the pear.
There was a night on a riverbank. It was cold, and I hadn’t eaten in two days, and I sat by the water until I couldn’t feel my hands. I’d been thinking for a long while about the guard. About how easy it had been for him. I thought, if I walk in here, nobody even has to take my name away. It’ll already be gone.
I took off the coat they’d given me and folded it on the bank. I still want to laugh at that, the care I took. I walked in up to my knees. The water was so cold I made a sound I didn’t recognize. Then I stood there with the current pulling at my legs, and I understood that if I went on, the guard would be right. There would be no one by that name, anywhere, and it would be because I’d finished the work for them.
I couldn’t do that. I wouldn’t call it courage. Spite, mostly, and I’ll take spite. I walked back out and put the coat on and sat shaking until the sky turned grey.
A woman I never saw again left bread on a wall near where I was sleeping. She didn’t speak to me. I ate it crying so hard I could barely swallow, and then I slept for a day.
When I could think again, I walked. I’m not sure toward what. One evening the land ran out and there was a cold sea, and a tower on the cliff above it with a great dead lens at the top, and the door at the bottom wasn’t locked.
I climbed it with my knees shaking. In the room under the lens, a candle was burning in a corner. I’ve never trimmed it. I’ve never lit it. It’s the same length it was that first night. I decided early not to think about that, and I’ve kept to it better than most decisions I’ve made.
I sat on the floor of that room and cried again, but it was a different crying. It was the first time in months I’d been somewhere nobody could take away from me, and I knew it was probably because nobody wanted it.
That was four winters ago. I started collecting. Accounts, ledgers, letters, anything people had thrown away or were afraid to keep. I copy them and bind them and put them on the shelves in order. It’s what I know how to do. It’s also the only way I’ve found to answer what they did: if the world is going to forget, somebody ought to be keeping the other paper.

I came down before light, the way I always do. The door was barred. I check it every night and again in the morning, and it was exactly as I’d left it, the bar in its brackets and the draught under the sill whistling the same thin note.
There was a bundle on the long table.
I stood at the bottom of the stair for what felt like a long time. Then I went round the room. The shutters were latched. The eleventh step has a loose stone that rings if you put your weight on it, and it hadn’t rung. I went back and checked the bar again, and my hands weren’t steady.
My first thought was that they’d found me. It was the only thing I thought for the first minute. Someone from the old district had come through the wall to remind me they could. I think I even looked for a note with my name on it.
Then I picked up the pages.
My right hand went cold. It wasn’t the morning air. It was cold from inside, as if something had been poured into it. It passed in a minute or so, and then my teeth started to ache, the way they do when you drink something too cold too fast. I told myself it was the sea air. I said so out loud, to the stairs.
Nine sheets, folded once, tied with a strip of undyed cord. I untied it, and I knew the handwriting before I’d read a word.
It was mine. I mean it was exactly mine. The slant, the hooked tail on my g that I got from a copybook with a printing flaw. I have looked at that hand every day of my life, and there wasn’t one place where someone had copied it. I’d have known. I’d have felt it, the way you feel a stranger’s hand on your arm.
I hadn’t written it. I sat down on the floor, because my legs wouldn’t hold, and I read.
It was a funeral. A terrace, white silk, so much incense I could almost smell it off the page. A man called Asterion stood at the edge of it with his fingers stained blue and violet, watching them lower a woman into the earth. The account called her his finest student. He had taught her to see a sunrise eighty years before, and he hadn’t changed at all, and a deacon behind him whispered that the master was a painting that refused to dry. Out past the terrace, low in the southern sky, one star was shivering, a slow beat like a heartbeat pushed through a narrow throat. A cold loneliness settled on the man, and he understood why he was still alive. The world was beginning to stutter, and it needed a witness who wouldn’t die before the sentence was finished.
I don’t know what the sentence was. I read that line a dozen times.
The date at the top was in a calendar so old that the districts had dropped it before my grandmother was born. I did the sum on my fingers like a child. Then I did it again with a pencil. It’s thousands of years. It’s older than the Concord. It’s older than anything anyone has ever shown me.
At the bottom of the last page there was a line on its own, pressed so hard into the paper that it had nearly torn.
Keep these. You will need to know how long we have.

I put the account on the shelf with the Primary Accounts. Under it I wrote source unknown, and then I stopped, and after a while I added hand: mine, and then I couldn’t stand to look at it and wrote pending underneath, as if that settled anything.
I’ve started a second book. Every time something happens that I can’t explain, I’m going to put the date in it, so that if I’m going mad I’ll at least have the evidence.
I don’t know what I feel. Fear, some. But there’s something else under it that I don’t like to look at. For four years the only voice that has spoken to me in this tower has been my own, and this morning there was another one on the table, and it was mine too, and it was asking me to keep going. I hate how glad I was.
Tonight I stood at the barred door with my back to the room, and I had the feeling that someone had stood right where I was standing not long before, wanting very much to be heard. I said, “Who’s there?” in my ordinary voice. The candle didn’t move. I said, “I’m here,” and felt ridiculous, and said it again.
[margin, unsteady] Don’t tell anyone. There’s no one to tell.


The pages, drawn

lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.title: Time, Entry II: The Keeper
lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.content:
Approximately 3,350 BCE.
Tam died in the spring.
He was the fisherman’s boy from the village below the cliff. He was nine when he first climbed my stair on a dare, and he stood in the doorway of the reading room with his fists clenched, waiting to be eaten. I gave him a piece of bread. He sat on the floor and I taught him his letters out of the margins of a tax ledger, because it was the only paper I had that day. By the time he was twelve he could read better than the priest.
I wasn’t supposed to go to the burying. I went anyway, in a grey cloth over my head, and stood at the back with the dogs. His granddaughter saw me. She nodded the way you’d nod at a statue, and looked away. She’s been taught not to look too long.
Here is what the village believes. They believe there’s a Keeper in the tower, and that the Keeper is always a woman, and that when one dies another takes her place and is called the same name. That’s how Tam’s mother explained it to him, and it’s how he explained it to his children. Nobody has ever said it to my face. I think they decided on it because the other explanation was worse.
I haven’t aged. I don’t know when I first noticed, only that there was a winter when I looked at my hands and they were the hands I’d had on the road. I’ve stopped counting years somewhere past the hundred and fortieth. The number frightened me, so I moved the count into the second book, where it can’t look back.
I held Tam’s hand when he was a boy. I buried him at the edge of the crowd. I think that’s what no one tells you about living this long. It isn’t the death. It’s that they keep growing past you, and you’re the only one still standing in the doorway.

The deliveries come more often now. Some months there are two, and some years there are none, and I’ve never found a pattern, though I’ve tried. The Primary Accounts take up three shelves. Most of what arrives is ordinary in its way: a harvest dispute, a trial record, a letter from a woman to a dead brother. All of it in my hand. All of it older than I am, or at least older than I can explain.
The cold in my right hand used to last a minute. Now it lasts an hour, and the ache in my teeth goes into the bones of my face. Twice I’ve bled from the nose onto a page. There is a feeling that comes before each one, the evening before, in the chest. I can only describe it as homesickness, for a place I’ve never been.
I tried to catch whoever it is. I sat up in the reading room every night for a month with the candle and a blanket. Twice I was sure I heard something on the stair. Each time I woke with my cheek on the table and a bundle at my elbow, and the bar still in its brackets, and the candle just as it was. I don’t remember falling asleep. I’ve stopped trying.
I leave a cup of tea out now. It’s cold in the morning and untouched. I don’t know why I do it.

Last night’s delivery was different.
I knew before I opened it. The cord was knotted twice, which it never is. Inside were four sheets in my hand, and at the top of the first, a line on its own, written large and fast, as though the writer hadn’t trusted herself to slow down:
Read this one first. I’m sorry.
The account underneath it was nothing I’d seen before. A man called Asterion stood in a high library, finishing a map. A drop of red paint on the end of his brush had stopped falling and begun to rise. It drifted up to join a thousand others, small bright spheres of ink floating toward the ceiling, and he said, very quietly, that gravity had lost its resolve. Then something struck. I couldn’t tell from the page what it was. A great white spire outside the balcony broke into clean-edged blocks, each one lifting slowly into the air as if the sky had decided to take it back. The ground opened below it like a mouth, and the light that came out of the mouth was violet. A boy beside him cried out that they were falling. The man said, no, boy. The earth is falling. We are merely being left behind.
The date was not in the old calendar. It was in a plain system I recognised, one the Concord uses. I worked out the difference. Then I worked it out again, sitting on the floor with the pages in my lap, because I could not make myself believe what I was adding up.
It was about three thousand three hundred years from now.
The last sheet was a letter. It was short.
I can’t tell you everything. I haven’t got long, and I’m not sure how much you can bear. This is real. It is coming. I’ve seen it more times than I’ll say. You have a great deal of time, and I think that is why you are still here. Read everything. Keep it in order. Look for who was warned and who wasn’t. I’m trying to stop it. I need you to help me.
I know you’re angry. I would be.
I was. I put the pages on the floor and I sat with my knees against my chest and I shouted at the shelves. I said, “How dare you.” I said, “I came here to be left alone.” I said it to my own handwriting, and my voice came back off the lens overhead and sounded like a stranger’s. The candle didn’t move.
When I was done I was shaking. I thought of the guard, and the pear, and the water at my knees. I thought: nobody has ever asked me for anything before. They told me, or they took. This was the first time anyone had asked.
And under that I felt something I didn’t want to feel. That I had been given a reason to be here. I have spent a hundred and forty winters being an accident that nobody noticed, and this letter was telling me I had been kept.
I’m not a hero. I was a clerk. But I’ve been a clerk for people who decided what the world was allowed to remember, and I’m tired of the world being decided.
[margin, written slowly] Four nosebleeds this month. Put it down to the damp. Told no one.
[margin, beneath it, pressed hard] I will read all of it.
I put out a fresh cup of tea before I went to bed. Then I stood in the doorway of the reading room with my hand on the cold bar, and I said, to the room, in my own ordinary voice:
“I’ll do it. I’ll try. But I want to see you.”
Nothing. The candle burned. The shelves held their shape in the dark.
“I mean it,” I said. “I want to see your face. I want to know what I look like at the end.”
I stayed there a long time. In the morning the tea was cold again, and a little lower in the cup than I had left it.


The pages, drawn

lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.title: Time, Entry III: The Man With the Brush
lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.content:
Approximately 3,350 BCE.
I scratched a line inside the cup. After five mornings of wondering whether I was imagining it, I marked the level of the tea with the point of my knife before bed, and when I came down it was a finger below the mark and cold all the way through. I wasn’t imagining it. Somebody drinks it, or something does, and whenever I’m awake the cup is empty and the tower is as empty as it ever was.
Two nights ago I left a note under the cup. Who are you? I wrote it in my own hand, which seemed the polite thing. The tea went down and the note went with it, and nothing came back. I stood over that table with both hands flat on the wood. Somebody in this tower is reading what I write to them, and I would like very much to know who gave them leave.
I’ve done what I said I would. I’m reading everything. It has taken most of the autumn, because I can’t open a page without wondering whether it’s the one the letter meant, the one that tells me who was warned and who wasn’t. The table isn’t big enough for the piles, so I sit on the floor, and I’ve slept there more nights than I’ve slept in the bed. A few days ago I woke up with a ledger on my face and a basket of fish at the foot of the stair, where Tam’s family has always left it. It had been there long enough that I threw it off the cliff. I’d forgotten about eating.
It was a name that stopped me. I was copying names onto the long wall, the only one without shelves, with a stick of charcoal, because that’s how I think: dates down the left and names down the right, as I would for a manifest. Late one night I wrote Asterion and found it was already there, three lines up, in my own writing.
I knew the name before I knew I knew it. It was at the bottom of the Concord charters that used to cross my desk with the trade papers. Asterion, founding authority. The old cartographer who drew the star lines. We all had the same joke about him, that he must have signed the first charter with a chisel, and nobody ever thought it was anything but a joke.
I had seen it the very first morning, in the funeral account. I saw it and I did nothing. I am extremely good at that. I told myself that names repeat, and that a man in a page eight thousand years old who happened to share one with a signature was no business of mine, and I filed him. When he turned up in the library account I put a line under the name and kept reading. It’s a talent. I had nine years of practice.
So I took the funeral account down and read it properly. The page says he is standing at the edge of a terrace with blue and violet paint on his fingers while they lower his best student into the ground. It says he taught her to see a sunrise eighty years before. Eighty years, and he hasn’t changed. Somebody behind him whispers that the master is a painting that refuses to dry.
The library account, eight thousand years later, has the same man holding the same brush.
I held my hands up to the lamp. They were the hands I’d had on the road.
I said his name out loud. It was the first name I’d said to the room since Tam’s, and I said it to the stairs, because they’re who I talk to. “He’s like me,” I said. The stairs had nothing to add.
I have lived in this tower a hundred and forty winters believing I was the only one. All that time he was across the water, losing students and burying them, and signing charters. And whoever is sending me these pages has known it, and put a funeral in my hands and not one line to say there is someone else. The letter told me to read everything. It never told me there was a man in it like me.
I was angrier than I’ve been since the gate.
The funeral page also mentions a star, low in the south, shivering. I realized I hadn’t looked at that corner of the sky once in a hundred and forty winters. I went out on the cliff with my coat held shut. It took me a while. Then I found it, and it was doing exactly what the page said, a slow even tremble that the wind didn’t explain. I stood there until my feet went numb. It was the first thing out of any of those pages that I had ever seen with my own eyes, and I don’t know what to do with the fact that it’s true. When I came in I barred the door twice.

Then three days of nothing, and a night with no wind. The feeling had been in my chest since supper, that homesickness for nowhere I’ve never got used to. In the morning the bundle was on the table with the bar still in its brackets. I knew before I touched it that I would bleed, and I did, onto my cuff, the sixth time this season. The cold went up past my elbow and my back teeth rang. I held a cloth to my nose until it stopped, and then I untied the cord.
It was a city so clean it hurt to read about. White stone and silver banners, and even the wind was arranged. The page says they have a name for how they do it, the Silent Veils, and I read that twice because it sounded like something my old employers would have been proud of. In the middle of the city there’s a fountain, and Asterion is standing at it beside the High Prelate, who tells him the world has finally been put in its proper place. No chaos. We have perfected the Reflection.
Asterion reaches out with his brush and touches the water, and the water pushes back. The page says it is hard, and that it shakes under the bristles. He tells the Prelate that he hasn’t perfected the world, he has silenced it. This water wants to be a river, not a monument. He says the city is running up a debt it can’t pay, and that one day the reflection will break and the dark will come for the pieces.
That is where the page ends. It doesn’t say what the Prelate answered.
I stood up and went to the window because my hands wouldn’t stay still.
It was the Prelate’s words that did it. I know that kind of talk. I spent nine years among people who spoke it, who believed a thing was safe once it had stopped moving. No chaos. We have perfected. I signed forms that said it in more words, and I said parts of it myself over dinner and was proud of how I sounded.
And Asterion, with his brush against the water, was telling a man like that that it would end. I don’t know what he meant by the dark. But the Prelate’s city has white stone and spires, and the library page has a white tower breaking apart. I laid the two pages side by side on the floor. The one says the reflection will break and the dark will come for the pieces. The other has the pieces, floating up. It could be the same city. It could be that every city in that country is made of white stone, and I’m a woman who has read too many pages in a row. But it is the first time in all those pages that anyone has said out loud that something was coming. I went through the shelves that afternoon looking for what happened next. There isn’t anything. The page stops on his line.
[margin] He told the Prelate something was coming. What? Page stops.
I wondered if the people who unwrote me had anything to do with a city like that. I don’t know. To me the Concord was only ever a name on a shipping form. But I’d bet this tower that someone in that white city keeps a drawer with a false bottom.
That night I understood the rest of it, with the lamp low. He’s alive. Right now, across the sea, there is a man who has buried everyone he ever cared for, and he is still out there at the edge of things with a brush in his hand. I don’t know what he says to people. I don’t know if anyone has ever listened.
I wanted to write to him so badly that it frightened me. I started four letters. I burned the first three. The one I kept says:
You don’t know me. I keep a tower on a cold coast and I have been reading you for months. I think you may be the only other one. I don’t know what to ask. I wanted you to know that someone has been paying attention.
I couldn’t sign it. I wrote the name the village uses and crossed it out, because I know what it is to have a name on a page that people aren’t allowed to read. It’s at the bottom of the desk drawer. I haven’t sent it. If anyone in that city knows my old employers, a letter from a woman who isn’t supposed to exist is the quickest way for them to find her.

The last one came three nights later, and it wasn’t like the others.
It was a single sheet, folded in four and tucked inside the cover of the book I’d been reading, where I would find it. No cord. I knew it was there because the cold bit into my hand when I opened the cover.
The right side of the page was gone in one smooth curve. There was no tear and no burn. When I held it to the lamp, the paper near the gap was colder than the rest.
The writing was mine, and it was the worst I’d seen. It sloped to the right and dug into the paper, which is what my hand does when I’m frightened. Every line stopped where the curve began. This is all there is:
In the three thousandth year since the Starfall
They have built a city in the hole. Rings of walls, and numbers on the doors. Nobody who lives in it has ever asked what it is a hole
They sell the light that comes up out of it. I watched them do it. It is the same light. It is the same
The Keep is still standing. Nobody remembers who
I couldn’t stay. It saw me the moment I
I had never seen the word. Starfall. I said it out loud once, to the room. A star falls. I thought of the library page, the ink rising and the white tower breaking and the ground opening with a violet light in it, and I didn’t need to think any further. The writer had put it first on the page, where you put a date everyone is expected to know, and there was only one day in all those pages that anyone would have a name for. The day in the library is the Starfall. Somebody has given it a name, and the name has a star in it.
I did the sum anyway. Three thousand years after.
So it has a name now, and I know no more than I did an hour ago. I know what it looks like from one balcony. I don’t know what causes it. I don’t know if it’s a war or a quake or something worse, or how far it reaches, or whether anyone besides one man in one library lives to write it down. I had thought of it as the end of the shelf. It had never crossed my mind that the pages would go on, that there would be years after it, and people living in them, and someone sitting in a room writing the date.
I laughed. It came up before I could stop it, and I put my hand over my mouth, and then the tears came too. The ground opens, and three thousand years later they build a city in it. I thought of every clerk I’ve ever known, every careful person with a stamp and a number, and I thought: of course they did.
Then I stopped laughing.
The Keep is still standing.
I read it until the words went strange. This tower, three thousand years after the Starfall, and somebody still living in it whom nobody remembers. If I’m the one writing these pages, then I’m still here, and I don’t know what happens to me in between. If I’m not, then someone else is sitting at this table with my handwriting, drinking my tea. I don’t know which is worse.
There was no room for the sheet on the wall. I taped a long strip of paper to the end of the last column and ruled it out past everything I’d written, and pinned the page at the very end, where the dates stop and the charcoal runs out. I can see it from the bed.
[margin, shaky] Every line stops. Whatever they saw, they never got to the end of it.
[margin, pressed hard] I’ll find out.
I put out a fresh cup before I went up. I marked the level.

lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.title: Time, Entry IV: The City in the Hole
lore-and-stories/stories/time/time---ent.content:
Approximately 3,338 BCE.
Twelve winters since the page with the missing edge, and nothing happened. I’ve decided to be grateful.
Seven deliveries in all that time, fewer than I used to get in a single spring. A tax roll from a town that’s under the sea now. A recipe for fish stew in my own handwriting, with more salt in the margin. I’ve made it eleven times and it is better with the salt. The cold in my hand lasts an hour each time. I bleed onto a cuff twice a year. I’ve got used to it the way you get used to a door that sticks.
I stopped leaving notes under the cup. You can only ask a cup who it is so many times. The tea still goes down a finger every night and I still mark the level with my knife. I’m not angry anymore. Some nights I say good night to it. It’s quiet up here.
Tam’s granddaughter has a grey head now. She still nods at me like I’m a statue. Her daughter leaves the fish.
I wrote to Asterion eleven more times and burned ten of them. The one I kept is in the drawer on top of the first, and neither has a name at the bottom. I read everything again from the first shelf and made a list of everyone he warned. It’s longer than I thought it would be. Nobody on it listened. I don’t know what that means. I think it might only mean that.
Every night I read the page with the missing edge, the one pinned where the charcoal stops. I know it by heart. I say they have built a city in the hole to the stairs. The stairs say nothing back. I tell myself I’ve stopped hoping for the rest of it. I say so every night, in the same voice I use to say I’m not hungry.

It came last night, and it hurt more than all the others put together.
It started at dawn with the homesickness in my chest, the usual one, but wrong. It was heavy. It sat on my ribs all morning while I swept and hauled water, and I couldn’t tell you now what else I did. By afternoon I couldn’t finish a thought. At dusk I put the kettle on because my hands still knew how.
The cold hit my right hand with the kettle in it. All at once, like someone had dropped my hand in the river and left the rest of me up here. The kettle fell off the hook and boiling water went over my ankle and I felt nothing. I felt my teeth. Every tooth in my head was ringing. Then it was in my jaw and behind my eyes, and I was on the floor with my cheek on the stones and my hand curled against my chest like a dead bird.
I tried to say something to the stairs. It came out as a noise.
Then the blood. My nose first, and I think my ear. I lay there and couldn’t remember what order you breathe in. I thought, this is it, I’m going to die on the kitchen floor next to a kettle. I thought of the guard and the pear. Nobody would know for a week. Tam’s family would find the fish still sitting in the basket, and there would be no one by that name, anywhere, and I’d have done their work for them by being too stubborn to leave. It was a very neat thought. I hated how neat it was. I held onto it anyway.
I don’t know how long I was down. When I could see again the lamp was out and the room was grey, and my hair was stuck to the floor. My hand was still curled up. I opened it with the other one, a finger at a time, like it belonged to somebody else. The cold was gone. The hand was pink and numb, like something that had been boiled.
The bundle was on the table. Of course it was.
I didn’t go to it. I washed first. I knelt over the basin and scrubbed the blood out of my hair and from under my nails. I was shaking so hard I had to stop and hold the edge. I stayed there until it passed.
Then I thought about the cup.
I thought about the note I left under it. Who are you? In my own hand, because it seemed polite. I thought about telling the stairs that somebody was reading my words and I’d like to know who gave them leave. I thought about the night I shouted how dare you at the shelves, as if whoever sends these was sitting somewhere with a blanket and a plate, deciding how much I could take.
I was angry, and it was cheap.
I dried my hair and sat down at the table. The bundle was bigger than any I’ve had, a thick stack knotted three times in the cord, and in the middle of it, wrapped in a scrap of oiled cloth, something hard. The right hand wouldn’t close, so I untied the cord with my teeth. I said to the room, “All right. I’ll read every word. I won’t ask who gave you leave.” Then I said, “I’m sorry.” It needed saying.
The cup was down a whole finger when I looked.
The hard thing in the cloth is the first object any of them has ever brought me.
It’s a plate of grey metal about as long as my hand and wrist together, bent a little along its length like a piece of pipe split down the middle. The surface is ribbed, with close lines running down it like the gills of a fish. At one end there’s a narrow slit with a light in it, faintly violet, the colour of the page I keep pinned on the wall. The light gets brighter when I bring my thumb near and dimmer when I take it away. The metal is warm, the way something asleep is warm. On the underside there are stamped marks in the trade script I half know from the Concord’s shipping forms. One word, RENOVA, which means nothing to me. A long number. A small circle with a crown. Inside the bend there’s a row of tiny prongs, like teeth with nothing to bite.
I turned it over for a long time. I don’t know what it’s for. I put it face down on the shelf over my bed and it’s still glowing through the cloth, a little violet seam in the dark. I thought about carrying it to the edge of the cliff. I didn’t. I don’t like not knowing what a thing does.
Seventeen sheets, all in my hand, all in the first person. Somebody telling me where they went. This is how it starts.


It was afternoon, and I was standing on a road in a grey coat a size too big.
The road was black glass, cracked into plates. The ground on both sides was warm, and I could feel it through my boots. Out across the flat, columns of smoke went straight up, and at the foot of the nearest one a crowd of people in rags were picking through the dirt with crowbars and sacks, like hens at spilled grain. Whatever they were picking at was still glowing. A man pulled out a lump the size of a loaf, violet inside like a bruise, and three others jumped on him for it. The sky was far too big. There was no mountain in it and no tree, nothing at all to hold it down.
I had my right hand pressed against my chest. It hurt. I was frightened and I kept very still, the way you do when you’re frightened of a whole place. “I’m here,” I said, out loud, to the empty road.
A boy of eight or nine was watching me from a tower made of scrap, with a spyglass in his fist. “Get off the road!” he shouted. There was a lantern on top of the tower. He told me the lamp meant the sky was quiet. Then he told me the sky was never quiet, only less loud, and I was standing in a bad place to stand.
“Where is this?”
“Hollowfall,” he said. “Are you simple?”
I went on.


A man was sitting by the road with a cart of glass jars. Each one was stoppered and labelled in shaky letters: FRESH AIR. TWO COINS. He offered me a breath of last Tuesday. “The good stuff,” he said. “Take a deep one.” I asked what was wrong with the air here. He looked at me so tenderly that I bought one.
Further on there was a plank bridge over a dry ditch, and on the bridge stood a very small, very angry man in a helmet made from a kettle. He wanted a toll. For the ditch, he said. Out of respect for the ditch. I gave him a button. He weighed it in his palm and scowled and said he couldn’t make change from a button. He dug around in a sack and pushed a bundle into my hands, wrapped in oiled cloth. “Fell off a truck,” he said. “Fits anybody with a fitting. Not that you’ve got one.”
“What’s a fitting?”
He laughed so hard he had to sit down on the bridge. I left him there, wheezing.


I stopped here. I looked at the shelf above my bed. The cloth is still on the plate and there’s still a little violet showing through it. I didn’t do anything. I looked at it and I looked at the page, and then I picked the page back up.


At a crossroads two men sat by a fire with a pot on it. They were the politest people I met all day. They stood up when I came near. They called me ma’am and asked me to sit and said there was plenty. I said I was expected somewhere. I didn’t ask what was in the pot. There was a boot beside the fire. I looked at the sky until I was past it.


I went and drank a cup of water standing up.


There were harder faces. A woman sat against a wall with a long cut down her cheek, watching the road as if every person on it was a question. Where her left forearm should have been there was something grey and jointed like a crab’s leg, with a faint violet light in the joints. I had no word for it, so I looked away. At a squat concrete house, another woman with flour on her hands put a cup of water into mine without asking where I’d come from, and told me not to take the west road after dark. Everyone I passed looked up at the sky every few steps, the way you check a pot on a stove.
Toward evening I came to a line of tall poles across the land. There was one every hundred paces, and on top of each a violet lamp, humming. A man on a ladder was mending one. He said it was the last pylon, and that the sky was different past it. I looked up as I crossed the line, and it was. The sky went flat and faintly bright, like looking up through still water. Where the wind touched it I could see it ripple. “The Wall,” the man said. Everything inside was safe, he told me, and everything outside wasn’t, and it cost money to know which side you were on. I asked what held it up. “Magic,” he said, the way you’d say weather.
After the poles, the light was different.
I came into a place of half lit streets just as the lamps were coming on, and half of them didn’t. Little glass bulbs hung on hooks by every door, glowing violet like lanterns. I watched a woman take one down and press it to her wrist before going out. A man was crossing the street in front of me, in the middle of a sentence, one arm raised to make a point, and the arm stopped. The rest of him kept talking. The arm hung in the air like a puppet’s with the string cut. People stepped round him and nobody looked. After a minute it dropped, and he finished his sentence. I asked a woman beside me if he was ill. She looked at me as though I’d asked if the sun was warm.
“He’s behind,” she said. “On the arm.”


Behind on what? I’ve read that line eleven times. I wrote it in the second book. Behind, on the arm. I don’t know what it means.


At the end of that street was a wide road with a name chalked on a board at the corner. CONTRACT ROW. Every wall was a board and every board was covered in chalk. Jobs, written out in the open for anyone to read. HAUL THIS. FIND MY DOG. Some had prices next to them that I didn’t like. Halfway down was a shop with a painted teapot over the door, and there was no tea in it.


A truck stood at the curb, six wheels, old and dented, with one door bent and tied shut with wire. Down the side, in red paint that someone had done by hand and done badly, it said FRESH MEAT SQUAD.
Four people came out of the shop. A tall, tired man, laughing and crying at once with his hand over his face. A young man with a bandaged hand and a split eyebrow, shouting at the whole street, “Free as a bird!” and walking backwards in front of a narrow, quiet woman with a long gun on her back. “Don’t,” said the woman, flat as a table. Behind them a round man in a clean shirt waved from the doorway with a ledger in one hand and a box of matches in the other.
The young man talked the way a tray falls, loud and all at once. When he saw me he stopped talking, which seemed to cost him, and tipped an imaginary hat.
“Mornin’, ma’am.”
“It’s afternoon.”
“That too.” He squinted at me. “You’s lost, ain’t you? Everbody that stands like that’s lost. Center’s thataway. Ride the Ring Line till the lights git ugly.”
The quiet woman looked at me a beat too long. I think she was checking something she half remembered. Then she turned away, and the young man was talking again, and the truck coughed and pulled out. I watched it to the corner. I didn’t know what they’d won. Someone had been let out of a debt. I could tell from the way the tall man walked.


I liked them. I’ve known those four for one page and I wish I knew what they did next.


At the end of the Row there was a low stone house with a lantern over the door. Above the door, in neat white letters painted by a patient hand: THE VIGIL.
There was a line outside it. Mothers with children, and old men. A woman at the door gave every child a heel of bread and every grown person a paper bag of dull violet stones. “Cheap and clean enough,” she said. “Pay what you have.” Next to the house was a small square where people stopped to set a pebble on a worn paving stone and say a name softly. Jade. I asked who she had been. “Ask somebody else,” they told me, not unkindly.


I had to stop. I know that word.
It’s the word on the three who came into my house and sat in my chair and read my pages. They walked me out before dawn and gave me a coat that wasn’t mine. And on this page they hand out bread, and the children take it from them and aren’t afraid.
I don’t know if they’re the same people. Names outlive the people who carry them. I know that better than most. But I got up and walked out of the room and walked back in, and I couldn’t tell you whether the bread makes it better or worse.


I asked the woman at the door if she’d ever heard of a keep. A tower on a cold coast, far south, with a dead lens at the top. She said there was a story like that. A light in the south that somebody keeps. Nobody goes. Nobody remembers who. She said it the way you tell a child a story, and turned to the next in line.


I know that line. It’s on my wall. I looked at it from here and I didn’t need to read it.


The Ring Line was a train that ran in a circle, and I got on without a ticket because the crowd carried me.
